བརྗོད་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། རྗོད་#པའི་རྣམ་པ་དང་བྲལ་ཞིང་བརྗོད་དུ་མེད་པ་སྣང་བ་དང་བཅས་པར་འགྱུར་བ་དང་བྲལ་ཏེ། སོ་སོ་རང་གིས་རིག་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་གྲུབ་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་དེ་ནི་ཆོས་#ཀྱི་མིག་ཅེས་བྱའོ། །དེ་ལ་མིག་མིག་གིས་སྟོང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་མིག་ཅེས་
བྱ་བ་ནི་ཆོས་ཉིད་ཀྱི་མིག་གོ། །མིག་གིས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཀུན་བརྟགས་པ་དང་། རྣམ་པར་བརྟགས་པའི་མིག་གིས་སོ། །སྟོང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བྲལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཐ་ཚིག་གོ། །དེ་བཞིན་དུ་རྣ་བ་རྣ་བས་སྟོང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལ་ཡང་སྦྱར་བར་བྱའོ། །འོ་ན་བརྗོད་
དུ་མེད་པའི་དོན་དམ་པ་ནི་མིག་གི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །གལ་ཏེ་མིག་གི་#ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཡིན་ན་ནི་བརྗོད་དུ་ཡོད་པ་ཉིད་དུ་འགྱུར་ན་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཆོས་ཉིད་ཀྱི་མིག་ཅེས་བྱ་ཞེ་ན། དེ་ནི་བདེན་མོད་ཀྱི་འོན་ཀྱང་མིག་ལ་སོགས་པ་དང་། གཟུགས་དང་སྒྲ་ལ་སོགས་པ་འདུས་བྱས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་
གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ཐམས་ཅད་གྱུར་པའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་གྲུབ་པའི་རྣམ་པ་ལ་ནི་ཐ་དད་དུ་དབྱེ་བ་མེད་དེ། རྣམ་པ་གཅིག་པ་ཡིན་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་གང་གི་ཚེ་རབ་ཏུ་བསྟན་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རྣམ་པར་ཕྱེ་སྟེ། སྨྲ་བར་འདོད་པར་གྱུར་པ་དེའི་ཚེ་ཐབས་གཞན་མེད་པས་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་
སྒྲའི་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད། དྲིའི་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་སྒྲ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་སོ་སོར་ཕྱེ་སྟེ་བསྟན་པ་ཙམ་དུ་ཟད་ཀྱི། དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་དེ་ནི་དེ་དག་གི་རྣམ་པ་དང་། དེ་དག་ཏུ་བརྗོད་པར་གྱུར་པ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལྟར་ན་ཆོས་ཉིད་ཀྱི་མིག་ལ་སོགས་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་དག་ནང་གི་
མིག་#གི་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་དང་བྲལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་ནང་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ཅེས་བྱའོ། །དེ་ལྟར་ནང་གི་དངོས་པོ་ལ་ཟ་བ་པོར་འཛིན་པ་བཟློག་ནས་ཕྱི་རོལ་གྱི་དངོས་པོ་ལ་བཟའ་བར་འཛིན་པ་བཟློག་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཕྱི་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་རྣམ་པར་གཞག་སྟེ། བཟའ་བར་འཛིན་པ་ཡང་ཕྱི་
རོལ་པ་རྣམས་ནི་#གཟུགས་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལ་བདག་གིར་ལྟ་བར་འཛིན་ཏོ། །ཆོས་འདི་པ་རྣམས་ནི་ཡུལ་ཉིད་དུ་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་པས་འཛིན་ཏོ། །དེ་ལ་སྔ་མ་བཟློག་པའི་ཕྱིར་གཟུགས་བདག་དང་། བདག་གིས་སྟོང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དང་སྒྲ་བདག་དང་བདག་གིས་#སྟོང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་
english:
Being free from that which is to be expressed and the mode of expression, and being free from the appearance of the inexpressible as something that changes, the nature of perfectly established self-cognition <note>original: "so so rang gis rig pa", referring to reflexive awareness or pratyatmanivedana</note> is called the Eye of Dharma <note>original: "chos kyi mig"</note>. Regarding the statement that the eye is empty of the eye, the word eye refers to the Eye of Reality <note>original: "chos nyིd kyi mig", the ultimate nature of the visual faculty</note>. The phrase by the eye refers to the conceptualized <note>original: "kun brtags pa", the imagined nature</note> and the designated eye. The word empty is a synonym for being free from these. The same logic should be applied to statements such as the ear is empty of the ear and so forth.

One might ask: If the inexpressible ultimate truth is not the essence of the eye, but if it were the essence of the eye, it would then become expressible. Why then is it called the Eye of Reality? This is true; however, for all conditioned phenomena such as the eye and so forth, or form, sound, and so forth, there is no differentiation within the aspect of their perfectly established nature <note>original: "yongs su grub pa", the pariniṣpanna nature</note> through the process of transformation. Although it is of a single aspect, when one wishes to explain and differentiate for the sake of teaching, there is no other method. Thus, one merely differentiates and teaches using terms like the suchness <note>original: "de bzhin nyid", the ultimate reality or tathatā</note> of form, the suchness of sound, the suchness of smell, and so forth. Nevertheless, that suchness does not possess their specific characteristics, nor is it expressed as them.

In this way, because the Eye of Reality and the others are free from the essence of the internal sense source <note>original: "skye mched", ayatana</note> of the eye and so forth, it is called internal emptiness <note>original: "nang stong pa nyid"</note>. Having thus reversed the apprehension of internal things as a consumer <note>original: "za ba po", the subject or enjoyer</note>, internal emptiness is established to reverse the apprehension of external things as the consumed <note>original: "bza' bar 'dzin pa", the object of enjoyment</note>. Regarding the apprehension of things as the consumed, outsiders <note>original: "phyi rol pa", non-Buddhists</note> apprehend form and so forth by viewing them as mine. Those within this Dharma <note>original: "chos 'di pa", Buddhists</note> apprehend them as objects through conceptualization. To reverse the former, it is said that form is empty of self and mine, and sound is empty of self and mine <unclear>…</unclear>

<summary>This page explains the concept of the Eye of Dharma and the Eye of Reality, clarifying how ultimate truth is empty of conceptual designations. It details the distinction between internal emptiness and external emptiness to refute the dualism of subject and object.</summary>
<keywords>Eye of Dharma, Suchness, Internal Emptiness, External Emptiness, Perfectly Established Nature, Subject-Object Dualism</keywords>

<margin>蘇註</margin>不知道而務學聞見日多而無以一之未免為累也孔子曰多聞擇其善者而從之多見而識之知之次也苟一日知道顧偽偽為無一非妄去妄復性是謂之損孔子謂子貢曰女以予為多學而識之者與曰然非與曰非也予一以貫之夫忘心以純復性無謂損矣而妄之不猶存以及其兼忘此心以純復性無餘然後去為而不失於無為矣人皆有欲取天下終事理之心故造事而求之心見於外而物惡之故難不可得聖人無為故無事其心見於外而物安之雖不取天下事理而為之而天下事理順安於是矣

<margin>呂註</margin>為學未聞道者也未聞道而求之不得不博故曰益為道者已聞道者也已聞道而為之不得不無為而已故曰損而又損者未免乎有為也并其損之者而損焉而後至於無為無為者寂然而不動之謂也無不為者感而遂通天下之故之謂也無為而至無為此之謂經學無憂謂之神神之為方也道之謂也至神其孰能與於此也由此觀之取天下常以無為及其有為不足以取天下可知已

<column-break/>

<margin>黃茂材註</margin>無所不知而後可以言學故學欲日益無所不為而後可以言道故道欲日損然益者可以進求而損者或難於強致唯至明者方能瞥地脫落乃至無為之地故能無所不為而應用不窮施於天下綽綽然矣

<margin>息齋註</margin>為學所以求知故日益為道所以去妄故日損知不極則損不全故日益者為日損之地也若損之又損妄去真全則無為矣至於無為則凡有為未嘗不無此又未易以損益論也及其無為之至雖天下之多而一貫之也若以有事而生事難暇前之一物尚膠纒乖錯而況天下之多乎

聖人無常心以百姓心為心善者吾善之不善者吾亦善之德善矣信者吾信之不信者吾亦信之德信矣聖人在天下惛惛為天下渾其心百姓皆注其耳目聖人

english:
<margin>Commentary by Su</margin>
If you do not know the Way and focus on learning, the things you hear and see increase daily, but there is no way to unify them, and you inevitably suffer the burden. Confucius said: "Hear much, select the good and follow it; see much and remember it. This is the second level of knowledge." If one day you know the Way, look back at your hypocrisy; there is nothing that is not delusion. To remove delusion and return to one's nature is called "decreasing." Confucius said to Zigong: "Do you think I have learned much and remembered it?" Zigong said: "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said: "No, I unify it with a single thread." Forgetting the heart and purely returning to one's nature is what is called decreasing. If delusions still remain, one proceeds to forget both self and others, making the heart pure and returning to nature without remainder. Then, one removes action and does not lose the state of non-action. Everyone has the desire to take the world and occupy their heart with logic. Therefore, they create affairs and seek them. When the heart is revealed externally, things hate it. Therefore, it is difficult to obtain. The sage has no action, so he has no affairs. When his heart is revealed externally, things are at peace. Although he does not take the world's affairs, he acts for them, and the world's affairs are naturally harmonious and peaceful.

<margin>Commentary by Lü</margin>
Studying without having heard the Way is not yet having heard it. Not having heard the Way, you have to be broad in your studies to seek it. Therefore, it is called "increasing." One who practices the Way has already heard the Way. Having heard the Way, one has to do nothing but non-action. Therefore, it is called "decreasing." Decreasing and decreasing again is because you haven't yet avoided action. By even removing the "decreasing," one arrives at non-action. Non-action is what is called "still and motionless." "There is nothing that cannot be done" is what is called "responding and passing through all matters of the world." To arrive at non-action from non-action—this is what is called the classic. Learning without worry is what is called spirit. The method of spirit is the Way. Who can equal this ultimate spirit? Looking at it from this perspective, "To win the world, one should always be free of affairs; when one interferes, one is not fit to win the world"—this can be known.

<column-break/>

<margin>Commentary by Huang Mao-cai</margin>
Only after one knows everything can one speak of learning; therefore, learning desires to increase daily. Only after one does nothing can one speak of the Way; therefore, the Way desires to decrease daily. However, those who increase can progress, while those who decrease may find it difficult to force. Only the one with ultimate clarity can suddenly drop away everything and arrive at the land of non-action. Thus, he can do nothing that is not done, and his applications are inexhaustible. His governance of the world is effortless and ample.

<margin>Commentary by Xizhai</margin>
Learning is for seeking knowledge; therefore, it increases daily. The Way is for removing delusion; therefore, it decreases daily. If knowledge is not ultimate, then the decrease is not complete. Therefore, "increasing" is the place where "decreasing" occurs. If you decrease and decrease again, and delusion is removed while the truth is complete, then there is non-action. When you arrive at non-action, then even if there is action, there is never a time it is not without it. This is not easily discussed in terms of increase and decrease. When he arrives at non-action, even though the world is vast, he unifies it with a single thread. If you create affairs, you will have no time to rest. One thing alone is already gluey, tangled, and contradictory; how much more so is the complexity of the world?

"The sage has no fixed heart. He takes the hearts of the common people as his heart. To those who are good, I am good. To those who are not good, I am also good. Virtue is good. To those who are faithful, I am faithful. To those who are not faithful, I am also faithful. Virtue is faithful. The sage is in the world, dim and murky. He muddies his heart for the world. The common people all turn their eyes and ears to him. The sage..."

<summary>This page details the necessity of shedding intellectual clutter and active interference to reach the "non-action" of the sage. It presents the sage as a mirror for the world, unburdened by fixed agendas or personal desires.</summary>

<keywords>Learning, the Way, non-action, sage, heart, virtue, faithfulness, Su, Lü, Huang Mao-cai, Xizhai</keywords>

> Κόρῳ ἄχραντον νερτέροισι δαίμοσι,
> Κλήρῳ λαχοῦσαν Αἰπυτιδῶν ἀφ’ αἵματος,
> Θυηπολεῖτε νυκτέροισιν ἐν σφαγαῖς.
> Ἢν δ’ σφαγῇ τε, καὶ παρ’ ἀλλοίῳ, τότε
> Θύειν, διδόντας ἐς σφαγὴν ἑκουσίως.

Ταῦτα τοῦ θεοῦ δηλώσαντος, αὐτίκα ἐκληροῦντο ὅσαι παρθένοι τοῦ Αἰπυτιδῶν γένους ἦσαν. καὶ ἐπελάμβανε γὰρ Λυκίσκου θυγατέρα ὁ κλῆρος. Ταύτην Ἐπήβολος ὁ μάντις ἀπηγόρευεν ὡς οὐ δέοι θύειν· οὐ γὰρ εἴη Λυκίσκου· τὴν δὲ γυναῖκα ἣ Λυκίσκῳ συνῴκησεν, ὡς τεκεῖν οὐκ οἵα τε ἦν, ἐν τούτῳ τὴν παῖδα ὑποβαλέσθαι. ἐν ὅσῳ δὲ οὗτος διεδίδασκε τὰ ἐς αὐτὴν, ἐν τοσῷδε ὁ Λυκίσκος ἐπαγόμενος ἅμα καὶ τὴν παρθένον ηὐτομόλησεν ἐς Σπάρτην. ἐχόντων δὲ ἀθύμως τῶν Μεσσηνίων ὡς Λυκίσκον ἀποδράντα ᾔσθοντο, ἐνταῦθα σφίσιν Ἀριστόδημος ἀνὴρ καὶ γένος τοῦ Αἰπυτιδῶν, καὶ Λυκίσκου τῇ τε ἄλλῃ δόξῃ, καὶ τὰ ἐς πόλεμον ἐπιφανέστερος, ἐδίδου τὴν θυγατέρα ἑκὼν θῦσαι. τὰ δὲ ἀνθρώπων οὐχ ἥκιστα τὸ πρόθυμον πεπρωμένη κατὰ ταῦτα ἐπικρύπτει, καὶ ἡ ψηφίδα ἐπιλαβοῦσα ἰλὺς ποταμοῦ. ὅπου καὶ τότε Ἀριστοδήμῳ διασῶσαι Μεσσηνίους ἀγώνισμα ποιουμένῳ, τὸ ἐμπόδιον ἐπήγαγε τοιόνδε. ἀνὴρ τῶν Μεσσηνίων (τὸ δὲ ὄνομα οὐ λέγουσιν) ἐρῶν ἔτυχε τῆς Ἀριστοδήμου θυγατρός. τότε δὲ ἤδη ἔμελλε γυναῖκα ἄξεσθαι. οὗτος κατ’ ἀρχὰς ἐς ἀμφισβήτησιν Ἀριστοδήμῳ καθίστατο, ἐκεῖνον μὲν ἐγγυήσαντά οἱ μηκέτι εἶναι κύριον τῆς παιδός, αὐτὸς δὲ ἐγγυησάμενος κυριώτερος ἐκείνου γίνεσθαι. δεύτερα δὲ ὡς τοῦτο οὐχ ἑώρα οἱ κατορθούμενον, ἐπ’ ἀναίσχυντον τρέπεται λόγον, συγγενέσθαι τε τῇ παιδί, καὶ τεκύειν ἐξ αὐτῆς. τέλος δὲ ἐς τοσοῦτον Ἀριστόδημον προήγαγεν, ὡς ἐκμανέντα ὑπὸ τοῦ θυμοῦ τὴν θυγατέρα ἀποκτεῖναι. μετὰ δὲ ἀνέτεμνε, καὶ ἐπεδείκνυεν αὐτὴν οὐκ ἔχουσαν ἐν γαστρί. παρὼν δὲ Ἐπήβολος, ἐκέλευεν ἄλλον τινὰ τὴν θυγατέρα ἐπιδώσοντα γενέσθαι· τῆς γὰρ τοῦ Ἀριστοδήμου, πλέον αὖ σφισιν ἀποθανόσης οὐδέν· φονεῦσαι γὰρ τὸν πατέρα αὐτὴν, θεοῖς δὲ οἷς ἡ Πυθία προσέταξεν, οὐ θῦσαι. τοιαῦτα εἰπόντος τοῦ μάντεως, τὸ πλῆθος τῶν Μεσσηνίων ὥρμησεν ἀποκτενοῦντες τὸν μνηστῆρα τῆς παιδός, ὡς Ἀριστοδήμῳ τε μίασμα εἰκαῖον προσάψαντα, καὶ σφίσι τῆς σωτηρίας τὴν ἐλπίδα ἀμφίβολον πεποιηκότα. ἦν δὲ ὁ ἀνὴρ οὗτος ἐς τὰ μάλιστα τῷ Εὐφάῃ φίλος. πείθει τοὺς Μεσσηνίους Εὐφάης, τόν τε χρησμὸν ἔχειν τέλος ἀποθανούσης τῆς παιδός, καὶ σφίσιν ἀποχρᾶν τὸ ὑπὸ Ἀριστοδήμου πεποιημένον. λέγοντος δὲ ταῦτα, ἔφασαν τὰ ὄντα λέγειν ὅσοι τοῦ Αἰπυτιδῶν γένους ἦσαν· ἀπεπαύετο γὰρ σφίσι ὁ δέος ὁ ἐπὶ τῇ θυγατρί, ἕκαστός τε ἔσπευδε, καὶ οἱ μὲν τῶν βασιλέων τῇ παραινέσει πειθόμενοι, τὴν ἐκκλησίαν διαλύουσιν· καὶ ἀπ’ αὐτῆς πρός τε θυσίας καὶ θεῶν ἑορτὴν τρέπονται. Λακεδαιμόνιοι δὲ ἀκούσαντες τὸν γενόμενον Μεσσηνίοις χρησμόν, ἀθύμως διέκειντο καὶ αὐτοί, καὶ οἱ βασιλεῖς, ἔς τε τὰ λοιπὰ καὶ ἀρχὴν ὀκνοῦντες μάχης. Ἔτει δὲ ἕκτῳ μετὰ τὸν ἐξ Ἰθώμης Λυκίσκου δρασμὸν οἱ Λακεδαιμόνιοι (τὰ γὰρ ἱερὰ ἐγίνετο αὐτοῖς αἴσια) στρατεύουσιν ἐπὶ τὴν Ἰθώμην. οἱ δὲ Κρῆτες οὐκέτι παρόντες σφίσιν ἔτυχον. ὑστέρησαν δὲ καὶ οἱ τῶν Μεσσηνίων σύμμαχοι. δι’ ὑποψίας γὰρ οἱ Σπαρτιᾶται καὶ ἄλλοις ἤδη Πελοποννησίων, καὶ Ἀρκάσιν ἦσαν καὶ Ἀργείοις μάλιστα. καὶ οἱ μὲν Ἀργεῖοι κρύφα ἔμελλον τῶν Λακεδαιμονίων ἀφίξεσθαι, καὶ ἰδίᾳ δὴ μᾶλλον μετὰ δόγματος κοινοῦ. τοῖς δὲ Ἀρκάσιν ἡ στρατεία μὲν ἀπείρητο ἐκ τοῦ φανεροῦ. παρέτυχον δὲ οὐδ’ οὗτοι. τοὺς γὰρ Μεσσηνίους καὶ ἄνευ συμμάχων κινδυνεῦσαι προήγαγεν ἡ δόξα τοῦ χρησμοῦ. τὰ μὲν οὖν πολλὰ οὐδέν τι ἐγένετο διάφορα, ἢ καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς προτέρας μάχης· ἥ τε ἡμέρα καὶ τότε μαχομένους προαπέλιπεν. οὐ μὲν τοι βιασθῆναί γε οὐδέτερον κέρας, ἢ καὶ λόχον μνημονεύουσιν. ἐπεὶ μηδὲ τῷ τάξιν ὡς ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς ἐτάχθησαν, συμμεῖναί φασιν· ἀλλ’ ἀφ’ ἑκατέρων τοὺς ἀρίστους συνελθόντας ἐς μέσον, ταύτῃ τὸν πάντα ἔχειν πόνον. ὁ γὰρ Εὐφάης πλέον τι ἢ βασιλέα εἰκὸς ἦν, προθυμούμενος, καὶ ἀφειδῶς τοῖς περὶ τὸν Θεόπομπον ἐγκείμενος, θαύματά τε καὶ πολλά τε οὐκ ἰάσιμα λαμβάνει. λιποψυχήσαντα

> To the gods below, a pure maiden,
> Chosen by lot from the blood of the Aepytidae,
> Sacrifice in the slaughters of the night.
> But if she fail the slaughter, then from another,
> Sacrifice one given voluntarily to the death.

After the god had revealed these things, they immediately cast lots for all the virgins who were of the race of the Aepytidae; and the lot fell upon the daughter of Lyciscus. Epebolus the seer forbade her to be sacrificed, saying it was not right, for she was not the daughter of Lyciscus; rather, the woman who lived with Lyciscus, being unable to bear children, had substituted the child as her own. While he was explaining the circumstances regarding her, Lyciscus took the girl and deserted to Sparta. When the Messenians were disheartened upon learning that Lyciscus had fled, Aristodemus—a man of the Aepytid line, more distinguished than Lyciscus in general reputation and especially in matters of war—offered his own daughter to be sacrificed voluntarily. But fate often conceals human eagerness in such matters, much like the mud of a river catching a voting-pebble; and so, when Aristodemus was striving to save the Messenians, fate brought the following obstacle upon him. A certain Messenian man (whose name they do not mention) happened to be in love with the daughter of Aristodemus, and was then on the point of taking her as his wife. At first, he entered into a dispute with Aristodemus, claiming that since the girl had been betrothed to him, Aristodemus was no longer her master, and that he, as her betrothed, had more authority over her than the father. Secondly, when he saw that this was not succeeding, he turned to a shameless story: that he had been intimate with the girl and that she was pregnant by him. Finally, he drove Aristodemus to such a point that, driven mad by rage, he killed his daughter. Afterwards, he cut her open and showed that she was not with child. 

Epebolus, being present, ordered that someone else should give a daughter; for he said that the death of Aristodemus's daughter had profited them nothing, because her father had murdered her, but had not sacrificed her to the gods whom the Pythia had commanded. When the seer said this, the multitude of the Messenians rushed to kill the girl's suitor, on the grounds that he had brought a needless pollution upon Aristodemus and had made their hope of safety uncertain. But this man was a very close friend of Euphaës. Euphaës persuaded the Messenians that the oracle had its fulfillment in the girl's death, and that what had been done by Aristodemus was sufficient for them. When he said this, all those who were of the Aepytid race said that he spoke the truth; for the fear concerning their own daughters was ended, and each man was eager for it to be so. The kings, following this advice, dissolved the assembly, and from there they turned to sacrifices and a festival to the gods. 

The Lacedaemonians, hearing of the oracle that had come to the Messenians, were also disheartened—both they and their kings—being hesitant for the future and reluctant to begin a battle. In the sixth year after the flight of Lyciscus from Ithome, the Lacedaemonians (as the sacrifices had become favorable to them) marched against Ithome. The Cretans happened to no longer be present with them, and the allies of the Messenians also arrived too late. For the Spartans were already held in suspicion by others of the Peloponnesians, and especially by the Arcadians and Argives. The Argives intended to arrive secretly from the Lacedaemonians, and by private arrangement rather than by public decree; as for the Arcadians, the expedition had been openly forbidden to them, yet they were not present either. For the expectation of the oracle led the Messenians to risk battle even without allies. For the most part, the battle was not much different from the previous one; the day failed them while they were still fighting. They do not record that either wing or any company was forced back, for they say that the ranks did not remain as they had been stationed at the beginning; rather, the best men from both sides came together in the center, and there the whole weight of the labor fell. For Euphaës, showing more spirit than was expected even of a king, and pressing unsparingly upon those around Theopompus, received many incurable wounds. Having fainted...

<meta>continues from the previous page: ...as indicated by the syllables</meta> *om ah hum phat svaha*. The phrase "offering and making requests" refers to the Guru. "In the same way as it was explained" refers to sources such as the *Compendium of Reality* <note>original: *Tattvasamgraha*</note> and others. "Vajrasattva" <note>Adamantine Being</note> here refers to Hevajra. The word "afterwards" means immediately following the empowerment. "Completely pure" means the stains of cyclic existence <term>samsara</term> have been purified. "One who possesses the form of wisdom" <note>original: *jnanamurti*</note> refers to an equality with the wisdom of the omniscient one.

Regarding the phrase "cyclic existence and complete purification": this refers to that wisdom in which there is not even the slightest difference between existence and nirvana. This is the "surpassing" state, with the intended meaning being that it is utterly beyond all conceptual elaboration. This very point will be clearly demonstrated by the two verses beginning with "in supreme joy."

"Supreme joy" <term>paramananda</term> is the supreme transcendent wisdom; it is the wisdom characterized by clear light. "There is no meditation there" means there is not even a single thing to be meditated upon. The "meditator" is the mind, and that too does not exist. "Body" is the physical body. "Objects" are the things that appear. "Subjective perceivers" are the eyes and the other senses. Likewise, flesh, blood, and so forth also do not exist. Having thus established that the obscuration of disturbing emotions does not exist, the text says "there is no seeing" and so forth to show that the obscuration to knowledge also does not exist. This means that external objects such as things to be seen also do not exist.

In the phrase "without waves," "waves" refers to conceptual thoughts. When these are exhausted, it is "without waves." "Manifold" refers to appearing in various different forms. When those are absent, it is "without the manifold." The phrase "this was said" refers to these words spoken by the Bhagavan <gloss>Blessed Lord</gloss>. "Requested" refers to the questions asked by Vajragarbha. As for what meaning was requested, the text says "for what reason" and so forth. The intended meaning is this: by its very nature, the co-emergent essence is completely pure.

<summary>This page provides a technical commentary on the nature of Vajrasattva and the state of non-dual wisdom, explaining that in the ultimate state of supreme joy, both the objects of meditation and the meditator's mind are non-existent. It defines key terms related to the purification of cyclic existence and the cessation of conceptual thought.</summary>

Thus it happens that, like Atalanta, they go off the path to pick up the golden apple; meanwhile, however, they interrupt their course and let the victory slip from their hands. But in the true course of Experience, and in producing new works from it, Divine Providence and Order must be taken as the pattern. For God, on the first day of Creation, created only Light, and attributed an entire day to that work; nor did He create anything of material substance on that day. Similarly, from all-encompassing Experience, the invention of Causes and true Axioms must first be elicited: and light-bearing Experiments must be sought, not fruit-bearing ones. Axioms, however, correctly invented and established, instruct Practice not sparingly, but in abundance; and they draw after them whole hosts and companies of Works. But concerning the paths of experimenting, which are no less beset and obstructed than the paths of Judging, we shall speak later: for the present, having spoken only of common Experience as a poor Demonstration. Now, the order of things demands that we add certain remarks concerning those signs mentioned a little earlier (that the philosophies and contemplations in use are in a bad state); and concerning the Causes of a matter so wonderful and incredible at first glance. For the knowledge of signs prepares the way for assent: but the explanation of causes removes the wonder. These two things contribute much to making the extirpation of Idols from the Intellect easier and more gentle.

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into the illusions of witches, specifically resolving previous arguments about the physical reality of "missing" limbs before moving into a new question regarding the transformation of humans into animals.</meta>

<margin>
# Solutions to the arguments.
</margin>

The answer to the first argument is clear. There is no doubt that, just as men can kill other humans when God permits it, they can also truly and physically remove a limb or other body parts. However, in those cases, **demons** are not operating through the **witches** <note>original: "maleficas"</note> currently under discussion. This also provides the solution to the second point. But as for the claim that because God permits the **generative power** <term>vim generativam: the biological ability to procreate</term> of witches more than other powers, He therefore permits that a limb be truly and physically removed—this is not a valid rule for every case. Such an act would not be performed by way of **witchcraft** <note>original: "maleficii"</note>, nor do witches even desire this when they perform their works, because they want to retain the power to restore the limb whenever they wish and know how. From this, it is clear that the limb is not truly removed, but is taken away through the **art of illusion** <term>prestigiosa arte: the demonic skill of creating deceptive appearances</term>.

Regarding the third point about the transformation of **Lot's wife** <note>The biblical story from Genesis 19 where Lot's wife was turned into a pillar of salt</note>, we say that this was a real transformation and not done through the art of illusion; however, we are currently speaking of the deceptive arts. To the fourth point—that demons can introduce certain **substantial forms** <term>substantial forms: the essential nature that makes a thing what it is (e.g., "human-ness" or "snake-ness")</term> and therefore can also remove them—it is said regarding the **magicians of Pharaoh** <note>In Exodus 7, these magicians mimicked Moses's miracles</note> that they produced real serpents. Indeed, demons can produce certain effects regarding some "imperfect" creatures with the help of some other agent; however, they cannot do this to humans, for whom God has greater care. According to the scripture: *Is it for oxen that God is concerned?* <note>original: "Nunquid deo cura est de bobus." A reference to 1 Corinthians 9:9</note> Nevertheless, as has been stated, they can always harm humans truly and physically, or through the art of illusion, if God permits it. This also makes the solution to the final argument clear.

<margin>
# Question 10. Whether witches work upon men by transforming them into bestial forms through the art of illusion.
</margin>

Fourthly, the truth itself is declared regarding where humans are transformed into beasts. As to how this happens, it is argued that it is not possible for this to occur. In the **Canon Law** <note>original: "xxvi. q. v. Epi." referring to the Canon Episcopi, a famous 10th-century legal text on witchcraft</note> from the Council of Ancyra: "Whosoever believes that any creature can be changed for the better or the worse, or transformed into another species or another likeness, except by the Creator Himself who made all things and through whom all things were made, is beyond doubt an infidel and worse than a pagan."

<column-break/>

Let us also use the arguments of **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent medieval theologian</note> in the *Second Book of Sentences*, distinction 8, on whether demons can make impressions upon the **bodily senses** by deluding them with illusions. There, he first argues that they cannot. For that form of a beast which is seen must exist somewhere. But it cannot exist only in the sense, because the sense does not possess any **sensory image** <term>speciem: a mental representation of an object</term> unless it is received from real things. Furthermore, according to the legal authority cited above, there is no real beast there. Nor, again, can the form be in the thing that is seen (as when a woman appears to be a beast), because two **substantial forms** cannot exist in the same thing at one and the same time. Therefore, since that beastly form which is seen can exist nowhere, no **illusion of prestige** <term>illusio prestigiosa: a deceptive trick or hallucination</term> can occur in the eye of the beholder, since vision must necessarily be terminated by some form.

Furthermore, if it is said that the form exists in the surrounding air, this cannot be. Firstly, because the air is not capable of receiving a specific form or shape. Secondly, because the same air does not always remain around that person due to its fluid nature, especially when they are moving. Thirdly, because such a transformation would then be seen by everyone—which is not the case, since demons do not seem to deceive the visions of holy men, at the very least.

Furthermore, the sense of sight or the power of vision is a passive power. But every passive thing is moved by an active thing proportioned to it. Now, the active thing proportioned to the sense is twofold: one that originates the act (namely, the **object**), and another that conveys it (namely, the **medium**). But that form which is seen cannot be the object of the sense, nor can it be the medium conveying it. Regarding the first—that it cannot be the object—this is because it cannot be derived from any real thing (as touched upon in the preceding argument), since it is not in the sense as something accepted from a real thing, nor is it in the object itself, nor even in the air as a conveying medium (as touched upon in the third argument). Furthermore, if the demon moves the internal **cognitive power**, he either does this by presenting himself as an object...

<summary>This page addresses theological objections regarding the physical reality of demonic transformations, concluding that while God may allow real physical harm, most "transformations" of humans into animals are demonic illusions that deceive the senses rather than changing a person's actual essence.</summary>

If a courtesan refuses to approach a man under royal order, she shall receive one thousand lashes, or pay a fine of five thousand <term>paṇas</term>.

If she accepts payment and then develops animosity, the fine is double the payment.

If she steals the payment for staying, she shall pay eight times the amount, except in cases of illness or the fault of the man.

If a man causes her distress while she is under his protection, or forces her into water <note>a method of torture or suicide</note>, he shall be punished.

For one who steals the ornaments of a courtesan or her payment, the fine is eight times the value.

The courtesan must report her earnings, future prospects, and her male clients.

By this, the rules for actors, dancers, singers, musicians, storytellers, rope-dancers, magicians, bards, and other women who deal in such professions, as well as those who live in secret, are also explained.

They shall give five <term>paṇas</term> as a fee for a performance if they are newcomers.

Those who live by beauty shall pay double the monthly fee.

A courtesan shall have her slaves and those who live by the stage learn singing, instrumental music, reading, dancing, acting, writing, painting, playing the <term>vīṇā</term> <gloss>lute</gloss> and flute, drumming, the study of character, the knowledge of perfumes and garlands, the art of fascination, the art of completion, massage, and the arts of the courtesan. They shall earn their livelihood from the royal circle. The sons of courtesans and those who live by the stage shall be made into experts. This also applies to all aspects of rhythmic timing.

Women who are knowledgeable in signs and different languages should be used for secret missions and to observe the movements of others.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter on the Superintendent of Courtesans, in the Administration of Superintendents.

english: [...continued from previous page] in a raw state, applied. Olympias of Thebes added hyssop and saltpeter. The ash of stag horn is drunk. It is also useful for one suffering from uterine trouble. It is also applied as a salve, and bull bile mixed with two <term>oboli</term> <gloss>small weights</gloss> of opium is applied. It is also useful to fumigate the womb with stag hair. They report that when hinds sense they are pregnant, they swallow a small stone, which is found in their excrement or in the womb (for it is also found there), and is kept by the pregnant woman as an amulet. Small bones are also found in the heart and womb that are very useful for pregnant women and those in labor. Regarding the pumice stone found in the same way in the uterus of cows, we have spoken of this in the nature of cattle. Wolf fat applied softens the womb. It can even be effective against harmful applications to alleviate their pains. And it is not useless. Or, if she is beginning to labor, let her stay near what she has eaten. So much so that it can even be effective against harmful applications. And it is truly a small thing to mention that it supervenes. There is great use of the hare for women. Dried lung, drunk, helps the womb. For fluxes, the liver with Samian earth in water, drunk. For the afterbirth, rennet. They avoid bathing on the previous day. Also, a salve made with saffron and leek juice, applied on a fleece, expels dead fetuses. If hare wombs are taken in food, they think male children are conceived. They believe this is also accomplished by their testicles and rennet. They believe that a hare's uterus, removed and given to those who have ceased to bear children, brings back fertility. Furthermore, the <term>magi</term> <gloss>Persian wise men</gloss> suggest a hare's conception for a man to drink. Likewise, nine grains of dung for a virgin, so that her breasts remain firm forever. Also with rennet. For this reason, smeared with honey, it is used on blood where they do not want hair to grow back after it has been plucked. For swelling of the womb, boar or swine dung mixed with oil is useful to apply. It is more effective if flour of dry dung is spread on it or added to a drink, in case it torments pregnant women or those who have just given birth. Drunk with honeyed wine, sow's milk aids the labor of women. Drunk by itself, it fills the failing breasts of those who have just given birth. The same, smeared with the blood of a female sow, makes the breasts grow less. If they are painful, soothe them with a drink of donkey milk. Taken with added honey, it also aids their purging. The old fat of the same animal also heals ulcerations of the womb, and applied on a fleece, it softens the hardness of the womb. Used by itself, whether fresh or old, applied in water, it has the power of a <term>psilothrum</term> <gloss>hair-removing agent</gloss>. The old spleen of the same animal, applied in water, increases the supply of milk in breasts. It stiffens the face. Donkey hooves burned as incense hasten labor, so that it may even induce an abortion; it is not used otherwise, for it kills the living fetus. If the dung of the same animal is applied while fresh, it is said to sedate fluxes of blood miraculously. And also the ash of the same dung, which, applied, is also useful for the womb. Horse foam, applied for forty days, causes the first hairs to stop growing before they are born. Likewise, stag horn, as taught. The horns are better if they are fresh. Wombs washed with mare's milk are aided. If one senses the fetus is dead, spleen drunk in sweet water expels it. Likewise, burning the hooves or using dry dung. It stops the face from drooping if infused with butter. Bull bile mixed with rose oil opens a hardened womb, applied externally on a fleece with turpentine resin. They also say that by burning the dung of a bull, drooping wombs are drawn back and labor is aided. Conception [is aided] by drinking cow's milk. It is certain that sterility occurs due to the trauma of labor. Olympias of Thebes affirms that this is corrected by bull bile, the fat of geese, and verdigris, with honey added to the medicated parts before intercourse. If calf bile is sprinkled on the womb during intercourse in purgings, it softens the hardness of the belly and diminishes the flux; if the navel is pricked, it is useful for the whole womb. They set the measure of bile at one <term>denarius</term> <gloss>a silver coin weight</gloss>, mixed with a third of a <term>denarius</term> of celery seed and almond oil, such that it seems sufficient; they apply this on a fleece. Male calf bile, ground with half the amount of honey, is used for the womb. If they eat calf meat roasted with birthwort around the time of conception, they promise that they will bear male children. Calf marrow, boiled in wine and water with fat, is useful for ulcerations of the womb. Likewise, fox fat, and cat excrement applied with resin and rose oil. It is thought very useful to fumigate the womb with goat horn. The blood of wild goats with sea palm pulls out hair. The bile of others, however, softens the callus of the womb when sprinkled, and makes conception possible after purging. The power of a <term>psilothrum</term> <gloss>hair-removing agent</gloss> is also brought about in this way: after the hairs are plucked, it is kept applied for three days. Midwives promise that a flux, however immense, is stopped by drinking goat urine, and if dung is applied. The membrane of goats, boiled in water and taken as a drink in wine, expels the afterbirth. It is thought useful to fumigate the womb with the hair of kids. And in a flux of blood, rennet is to be drunk, or henbane seed is to be applied. Aeschines says that if the loins of a buck are pricked with the blood of a wild black bull, a woman will lose interest in sex. The same [author] says that goat urine mixed with spikenard is a drink of love, because of the fragrance. For infants, nothing is more useful than butter, by itself and with honey, both for teething, and for the gums, and for ulcers of the mouth. A wolf's tooth, worn as an amulet, prevents fears in infants and diseases of teething. A wolf's skin does the same. Their largest teeth, when worn by horses, are said to provide indefatigable speed. If a hare's rennet is applied to the udder, it will stop an infant's loose bowels. A donkey's liver, with a little all-heal <note>a plant of the genus *Valeriana*</note> added and dropped into the mouth, protects infants from epileptic diseases and others. They instruct that this be done for forty days. A donkey's skin thrown over them makes infants fearless. The teeth that first fall out from horses provide easy teething for infants when worn as amulets. It is more effective if they have not touched the earth. Calf spleen is to be eaten in honey. And it is to be applied for pain of the spleen. For running ulcers, with honey. Calf spleen boiled in wine, ground, and applied [is good] for little ulcers of the mouth. The <term>magi</term> <gloss>Persian wise men</gloss> instruct that goat brain be passed through a gold ring before being dropped into the mouths of infants who have not yet been given milk, against epilepsy and other infant diseases. Goat dung, worn in a cloth as an amulet, calms restless infants, especially girls. Gums rubbed with goat milk or hare brain make teething easy. Cato thinks that sleep is induced by eating hare. The common people also believe it grants grace to the body for nine days. Yet there must be some cause beneath such a great persuasion. The <term>magi</term> <gloss>Persian wise men</gloss> say that the bile of a sacrificed goat, merely smeared on the eyes or placed under a pillow, is said to entice sleep. Ash of goat horn in myrtle oil, when rubbed on, inhibits sweats. Boar bile, applied, stimulates sexual intercourse. Likewise, boar marrow drunk. Donkey fat mixed with the fat of a male goose, applied. Likewise, regarding the intercourse of horses, Virgil...

<header>PHILOCALIA, CHAPTER XIX.</header>

<column-break/>
...into different flights and different cries, and for the rest, into these or those movements. Others say their souls are more divine and better suited for this, which is most implausible. Celsus therefore, wishing to prove from the proposed subjects that irrational animals are more divine and wiser than humans, should have established through many arguments that such divination exists. After this, he should have more effectively and demonstrably rejected the arguments of those who abolish such divinations. He should also have demonstrably refuted the arguments of those who say that these movements in animals are caused by gods or demons for the purpose of divination. Finally, he should have established that the soul of irrational animals is more divine than the human soul. For in this way, we have stood against the persuasive arguments of one who acts as a philosopher on such matters, as far as we were able. We refute the claim that irrational animals are wiser than humans, and we demonstrate as false the claim that they possess thoughts regarding the divine...

<column-break/>
...into different flights and different cries, and for the rest into these or those movements: others [claim] their souls are more divine and more suited to divination, which is least of all credible. It was necessary, therefore, for Celsus, who wanted to show from the proposed matters that brute animals are more divine and wiser than humans, to show and prove through many [arguments] that such divination exists. Then, afterward, to reject more strongly and with demonstration the statements of those who remove such prophecies, and to pull down with firm arguments the discourses of those who said that such movements for the purpose of divination are excited in animals by gods or demons; then, finally, to prove that the soul of the brutes is more divine than the human. Thus, indeed, against his disputation—he who plays the philosopher in such matters—we have set ourselves up as far as we were able. We overturn that [claim] that brutes are wiser than humans; [and] that other [claim], that they have thoughts about God, [we refute].

<summary>This page contains a portion of Origen's critique of Celsus regarding the alleged wisdom and divinity of animals, specifically challenging the idea that animal behavior serves as a valid source of divine divination.</summary>

english:
<meta>continues from previous page: Nearchus says a four-month voyage</meta> stadia, not defining length or width, but saying it is a voyage of twenty days from the mainland. He says the ships sail poorly because they are badly equipped with sails and are constructed without <term>en koiliois metron</term> <gloss>rib-frames</gloss> or keels. There are other islands between it and India, though it is the furthest south. He claims amphibious sea monsters live around it, some resembling oxen, some horses, and some other land animals. Regarding Taprobane <gloss>Sri Lanka</gloss>, see von Bohlen, page 29 and following.

### 14.

Strabo, Book 15, page 692: Concerning <term>bosmoron</term> <gloss>a type of grain</gloss>, which Onesicritus says is a grain smaller than wheat and grows in the lands between rivers. It is roasted when it is threshed, and the people take an oath not to carry it away from the threshing floor unroasted, so that the seed cannot be exported.
Compare Diodorus, Book 2, chapter 36, where the books show the spelling "bosporon." See Stephanus's Thesaurus under "bosmoron." — "grain": so says the author of the Epitome; the manuscripts of Strabo say "septos."

### 15.

Strabo, Book 15, page 694: India produces many remarkable trees, among which is one with branches that lean downward, and leaves no smaller than a shield. Onesicritus, going into more detail about the territory of <term>Musicanus</term> <gloss>a ruler in the Indus valley</gloss>, which he says is the southernmost part of India, describes certain large trees whose branches grow upward for twelve cubits, then take the rest of their growth downward, as if bent, until they touch the ground. Then, spreading through the earth, they take root like layers, and then rising up, they form a trunk. From this, they bend down again in the same manner of growth, making another layer, and then another, and so on in succession, so that from a single tree a long sunshade is formed,

<column-break/>

resembling a tent with many pillars. He also mentions the size of the trees, saying the trunks are so large that five men can hardly embrace them.
Compare Aristobulus, Fragment 30, where it is said that Aristobulus described trees of such magnitude that fifty horsemen could rest under the shade of one; Strabo adds: "but this man (Onesicritus) says four hundred." Nearchus, Fragment 40; Diodorus, Book 17, chapter 90.

### 16.

Strabo, Book 15, page 693: The fact that the rivers overflow and the land winds do not blow is confirmed by what was said by Onesicritus. For he says the coastline of India is swampy, especially at the mouths of the rivers, because of the silt, the floods, and the dominance of the sea winds.
"The argument of this fragment confirms what was narrated by Aristobulus regarding the flooding of Indian rivers in Fragment 29." — GEIER. See below, Fragment 20.

### 17.

Strabo, Book 15, page 695: Regarding this (the idea that water from the clouds is already decocted when it is poured out), those around Aristobulus would not agree, as they claim it does not rain on the plains. But to Onesicritus, it seems that this water is the cause of the physical peculiarities in animals. He offers as evidence that the colors of foreign livestock change to the local color when they drink it. This point is well made; but he is no longer correct when he places the cause of the Ethiopians being black and curly-haired simply in the water, and

<column-break/>

reproaches Theodectes for attributing the cause to the sun itself, as that author says:

<note>original: 
"Whose sun at the near-border changing
a dark flower of soot leaped forth
into men's bodies and curled their hair
with the contracts of fire that stunted their forms."</note>

Yet Onesicritus might have some reasoning; for he says the sun is no closer to the Ethiopians than to others, but is rather more directly overhead <term>kata katheton</term> and for this reason burns more. Thus, he says it is not well said that the sun is "near-bordering" to them, since it is at an equal distance from everyone. He also argues that heat is not the cause of such a condition, since it is not so for those in the womb, whom the sun does not touch.

<sig>B iv</sig>
caloric. The change that occurs in the thermometer, therefore, announces only a displacement of caloric, a change that has happened to a system of bodies of which it is a part. It indicates at most only the portion of caloric it has received, but it does not measure the total quantity that has been released, displaced, or absorbed. The simplest and most exact means to fulfill this latter objective is the one imagined by M. de la Place <note>Pierre-Simon Laplace, a prominent mathematician and physicist</note>, and which is described in the *Memoirs of the Academy*, year 1780, page 364. One also finds a summary explanation of it at the end of this work. It consists of placing the body, or the combination from which the caloric is being released, in the middle of a hollow sphere of ice. The quantity of melted ice is an exact expression of the quantity of caloric that has been released. The <term>Sufi</term> <gloss>mystic</gloss> sat at the foot of the wine jar in the corner of the monastery,
Until he saw the <term>muhtasib</term> <gloss>market inspector</gloss> carrying a jug on his shoulder.

I asked the wine-seller at dawn about the state,
Of the Sheikh, the judge, and the drinking of the Jews.

He said, "The matter is unspoken, even if you are a confidant,
Hold your tongue, keep the veil, and drink wine."

O cupbearer, spring is arriving and the money for wine is gone,
Think of something, for the blood of the heart is boiling with grief.

Your love is poverty, youth, and the new spring,
Accept my excuse and cover my sin with the skirt of your grace.

How long will you use your tongue like a candle?
The butterfly of desire has arrived, O silent lover.

O King of form and meaning, whom no eye has ever seen,
And no ear has ever heard the equal of.

Stay as long as the blue robe accepts it,
May your young fortune live from the ancient heaven.

Yesterday, a sharp-witted expert told me in secret,
That one should not hide anything from the wine-seller.

He said, "Take things easily, for by nature,
The world treats those who struggle hard with severity."

And then he offered a cup whose luster caused,
Venus to dance in the heavens and the harpist to perk up her ears.

With a bloody heart, bring a smiling lip like the cup,
Do not cry out like a harp when you receive a wound.

Until you become intimate, you will not hear the secrets of this veil,
The ear of the uninitiated is no place for the message of <term>Soroush</term> <gloss>the messenger angel</gloss>.

english:
# VTOPIAE THOMAE MORI

to exercise authority over beggars, but rather over the wealthy and happy. Fabricius, a man of upright and lofty spirit, certainly understood this himself when he replied that he would rather rule over the rich than be rich himself. And indeed, for one man to flow in pleasure and delicacies while others are groaning and lamenting on all sides, this is not being a king, but a jailer. Finally, just as he is a most unskilled physician who knows not how to cure a disease except by causing another, so he who does not know how to correct the lives of citizens except by taking away the comforts of life should admit that he does not know how to rule free men. Rather, he should change his own laziness or pride; for it is generally through these faults that the people either despise him or hate him. He should live harmlessly from his own means, adjust his expenses to his revenues, curb crimes, and prevent them through the proper upbringing of his people rather than allowing them to grow, only to punish them later. He should not rashly revoke laws that have fallen into disuse, especially those that have been long abandoned and never missed. Nor should he ever take anything in the name of a crime that a judge would not allow a private citizen to take, as if it were unjust and crafty. Here, if I were to propose to them the law of the Macarenses, who themselves are not far from Utopia, whose King, on the very first day he enters upon his rule, is bound by a solemn oath, after great sacrifices have been offered, never to have more than a thousand pounds of gold, or its equivalent in silver, in his treasury. They say this law was instituted by a certain excellent King, who cared more for the advantage of the country than for riches

english:
He has no other than him. So I asked the judge: "Do you know his father?" May God protect his end. He said: "And can Abu Zayd be unknown? The one who was wounded by a tyrant <term>jabbar</term> <gloss>oppressor or giant</gloss>, and who has news and more news with every judge." At that moment, I shaved my head <note>a sign of grief or resolution</note> and woke up, but only after the time had passed. I became certain that for all of it, his evil was a trick and the house of a poem. My gaze was lowered by what I met. I swore that I would not deal with the likes of them as long as I lived. Then I did not cease to sigh over the best of my deal and the eloquence among my companions. The judge said to me, when he saw what had been transacted and it became clear that a free man had passed by: "O you, that of your wealth which has admonished you is not lost. Nor has he sinned against you who has awakened you. So take a lesson from what has come to you. Let your companions remember what befell you, so that you may forever banish your dirhams <gloss>silver coins</gloss> for the sake of memory. He who is tested and remains patient, the lesson is revealed to him and he takes heed." So I bid him farewell, not asking out of shame and sadness. The tail of loss and deception followed, and I intended to confront Abu Zayd with the news directly.

Caudæ uero imaginem faciebant consimilem, quando luna in cauda erat eclipsata, aut à Saturno uel Marte male affecta: faciebantq́; illam ad anxietatē & infirmitatem inducenda: & uocabant illā malum genium. <meta>This page continues the discussion of planetary and celestial talismans from Book 2. It transitions from the seven classical planets to the lunar nodes (the Dragon’s Head and Tail) and begins the sequence of the twenty-eight Mansions of the Moon, detailing the specific images, materials, and rituals used to harness their influences.</meta>

CLXXXVI.
->ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY<-

### On the images of the head and tail of the Moon’s dragon. Chapter 45.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting a serpent or dragon coiled into a circular shape resembling the Greek letter Theta (Θ). The creature has the head of a bird (hawk) and a pointed tail. Within the circular body, there is a central vertical line crossed by a shorter horizontal line, with small astrological or symbolic marks at the terminals.</image-desc>

They also used to make an image of the head and tail of the Moon's dragon <note>original: "capitis & caudæ draconis Lunæ"—referring to the North and South Nodes of the Moon, where its orbit intersects the ecliptic</note>; specifically, the likeness of a serpent between the aerial and fiery circle, with the head of a hawk surrounding them, in the likeness of the Greek letter theta <note>original: "thita" (Θ). The serpent biting its tail is a common symbol for the Nodes in Renaissance magic.</note>. They made this when Jupiter, along with the Head <note>The North Node, or "Caput Draconis"</note>, held the <term>midheaven: the highest point of the zodiac at the time of the calculation</term>. They affirm that this image contributes greatly to the success of petitions. They intended to represent a good and happy <term>daemon: a guiding spirit or celestial entity, not necessarily an evil "demon"</term> through this image, and they chose to figure it as a serpent. Indeed, the Egyptians and Phoenicians celebrate this animal as divine above all others, noting its divine nature because there exists within it a sharper spirit and a more abundant fire than in other animals. This is shown by its swift movement without any feet or hands or other limbs, and because it periodically renews its age and grows young again by shedding its skin.

However, they made the image of the Tail <note>The South Node, or "Cauda Draconis"</note> in a similar fashion when the Moon was eclipsed in the Tail, or was poorly affected by Saturn or Mars. They made this to induce anxiety and infirmity, and they called it an "evil genius" <note>original: "malum genium"—a malevolent spirit or influence</note>. A certain Hebrew man had enclosed such an image in a golden double-belt which Blanche, the daughter of the Duke of Bourbon, gave as a gift to her husband Peter, the first King of Spain of that name <note>Peter of Castile, known as "the Cruel" (1334–1369). Historical legend suggests he abandoned his wife Blanche almost immediately, with some accounts blaming a cursed belt.</note> (whether she was aware of it or was ignorant). When he was girded with it, it seemed to him that he was cinched by a serpent. Once the magic power inserted into the belt was discovered, he repudiated his wife for that reason.

### On the images of the Mansions of the Moon. Chapter 46.

They also made images in the individual <term>mansions of the moon: 28 divisions of the zodiac through which the Moon travels daily</term>. 

In the **first** mansion, for the destruction of someone, they made on an iron ring the image of a black man clothed and girded in hair-cloth <note>original: "cilicio"—a coarse garment made of goat's hair, worn for penance</note>, throwing a small spear with his right hand. They sealed this in black wax, smoked it with liquid storax <note>a fragrant resin</note>, and made imprecations. 

In the **second**, against the wrath of a prince and for reconciliation with him, they sealed in white wax and mastic the image of a crowned king, and smoked it with aloeswood. 

In the **third**, they made an image on a silver ring of square measure, the figure of which was a well-dressed woman sitting in a chair, with her right hand raised over her head. They sealed it and smoked it with musk, camphor, and "aromatic claw" <note>original: "ungula aromatica"—likely the operculum of certain sea snails, used in incense</note>. They asserted that this bestowed prosperity of fortune and every good thing. 

In the **fourth**, for revenge, separation, enmity, and ill-will, they sealed in red wax the image of a soldier sitting on a horse, holding a serpent in his right hand, and smoked it with red myrrh and storax. 

In the **fifth**, for the favor of kings and officials and for a good reception, they sealed in silver the head of a man, and smoked it with sandalwood. 

In the **sixth**, to place love between two people, they sealed in white wax two images embracing each other, and smoked them with aloeswood and amber. 

In the **seventh**, to acquire every good thing, they sealed in silver the image of a well-dressed man, with hands stretched toward heaven for...

<summary>This page describes the creation of talismans based on the Lunar Nodes (the Dragon's Head and Tail) and begins a catalog of the 28 Mansions of the Moon. It explains the ritual materials, imagery, and intended magical effects—ranging from political favor to destructive curses—associated with these celestial positions.</summary>

πίπτων κατακόπτει με πληγαῖς. ἐγὼ δὲ ὥσπερ ἐν μυστηρίῳ μηδὲν, μήθ’ ὅς τις ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἦν, μήθ’ ἧς χάριν ἔτυπτεν, ὑποπτεύσας δή τι κακὸν εἶναι, 9) ἐδεδοίκειν ἀμύνασθαι, καί τοι δυνάμενος. ἐπεὶ δὲ ἔκαμεν, 10) ὁ μὲν τύπτων, ἐγὼ δὲ Φιλοσοφῶν, λέγω πρὸς αὐτὸν ἀναστάς· Τίς εἶ ποτε ὦ ἄνθρωπε; 11) καὶ τί με οὕτως ἠκίσω; Ὁ δὲ ἔτι μᾶλλον ὀργισθεὶς ὅτι καὶ φωνὴν ἀφῆκα, ῥαπίζει πάλιν, 12) καὶ καλεῖ δεσμὰ καὶ πέδας. 13) δεσμεύουσιν ἔν με καὶ ἄγουσιν εἴς τι δωμάτιον.

### ΚΕΦΑΛ. κδ’.

Ἐν ᾧ δὲ ταῦτα ἐπράττετο, λανθάνει μου διαρρυεῖσα ἡ τῆς Λευκίππης ἐπιστολή· ἔτυχον γὰρ αὐτὴν ἔσω τοῦ χιτωνίσκου προσδεδεμένην ἐκ τῶν τῆς ὀθόνης θυσάνων 1) ἔχων. ἣ ἡ Μελίττη ἀναιρεῖται λαβοῦσα· ἐδεδίει γὰρ μή τινα τῶν πρὸς με αὐτῆς γραμμάτων ἦν. ὡς δὲ ἀνέγνω καθ’ ἑαυτὴν γενομένη, καὶ τὸ τῆς Λευκίππης εὗρεν ὄνομα, βάλλεται μὲν τὴν καρδίαν, 2) εὐθέως γνωρίσασα τοὔνομα· οὐ μὲν αὐτὴν ἐνόμιζεν εἶναι, τῷ πολλάκις αὐτὴν ἀκηκοέναι τετελευτηκέναι.

<header>ACHILLES TATIUS [Salm. p. 343.]</header>

falling upon me, he beat me with blows. I, as if in a mystery, suspecting nothing—neither who the man was, nor for what reason he was beating me—feared to defend myself, even though I was able to. When he was tired from beating me, and I was weary from philosophizing, I stood up and said to him: Who are you, man? And why have you treated me so cruelly? He, even more enraged that I had uttered a sound, slapped me again, and called for bonds and shackles. They bound me and led me into a small room.

### CHAPTER XXIV

While these things were happening, the letter from Leucippe slipped away from me unnoticed. For I happened to have it tied inside my tunic with the fringes of the cloth <note>original: "ὀθόνης θυσάνων"</note>. Melitte took it and removed it; she was afraid it might be one of her own letters to me. When she was by herself and read it, and found Leucippe's name, she was struck in the heart, recognizing the name immediately. However, she did not believe it was she, because she had frequently heard that she had died.

---

9) He threw me to the ground <note>original: "Ἀράσσει πρὸς τὔδαφος"</note>. In others <term>rhassei</term>. Or is it <term>rhyssei</term>? For <term>rhyssei</term> is also <term>katabalon</term>, to throw down, to settle on the ground. A wrestling term. SALMASIUS.

9) Suspecting that it was some evil <note>original: "Ὑποπτεύσας δή τι κακὸν εἶναι"</note>. Better: "suspecting that there was some evil." IDEM.

10) He was weary <note>original: "Ἔκαμεν"</note>. Terence, Adelphoe II. 2, where Sannio says: I never saw a contest worse matched than this has been today between us. I by getting beaten, he by beating, we are both exhausted. BODEN.

11) Who are you, man? <note>original: "Τίς εἶ ποτε, ὦ ἄνθρωπε"</note>. IDEM.

12) He slapped again <note>original: "Ῥαπίζει πάλιν"</note>. That is, he strikes at the cheek. This is better than above. FAB.

## HET SESTE HOOFT-STUCK.

### *De ontleedingh van de inwendige deelen van het Haft.*

Het ey, de wurm, ſijn voetſel, ſijn levens-tijt, ſijn uytterlijcke leeden, ende ſijn aerdt kortelijck beſchreven hebbende : ſoo kon ick nu bequamelyck ſijn veranderingh afhandelen. Dan alſoo de ſelve ſoo ſchielijck in ſijn werck gaat, dat ſe haaſt niet en beſtaat, als in het afftroopen van twee vlieſen, ende het uytrecken van ſommige leeden. Soo oordeel ick het beeter te ſijn, om ſoo veel te netter het onder-ſcheyt te verſtaan tuſſchen het *Aas* en het *Haft*; dat is tuſſchen de wurm ſwemmen-de, ende de ſelve wurm vliegende; eerſte-lijck ſijne inwendige leeden te beſchrijven; te meer alſoo wy de ſelve leeden, onder beyde de geſtalteniſſen van dit dierken, gewaar worden.

## THE SIXTH CHAPTER.

### *The dissection of the internal parts of the Dayfly.*

Having briefly described the egg, the worm <note>term: "wurm" — Swammerdam uses this to refer to the aquatic nymph or larval stage of the insect</note>, its food, its lifespan, its external limbs, and its nature: I could now conveniently treat its transformation. But since the same transformation proceeds so quickly in its operation that it consists of little more than the stripping off of two skins <note>original: "vlieſen" — membranes or pellicles shed during molting</note> and the stretching out of certain limbs: I judge it to be better—in order to understand more precisely the distinction between the *Aas* <note>term: "Aas" — the Dutch term for the aquatic nymph of the mayfly, which literally means "bait," as it was used by fishermen</note> and the *Haft* <note>term: "Haft" — the Dutch common name for the adult winged stage of the Ephemeron or Mayfly</note>; that is, between the swimming worm and the same worm flying—to first describe its internal organs; all the more so because we observe these same organs under both forms of this little creature.

### מסכת פרה

**פרק א**

**א** רבי אליעזר אומר עגלה בת שנתה ופרה בת שתים וחכמים אומרים עגלה בת שתים ופרה בת שלש או בת ארבע ר' מאיר אומר אף בת חמש כשרה הזקנה אלא שאין ממתינין לה שמא תשחיר שלא תפסל אמר רבי יהושע לא שמעתי אל שלשית אמרו לו מה הלשון שלשית אמר להם כך שמעתי סתם אמר בן עזאי אני אפרש אם אומרתם שלישית לאחרת במנין וכשאתה אומר שלישית בת שלש שנים כיוצא בו אמרו כרם רבעי אמרו לו מה הלשון רבעי אמר להם כך שמעתי סתם אמר בן עזאי אני אפרש אם אומרתם רביעי לאחר במנין וכשאתה אומר רבעי בן ארבע שנים כיוצא בו אמרו האוכל בבית המנוגע פרס מג' לקב אמרו לו אמור משמנה עשרה לסאה אמר להם כך שמעתי סתם אמר בן עזאי אני אפרש אם אומר אתה משלש לקב אין בו חלה וכשאתה אומר משמונה עשרה לסאה מיעטתו חלתו: **ב** ימי יום הגלילי אומר פרים בני שתים שנא' ופר שני בן בקר תקח לחטאת וחכמים אומרים אף בני שלש רבי מאיר אומר אף בני ארבע ובני חמש כשרים אלא שאין מביאים זקנים מפני הכבוד: **ג** כבשים בני שנה ואילים בני שתים וכולם מיום ליום בן שלשה עשר חדש אינו כשר לא לאיל ולא לכבש רבי טרפון קורהו פלגס בן עזאי קורהו נוקד רבי ישמעאל קורהו פרכדיגמא הקריבו מביא עליו נסכי איל ולא עלה לו מזבחו בן שלשת עשר חדש ויום אחד הרי זה איל: **ד** חטאת הצבור ועולותיה חטאת היחיד ואשם נזיר ואשם מצורע כשרין מיום שלשים והלאה ואף ביום שלשים ואם הקריב ביום השמיני כשרים הנדרים והנדבות הבכור והמעשר והפסח כשרים מיום השמיני והלאה ואף ביום השמיני:

**פרק ב**

**א** רבי אליעזר אומר פרת חטאת המעוברת כשרה וחכמים פוסלים רבי אליעזר אומר אינה נלקחת מן הגוים וחכמים מכשירים ולא זו בלבד אלא כל קרבנות הצבור והיחיד באין מהארץ ומחוצה לארץ מן החדש ומן הישן חוץ מן העומר ושתי הלחם שאינן באין אלא מן החדש ומן הארץ: **ב** פרה שקרניה וטלפיה שחורים יגור גלגל העין והשינים והלשון אינם פוסלין בפרה והננסת כשרה היתה בה יבלת וחתכה רבי יהודה פוסל רבי שמעון אוסר כל מקום שנוטל ולא העלה מקומו שער אדום פסולה: **ג** יוצא דופן ואתנן ומחיר פסולה רבי אליעזר מכשיר שנאמר לא תביא אתנן זונה ומחיר כלב בית ה' אלהיך ואין זו באה לבית כל המומים הפוסלים במוקדשים פוסלים בפרה רכב עליה נשען עליה נתלה בזנבה עבר בה את הנהר קיפל עליה את המוסרה נתן טליתו עליה פסולה אבל קשרה במוסרה עשה לה סנדל בשביל שלא תחליק פרש טליתו עליה מפני הזבובים כשרה זה הכלל כל שהו' לצורכה כשרה לצורך אחר פסולה: **ד** שכן עליה עוף כשרה עלה עליה זכר פסולה רבי יהודה אומר אם העלהו פסולה ואם מעצמו כשרה: **ה** היו בה ב' שערות שחורות

Rabbi Jose says: even if a vessel holds a <term>kor</term> <gloss>a large dry measure</gloss> and contains only a <term>revi'it</term> <gloss>a small liquid measure</gloss>, it is as if it were not immersed. **7** All foods combine to defile the body [if they are in the amount of] half a <term>pras</term> <gloss>a measurement of half a loaf</gloss>. All liquids combine to defile the body [if they are in the amount of] a <term>revi'it</term>. This is a stringency regarding one who drinks defiled liquids compared to one who eats [defiled food], that he considers other liquids as water. **8** If one ate defiled foods and drank defiled liquids, [if] he immersed and vomited [them up], they are defiled because they are not pure in the body. If he drank pure liquids, he immersed and vomited, they are pure because they are pure in the body. [If] he swallowed a pure ring, entered the tent of the dead, and stayed, and immersed and vomited it, it is as it was. [If] he swallowed a defiled ring, he immerses and eats of the <term>terumah</term> <gloss>priestly gifts</gloss>; [if] he vomited it, it is defiled. And with respect to [a ring or object] that is cut off as a human [would be], when it is visible, it is [considered] external; if it is not visible, he immerses and eats of his <term>terumah</term>.

### Massekhet Parah

**Chapter 1**

**1** Rabbi Eliezer says: a heifer in its first year, and a cow in its second. But the Sages say: a heifer in its second year, and a cow in its third or fourth. Rabbi Meir says: even one in its fifth year is valid. An old one is [also] valid, except that we do not wait for it, lest it turn black and become disqualified. Rabbi Joshua said: I have not heard [the tradition regarding] "third." They said to him: What is the meaning of "third"? He said to them: This is how I heard it, [without elaboration]. Ben Azzai said: I will explain it. If you say "third" to another in the count, when you say "third," [it means] three years old. Similarly, they said: "fourth-year vineyard" <note>Hebrew: <term>kerem revai</term></note>. They said to him: What is the meaning of "fourth"? He said to them: This is how I heard it, [without elaboration]. Ben Azzai said: I will explain it. If you say "fourth" to another in the count, when you say "fourth-year," [it means] four years old. Similarly, they said: One who eats in a house affected by leprosy [a volume of] half a loaf from three to a <term>kab</term> <gloss>a specific dry measure</gloss>. They said to him: Say, from eighteen to a <term>seah</term> <gloss>a larger dry measure</gloss>. He said to them: This is how I heard it, [without elaboration]. Ben Azzai said: I will explain it. If you say "from three to a <term>kab</term>," it is not subject to [the dough-offering of] <term>challah</term>; and when you say "from eighteen to a <term>seah</term>," it diminishes its <term>challah</term>. **2** Rabbi Jose the Galilean says: heifers [are used] at two years old, as it is written: "And you shall take a heifer of the herd for a sin offering." But the Sages say: even those of three years. Rabbi Meir says: even those of four and five are valid, except that they do not bring old ones out of respect. **3** Sheep in their first year, and rams in their second; and all are from day to day. A thirteen-month-old [animal] is not valid, neither as a ram nor as a sheep. Rabbi Tarfon calls it <term>palgas</term> <gloss>half-grown</gloss>; Ben Azzai calls it <term>noked</term> <gloss>pasture-dweller</gloss>; Rabbi Ishmael calls it <term>farkadigma</term> <gloss>a term of obscure Greek or Latin origin</gloss>. [If] they offered it, he brings upon it the drink offerings of a ram, but it does not count for him. [An animal] of thirteen months and one day, this is a ram. **4** The communal sin offering and its burnt offerings, the individual sin offering, the sin offering of the Nazirite, and the sin offering of the leper are valid from the thirtieth day onwards, and even on the thirtieth day. And if one offered on the eighth day, they are valid. Vows, voluntary offerings, the firstborn, the tithe, and the Passover sacrifice are valid from the eighth day onwards, and even on the eighth day.

**Chapter 2**

**1** Rabbi Eliezer says: a pregnant heifer for the sin offering is valid, but the Sages disqualify it. Rabbi Eliezer says: it is not purchased from Gentiles, but the Sages validate it. And not only this, but all communal and individual sacrifices come from the Land and from outside the Land, from the new crop and from the old, except for the <term>omer</term> <gloss>the sheaf offering</gloss> and the two loaves, which only come from the new crop and from the Land. **2** A cow whose horns and hooves are black; the eyeball, the teeth, and the tongue do not disqualify the cow. And a dwarf is valid. If it had a wart and he cut it off, Rabbi Judah disqualifies it; Rabbi Simeon forbids it. Any place where he removes [a part] and no red hair has grown in its place, it is disqualified. **3** [An animal born by] cesarean section, the fee of a harlot, and the price of a dog are disqualified. Rabbi Eliezer validates them, as it is written: "You shall not bring the fee of a harlot or the price of a dog into the house of the Lord your God," and this [cow] does not come to the House. All blemishes that disqualify [other] holy offerings disqualify the cow. [If] one rode upon it, leaned upon it, hung by its tail, crossed a river with it, folded the bridle upon it, or placed his cloak upon it, it is disqualified. But if he tied it with a bridle, made a sandal for it so it would not slip, [or] spread his cloak upon it to protect it from flies, it is valid. This is the general rule: anything that is for its own needs is valid; for the needs of another, it is disqualified. **4** If a bird sat upon it, it is valid; [if] a male mounted it, it is disqualified. Rabbi Judah says: if it caused it to mount, it is disqualified, but if it did so of its own accord, it is valid. **5** If it had two black hairs...

from there its powers, namely for expelling <note>In this context, expelling excess fluid from the body.</note> [fluid], are made stronger, and moreover, the doses of **precipitated Mercury** may be more easily formed for administration or absorption in the form of pills. This precipitated Mercury, therefore, is uniquely praised and recommended, and indeed performs very well. **Mercury of Life** or **flowers of butter of antimony** <note>original: "flores butyri antimonij"; despite the name "Mercury of Life," this was a preparation of antimony trichloride used as a potent purgative.</note>, which were discussed above, accomplish the same thing if 4 to 12 grains of it are administered over a full three-day period in an extract of **Hellebore** and **colocynth** <note>Colocynth, or bitter apple, is a powerful medicinal fruit used as a drastic purgative.</note>; it successfully expels the dissolved salt. 

Afterward, however, sweating and urination should be stimulated with a decoction of **sarsaparilla**, **holy wood** <term>lignum sanctum: another name for Guaiacum, a tropical wood used to treat various ailments by inducing sweat.</term>, or **asarum root**, always adding **spirit of Tartar**, or other diaphoretics <note>medicines that induce sweating</note> and diuretics, as mentioned above. Especially beneficial is the addition of the **secret remedy** <term>arcanum: a high-potency alchemical preparation believed to hold the essential 'secret' power of a substance.</term> of wormwood or blessed thistle. 

It must be noted, however, that the three-day administration of **Mercury of Life** often tends to cause a rectal prolapse in adults, which is thereafter rarely or even with difficulty cured. In treating **dropsy** <term>hydrops: an old medical term for edema, or the accumulation of excess watery fluid in the tissues or cavities of the body.</term>, it is necessary that such purgatives be applied right from the start of the treatment: afterward, diuretics and water-movers should follow. Otherwise, what is called <term>histeron proteron: a Greek phrase meaning "the latter first," or putting the cart before the horse.</term> would be practiced here; all the serum or water having flowed down to the kidneys and ureters, there afterward, on account of the heavy burden, very stubborn symptoms usually arise. 

Furthermore, in the preparation of the extract of **black Hellebore root**, it is safer to use the wine itself instead of spirit of wine <note>High-proof alcohol or brandy.</note>, with which the root itself should at least gently simmer without much bubbling; and this must be done with fresh wine until all the essential power has been extracted from the roots; afterward, by evaporating or distilling the liquid to the thickness of honey, it should be reduced to an extract. abandoning non-virtue is itself the "changing of the three robes." In that state, because it clears away the stains of the afflictions, conceptual thoughts, and signs, it is the "bathing three times." Burning the conceptual thoughts of the afflictions with the nature of the fire of primordial wisdom which is free from elaboration is itself the "fire offering." 

That very <term>bodhicitta</term> is <term>Hevajra</term>, and by its very nature of wisdom, it is the cycle of <term>Yoginis</term>; therefore, it is the "mandala deity." The support for these is the very cause for the abiding of meditative concentration; since that too is a quality of the mind, it is therefore the "mandala." In the section beginning "In brief...", the meaning of the previously spoken verses is summarized in a single phrase. "In brief" means that by the stated reasoning, those practices such as mantra recitation are summarized and maintained, so the mind becomes of a "collected nature"—this is the remaining word. 

"Mind" is the <term>bodhicitta</term> as previously described. "Collected" means that all phenomena are collected into a single taste. The one who has that nature is the "yogi," for apart from that nature, no self is perceived. This is the "supreme empowerment," because it visibly washes away the stains of afflictions and conceptual thoughts. The chapter that clarifies this empowerment is the Chapter on Empowerment. This concludes the explanation of the tenth chapter from the *Pearl Garland* <term>Muktāvalī</term>, a difficult-point commentary on the <term>Hevajra Tantra</term>.

To lead sentient beings into the teaching, one should perform the four "gazes": the gaze that causes to fall, the gaze of subduing, the gaze of summoning, and the gaze of stiffening. The characteristics of these are shown in order by four half-verses. There, whatever is looked at with a face directed straight ahead and a wrathful expression, with the two pupils shown at the forehead, is the "gaze that causes to fall." That which relies on the left and looks to the left is the "gaze of subduing." That which relies on the upper direction and looks to the right is the "gaze of summoning." That which relies on the tip of the nose and looks straight ahead is the "gaze of stiffening."

Ἐπειδὴ τοίνυν κατὰ τὴν ἐν τῷ ψαλμῷ διαμακαρισμὸν τῆς ἀντιλήψεως αὐτῇ παρὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ γινομένης, τὰς καλὰς ταύτας ἀναβάσεις ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ δίθετο, πάντοτε ἐκ δυνάμεως πορευομένη εἰς δύναμιν, καλῶς ἐπὶ τῆς τελειοτέρας καταστάσεως ῥοῶν παράδεισος αἱ τοῦ στόματος αὐτῆς ἀποστολαὶ ὀνομάζονται. Προσφυῶς δὲ τῷ ὑποκειμένῳ νοήματι ἡ λέξις τῆς ἀποστολῆς ἐφηρμόσθη. Τὸ γὰρ ἀποστελλόμενον ἀπὸ τοῦ πέμποντος εἰς τὸν ὑποδεχόμενον μεταβαίνει. Καὶ τοῦτο ἐκ τῆς συνήθους τοῦ ῥήματος καταχρήσεως, ἔστι μαθεῖν, ὡς καὶ τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον λέγει, ὅτι τοὺς μαθητὰς τοὺς πρὸς τὸ κήρυγμα τῆς ἀληθείας ἐκπεμπομένους, Ἀποστόλους ὁ Λόγος ὠνόμασε. Τί οὖν ἐστιν ὃ ἀποστέλλει τὸ στόμα τῆς νύμφης; Δῆλον ὅτι τὸν λόγον τῆς πίστεως, ὃς ἐν τοῖς ὑποδεχομένοις γενόμενος, παράδεισος γίνεται, διὰ τῆς ἀκοῆς ταῖς καρδίαις ἐμφυτευόμενος. Τὸ δὲ κατάφυτον καὶ συνηρεφὲς τοῖς δένδροις ἄλσος, παράδεισον εἴωθε καλεῖν ἡ συνήθεια. Ὡς ἂν οὖν καὶ τὸ γένος μάθοιμεν τῶν φυτῶν, ὅπερ διὰ τοῦ Λόγου ταῖς ψυχαῖς τῶν πεπιστευκότων κηπεύεται, ῥόας ὀνομάζει τὰ δένδρα ἧς φυτηκομεῖ ὁ Λόγος, ὁ παρὰ τοῦ στόματος τῆς νύμφης ἀποστελλόμενος. Ἡ δὲ ῥόα δυσεπιχείρητός ἐστι τῷ κλέπτῃ ἀκανθώδεις προβαλλόμενη τοὺς ὄρπηκας, καὶ τὸν καρπὸν αὐστηρῷ τινι καὶ πικραίνοντι κατὰ τὴν γεῦσιν τῷ καλύμματι περιέχουσά τε καὶ ὑποτρέφουσα· ὃς κατὰ τὸν ἴδιον καιρὸν μετὰ τὸ πεπανθῆναι, τοῦ ἐλύτρου περιῤῥαγέντος ἔνδοθεν διαφαίνεται, ἡδὺς μὲν τὴν ὄψιν καὶ εὐδιάθετος, μελιειδὴς δὲ τὴν γεῦσιν καὶ ἄλυπος, καὶ καταγλυκαίνων τῷ οἰνοειδεῖ χυμῷ τὰ γευστικὰ αἰσθητήρια. Διὰ τοῦτό μοι δοκεῖ ῥοῶν παραδείσεως ἐν ταῖς τῶν ἀκουόντων ψυχαῖς ὁ ἀποστελλόμενος ἐκ τοῦ στόματος τῆς νύμφης λόγος ἐργάζεσθαι, ἵνα διδαχθῶμεν διὰ τῶν λεγομένων, μὴ διά τινος ἐκλύσεως καὶ τρυφῆς κατὰ τὴν παροῦσαν ζωὴν μαλακίζεσθαι, ἀλλὰ τὸν κατεσκληκότα διὰ τῆς ἐγκρατείας αἱρεῖσθαι βίον. Ἀλλ’ ὅταν ὁ καιρὸς παράσχῃ τῆς ἀπολαύσεως τῶν καρπῶν τὸ ἐνδόσιμον, παγκαρπία τῆς τρυφῆς ἐκ παντὸς γένους τῶν ἀκροδρύων ῥόα γίνεται, οὐκ ἐν βραβύλοις ἢ βαλάνοις, ἥ τισι τοῖς τοιούτοις τῆς τῶν καρπῶν ἀπολαύσεως γινομένης· ἀλλὰ ποικίλη τις καὶ πολυειδὴς ἀρωμάτων φύσις ἐκ τῶν ἀκροδρύων εὑρίσκεται. Apposite autem subjectæ sententiæ adaptata fuit dictio emissionis. Nam quod emittitur, ab eo qui mittit, transit ad eum qui suscipit. Idque licet discere ex consueto usu verbi, quod, ut dicit Evangelium, eos qui mittuntur ad prædicandam veritatem, Verbum nominavit apostolos, id est missos. Quid est igitur quod emittit os sponsæ? verbum scilicet fidei; quod cum est in iis qui suscipiunt, fit paradisus qui plantatur per auditionem in cordibus. Nemus autem plantatum et frequens arboribus, paradisum solet vocare consuetudo. Ut ergo discamus etiam genus arborum, quæ per Verbum coluntur in hortis animarum eorum qui crediderunt, malos punicas nominat arbores, quas Verbum plantat et colit, quod emittitur ex ore sponsæ. Malum autem punicam difficiliter aggreditur, ut quæ spinosos proferat ramos, et quodam in gustu austero et amarescenti propugnaculo fructum contineat et nutriat: qui suo tempore, postquam matuerit, fracto cortice intus apparet, visu jucundus et bene affectus, gustui autem mellitus et nihil afferens molestiæ, qui sapore quodam vini simili gustus instrumenta afficit dulcedine. Propterea mihi videtur paradisus malorum punicarum, nempe sermo qui emittitur in animas auditorum ex ore sponsæ, efficere, ut doceamur per ea quæ dicuntur, non per dissolutionem aliquam et delicias in vita præsenti emolliri ac enervari, sed per continentiam, duram et asperam vitam eligere. Non est enim calor per se laudabilis, quando calor est fetida inflammatio, sed oportet puritatem per bonum odorem ferre testimonium de calore, ut sit sancto Spiritu fervens, qui est a tetro calore expurgatus.
