829. Quoniam Religio in ſupremis apud hominem reſidet, & ex ſupremis vivunt & lucent inferiora ejus, & quia Mahumedes verſatur in animis illorum una cum Religione, ideo ſemper aliquis Mahumedes in conſpectu illorum ponitur, ac ut vertant facies ſuas ad Orientem, ſuper quo eſt Dominus, ponitur ille infra Meditullium Chriſtianum: non eſt ipſe Mahumedes, qui Alcoranum conſcripſit, ſed alius qui munere ejus fungitur; nec eſt idem ſemper, ſed mutatur: quondam fuit unus ex Saxonia, qui captus ab Algirienſibus factus eſt Mahumedanus, is quia Chriſtianus etiam fuerat, aliquoties actus eſt ad loquendum cum illis de Domino, quod non fuerit Filius Joſephi, ſed Filius Ipſius Dei. Iſti Mahumedi ſucceſſerunt poſtea alii. In loco ubi repræſentativus ille Mahumedes ſedem habet, apparet ignis ſicut faculæ, ut noſcatur; ſed ille ignis non conſpicuus eſt aliis, quam Mahumedanis.

830. Ipſe Mahumedes, qui ſcripſit Alcoranum, non in conſpectum hodie venit; dictum mihi eſt, quod primis temporibus præfuerit illis, ſed quia voluit dominari ſuper omnia Religionis illorum ut Deus, quod e ſede ſua, quam ſub Pontificiis habuit, ejectus ſit, & ad latus dextrum juxta meridiem demiſſus. Quondam aliqua Societas ex Mahumedanis excitata eſt a malitioſis ad agnoſcendum Mahumedem pro Deo, ut ſeditio ſedaretur, ſublatus eſt Mahumedes ab infera terra, & oſtenſus, & tunc quoque mihi viſus eſt: apparuit ſimilis Spiritibus corporeis, quibus non perceptio interior eſt, facie ad nigrum vergente, & audivi illum loquentem hæc verba, *Ego ſum Mahumedes veſter*; & mox quaſi ſubſidens.

831. Mahumedani infeſti ſunt Chriſtianis primario propter fidem trium Perſonarum Divinarum, & inde cultum trium Deorum, totidem Creatorum, ac Chatolico-Romanis inſuper propter genuflexiones coram ſimulachris, & inde hos vocant Idololatras, & illos fanaticos, dicentes quod faciant Deum Tricipitem, & quod dicant unum ac muſſitent tres, proinde quod ſcindant Omnipotentiam, & ex una & unius faciant tres; & quod ita ſint ſicut Fauni cum tribus cornibus, uno pro quovis Deo, & inſimul tres pro uno, & quod ſic orent, ſic pſallant, & ſic e ſuggeſtibus ſonent.

832. Eſt Mahumedanis, ſicut omnibus Gentibus quæ agnoſcunt Deum unum, ac amant juſtum, & faciunt bonum ex Religione, ſuum Cælum, ſed extra Chriſtianum: aſt Cælum Mahumedanum in duos eſt diſtinctum, in Inferiori vivunt honeſte cum pluribus uxoribus, ſed inde non alii in Cælum ſuperius elevantur, quam qui abdicant pellices, & agnoſcunt Dominum Salvatorem noſtrum, & ſimul Ipſius Dominium ſuper Cælum & Infernum. Audivi quod illis impoſſibile ſit cogitare Deum Patrem & Dominum noſtrum eſſe unum, ſed quod illis poſſibile ſit credere, quod dominetur ſuper Cælos & Inferna, quia Filius Dei Patris eſt: hæc Fides apud illos eſt, per quam aſcenſus in ſuperius Cælum illis a Domino datur.

833. Quod Religio Mahumedana recepta ſit a pluribus Regnis, quam Religio Chriſtiana, poteſt ſcandalo eſſe illis, qui de Divina Providentia cogitant, & ſimul credunt, quod non aliquis ſalvari poſſit, quam qui Chriſtianus natus eſt: at Religio Mahumedana non eſt ſcandalum illis, qui credunt quod omnia ſint Divinæ Providentiæ; hi inquirunt, in quo eſt, & quoque inveniunt. Eſt in hoc, quod Mahumedana Religio agnoſcat Dominum pro Maximo Propheta, Sapientiſſimo omnium, & quoque pro Filio Dei; at quia modo Alcoranum Librum religionis ſuæ fecerunt, & inde Mahumedes, qui illum conſcripſit, cogitationibus illorum inſedit, & aliquo cultu illum proſequuntur, ideo parum de Domino noſtro cogitant. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the spiritual state of various religions, transitioning from the Roman Catholic state to that of the Muslims (referred to here as Mohammedans) in the spiritual world.</meta>

### THE NEW HEAVEN AND THE NEW CHURCH. 493

...confession of the Lord and the One God; for that joins souls to Heaven and creates a distance from the East, above which is the Lord.

829. Since religion resides in the highest parts of a person, and from those highest parts the lower things live and shine, and because **Mohammed** is present in their minds alongside their religion, someone representing Mohammed is always placed in their sight. So that they may turn their faces toward the East, above which is the Lord, he is placed below the **Christian Center** <term>Meditullium: a central or middle region in Swedenborg's spiritual geography</term>. This is not the actual Mohammed who wrote the **Quran** <note>original: "Alcoranum"</note>, but another person who performs his office; nor is it always the same person, but he is changed. Once it was a man from **Saxony** who, having been captured by the **Algerians**, became a Muslim. Because he had also been a Christian, he was occasionally moved to speak with them about the Lord, saying that He was not the son of Joseph but the Son of God Himself. Other men succeeded this Mohammed later on. In the place where that representative Mohammed has his seat, a fire appears like torches so that he may be recognized; but that fire is not visible to anyone other than the Muslims.

830. The actual Mohammed who wrote the Quran does not come into view today. I was told that in the earliest times he presided over them, but because he wished to rule over everything of their religion like a God, he was ejected from his seat—which he held under the Papists—and sent down to the right side near the south. Once, a certain society of Muslims was incited by malicious spirits to acknowledge Mohammed as God. To settle the sedition, Mohammed was brought up from the **lower earth** <term>Infera Terra: a region of the spiritual world for preparation or vastation</term> and shown to them, and I saw him then as well. He appeared similar to **corporeal spirits** <note>spirits focused only on the physical or external senses</note> who have no interior perception; his face verged toward black. I heard him speak these words: *I am your Mohammed*; and soon he seemed to sink back down.

831. Muslims are hostile to Christians primarily because of the belief in three Divine Persons, and the resulting worship of three Gods and three Creators. They are hostile to **Roman Catholics** in addition because of their kneeling before images; hence they call the latter **Idolaters** and the former **fanatics**. They say that Christians make a **three-headed God** <note>original: "Tricipitem"</note>, and that they say "one" but whisper "three"; consequently, they say Christians tear apart Omnipotence and make three out of the one and only. They say Christians are like **Fauns** <note>mythological half-human, half-goat creatures</note> with three horns, one for each God, and yet three for one; and that they pray this way, sing this way, and sound this way from their pulpits.

832. Like all nations that acknowledge one God, love what is just, and do good based on religion, Muslims have their own Heaven, but it is outside the Christian one. However, the Muslim Heaven is divided into two: in the lower one, they live honestly with multiple wives, but no one is elevated from there into the higher Heaven except those who give up their concubines and acknowledge the Lord as our Savior, and at the same time acknowledge His dominion over Heaven and Hell. I heard that it is impossible for them to think that God the Father and our Lord are one, but that it is possible for them to believe He rules over the Heavens and the Hells because He is the Son of God the Father. This is the faith among them through which the Lord grants them ascent into the higher Heaven.

833. The fact that the Muslim religion has been received by more kingdoms than the Christian religion can be a scandal to those who think about **Divine Providence** and simultaneously believe that no one can be saved except a person born a Christian. But the Muslim religion is not a scandal to those who believe that all things are of Divine Providence; these people search for the reason why it is so, and they find it. It is in this: that the Muslim religion acknowledges the Lord as the Greatest Prophet, the wisest of all, and also as the Son of God. But because they have made the Quran the book of their religion, and consequently Mohammed (who wrote it) resides in their thoughts and they follow him with a certain worship, they think little about our Lord. So that it may be fully known that this religion was raised up by the Lord's Divine Providence to destroy the idolatries of many nations, it will be described in some order; but first, concerning the origin of idolatries. <note>Decorative initial letter Γ</note>For they are full of many devices, and they are quick to perceive when they encounter unexpected snares. The <term>phlemys</term> <gloss>a type of fish, likely a species of bass or similar</gloss> is particularly clever, guileless, and prudent. It does not love the surfeit of sleep, but is sharp in its spirit and in its eyes. It endures winter twice over, and the harsher seasons, and loves the labors and the sea. For thus lives the brave and friendly [creature] of Hermes. The hunting is most fitting in the seasons of autumn, when the morning star rises. In winter, as it scatters along with the rays of the sun, it is captured, and all day long in the burgeoning spring, by manifold nets, it is raised when the season is full.

english: is the **seventy-fifth**. "By the Blessed One, it was said thus" is the **seventy-sixth**. Blessed One, "if a beginner person is to seek for the emptiness of essence, how should they be instructed and advised?" is the **seventy-seventh**. All these inquiries should be understood as being for the benefit of the non-returning Bodhisattvas present in that circle, and for the benefit of future generations. **Twenty-third volume** <note>term: bam po</note>. Regarding that, Subhūti, "form is profound" means that here, the suchness of form is expressed by the word "form." Therefore, when it was asked, "how is it profound?", [it means] "Subhūti, form is profound just as the suchness of form is [profound]." This shows it to be only suchness. The meaning is that form is called profound by the same manner in which suchness is profound. When it was asked, "Blessed One, what is the suchness of form?", what was intended? Suchness is without any characteristics. It neither has the characteristics of form and so on, nor is it dependent upon form and so on. Thus, the question was: "How can the suchness of form or the suchness of feeling be expressed by the words 'form' and so on?" "Subhūti, in that suchness of form, there is no form; yet apart from form, there is no suchness." This means that after abandoning the imagined <note>term: parikalpita</note>, the thoroughly established suchness <note>term: pariniṣpanna</note> that exists apart from the imagined is free from all characteristics, and it is improper to express it with terms like "form." For the sake of indicating the state of that suchness which ordinary foolish beings cannot distinguish from the imagined "form" and so on, it is designated through the convention of terms like "form."

### Canto 40
### The Duel between Ravana and Sugriva

Then Rama, surrounded by the monkey chiefs, ascended the two-yojana plateau of Suvela's summit. 1
Staying there for a moment and looking in the ten directions, he saw Laṅkā, built by <term>Vishvakarma</term> <gloss>the divine architect</gloss>, well-arranged and beautiful with pleasant forests. 2
He saw the unreachable lord of the demons, seated on the peak of the gate, wearing a white fan, decorated with a victory umbrella, anointed with red sandalwood, and adorned with gem ornaments. 3-4
He looked like a blue cloud, his garments covered in gold, his chest scarred by the tusks of <term>Airavata</term> <gloss>Indra's elephant</gloss>. 5
He was dressed in red silk, like the color of the sun at twilight, resembling a mass of clouds in the sky. 6
While the monkey kings and Rama were looking on, Sugriva, upon seeing the demon king, suddenly stood up. 7

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 245 regarding the physics of combustion and the "Crucial Instance" (a decisive experiment) to determine why gunpowder is so explosive. Bacon is currently discussing how certain substances react violently to heat because they naturally shrink away from flame.</meta>

# VERULAMII

->246<-

...flame <note>original: "flammam"; completing the word from the previous page.</note> they flee and shrink from, such as all **Salts**. For we see that if they are thrown into the **Fire**, the **Watery Spirit** <note>original: "Spiritum Aqueum"; in the science of this time, a "spirit" was a volatile substance or gas trapped within solids or liquids.</note> bursts out with a crash before the **Flame** is caught. This also happens gently in leaves that are a bit more stubborn, where the watery part bursts out before the oily part catches **Flame**. But this is seen most clearly in **Quicksilver** <note>original: "Argento vivo"; mercury.</note>, which is not poorly called **Mineral Water**. For this substance, without any actual catching of fire, through simple **Eruption** and **Expansion**, almost equals the strength of **Gunpowder** <term>Pulveris Pyrii</term>; it is even said that when mixed with gunpowder, it multiplies its power.

Similarly, let the <term>Nature under Investigation</term> <note>original: "Natura Inquisita"; the specific phenomenon Bacon is currently analyzing using his scientific method.</note> be the **Transitory Nature of Flame** and its **Momentary Extinction**. For the nature of flame does not seem to be fixed or consistent here in our world, but is generated at almost every single moment and immediately extinguished. It is clear that in **Flames** which continue and endure here, that duration is not the result of the same **Flame** existing as a single **Individual entity** <term>Individuo</term>, but occurs through a succession of new flames generated one after another; the flame by no means remains numerically the same. This is easily perceived from the fact that once the nourishment or fuel of the flame is withdrawn, the flame immediately perishes. The <term>Crossroads</term> <note>original: "Bivium"; a "fork in the road" or "crucial instance" where the researcher must choose between two competing explanations for a phenomenon.</note> concerning this nature is as follows: This **Momentary Nature** either occurs because the **Cause** that first generated it is diminishing—as happens with **Light**, **Sounds**, and so-called "violent" **Motions**—or it is because the **Flame**, though it could by its own **Nature** remain here with us, is from the con- <note>The text cuts off mid-word to be continued on the next page.</note>

པ་དེས་འགྲུབ་སྟེ། ལྷན་ཅིག་སྐྱེས་པ་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་བྱའོ། །དེ་ལ་གནས་ན་རྣལ་འབྱོར་པ་ཕྱག་རྒྱ་ཆེན་པོའི་དངོས་གྲུབ་འགྲུབ་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞེ་ན། ཕྱག་རྒྱའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་པ་སྟེ། རུང་བར་བྱས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རིག་པ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཕྱག་རྒྱ་ཆེན་པོའི་དངོས་གྲུབ་འགྲུབ་སྟེ་མཚན་ཉིད་
འགྲུབ་པ་ནི་གཙོ་བོའི་རྒྱུ་ཉིད་ཡིན་ལ། ཕྱག་རྒྱའི་སྦྱོར་བ་ནི་དེའི་ལྷན་ཅིག་བྱེད་པའི་རྐྱེན་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་ཡང་འདིར་དམ་ཚིག་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །རིག་པ་དང་སྐྱེས་བུའི་དངོས་གྲུབ་དང་། ཕྱག་རྒྱ་ཆེན་པོའི་དངོས་གྲུབ་ནི་རིགས་པའི་སྐྱེས་བུའི་དངོས་གྲུབ་སྟེ། འདིར་རིགས་ཀྱི་རིག་པ་མ་གཏོགས་
རྟོགས་པར་མི་སྲིད་པས་སོ། །དང་པོའི་ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་གསུམ་གྱི་དུས་སུ་དེ་མི་དགོངས་ཏེ། དེའི་ཚེ་རྣམ་པར་གཡེང་བར་བྱེད་པ་ཉིད་དོ། །འདི་ལྟར་ཞེས་པ་ནི་འདི་ལྟར་དབང་བསྐུར་བ་སྦྱིན་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་། འདི་ལྟར་ཡང་ཕྱག་རྒྱས་རྣལ་འབྱོར་པ་འགྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་དགོས་པ་འདིས་ཏེ། 
སློབ་མ་དབང་བསྐུར་བ་དང་། དངོས་གྲུབ་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བའི་དོན་དུ་དཀྱིལ་འཁོར་གསུངས་ཞེས་པ་ནི་དམ་ཚིག་གི་དཀྱིལ་འཁོར་དང་སྒྲུབ་པའི་དཀྱིལ་འཁོར་ཏེ། དེ་བསྟན་ཞེས་པའི་དོན་ཏོ། །དཀྱིལ་འཁོར་གྱི་ཁྱད་པར་ཟུང་བཞི་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་ནི་གོ་སླའོ། །ཤར་དུ་གཞག་
ཅེས་པ་ནི་དགོད་པའོ། །དཀྱིལ་འཁོར་བདག་པོའི་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པས་སྔོན་དུ་བསྙེན་པ་གསུངས་སོ། །དཀྱིལ་འཁོར་པའི་ཞེས་པ་ནི་དཀྱིལ་འཁོར་པ་སོ་སོའི་འོ། །གང་དུ་བརྗོད་པའི་ཞེས་པ་ནི་ཨོཾ་བཛྲ་རཀྵ་རཀྵ་ཧཱུཾ་ཕཊ་སྭཱ་ཧཱ། ཞེས་པ་འདིས་སོ། །སྔོན་དུ་ཞེས་པ་ནི་ས་སྦྱོང་བའི་སྔོན་
དུའོ། །ཨ་ལ་སོགས་སྔགས་ཞེས་པ་ནི་ཨོཾ་ཨ་ཀཱ་རོ་མུ་ཁཾ་སརྦ་དྷརྨཱ་ཎཱཾ། ཨཱདྱ་ནུཏྤན་ན་ཏྭཱཏ་ཨོཾ་ཨཱཿཧཱུཾ་ཕཊ་སྭཱ་ཧཱ། ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་སྔགས་འདིས་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་དོན་ཏོ། །སྲུང་བ་ཞེས་པ་ནི་ར་བ་དང་དྲ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའོ། །འདིས་ཞེས་པ་ནི་བྲི་བ་ན་ཡང་བླ་མ་ལ་མཆོད་པ་དང་གསོལ་བ་གདབ་པར་
བྱའོ། །འདིར་ཞེས་པ་ནི་རྟེན་གྱི་དཀྱིལ་འཁོར་བྲིས་བར་རོ། །རྡོ་རྗེ་སེམས་དཔའ་ནི་སེམས་བརྟན་པ་སྟེ་དེས་བསྙེམས་པའོ། །གཡས་བརྐྱང་ཞེས་པ་ནི་གཡས་བརྐྱང་བའོ། །རྐང་པ་ཞེས་པ་ནི་རྗེ་ངར་རོ། །དཀྱིལ་འཁོར་ཞེས་པ་ནི་དཀྱིལ་འཁོར་དུའོ། །ཕྱི་ནས་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཞེས་པ་ནི་བསྐྱེད་

Aṅguttara-Nikāya. XI.

Just as, venerable sir, a dust-cloth wipes clean things and wipes dirty things, wipes away excrement and wipes away urine, wipes away spittle and wipes away pus, and wipes away blood, yet the dust-cloth is not thereby troubled or disgusted: even so, venerable sir, do I dwell with a mind like a dust-cloth, extensive, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, without ill will. Whoever, venerable sir, has not established mindfulness of the body regarding his own body, he might offend a fellow practitioner here and depart on his travels without seeking forgiveness.

Just as, venerable sir, a young outcaste boy or girl, carrying a basket <note>original: "kaḷopihattho"</note> and wearing rags <note>original: "nantikavāsī"</note>, enters a village or town having set up a lowly mind: even so, venerable sir, do I dwell with a mind like a young outcaste, extensive, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, without ill will. Whoever, venerable sir, has not established mindfulness of the body regarding his own body, he might offend a fellow practitioner here and depart on his travels without seeking forgiveness.

Just as, venerable sir, a bull whose horns have been cut, who is gentle, well-tamed, and well-trained, wandering from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads, does not harm anyone with his foot or his horn: even so, venerable sir, do I dwell with a mind like a bull with cut horns, extensive, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, without ill will. english:
This means that the term "emptiness" is used to describe the emptiness of the impermanence of form. The same should be applied to all other phenomena.

After showing the accomplishment of non-abiding in this way, in order to show the faults of abiding, the text says: "Furthermore, O Bhagavan, when a <term>bodhisattva mahasattva</term> practices the Perfection of Wisdom, if through lack of skillful means they abide in form with a mind fallen into grasping at a self and grasping at things as 'mine', they are practicing the conceptualization of form, and are not practicing the Perfection of Wisdom," and so forth.

If, through lack of skillful means, one grasps inappropriately and does not know that phenomena are by nature without objective existence, and thus abides in form thinking "I am the essence of form," or "this form is me," or "this is the characteristic of suitability to be form," then that is the conceptualization of form. This means one is practicing according to the phenomena of mental formations that follow the conceptualization of form, rather than practicing the Perfection of Wisdom which follows the characteristic of emptiness.

To show the faults of practicing with conceptualization, it says: "practicing with conceptualization is not the meditation on the Perfection of Wisdom," and so forth.

One might ask: "Why is it that if one practices with conceptualization through lack of skillful means, having fallen into grasping at self and 'mine', one will not practice the Perfection of Wisdom, nor enter the yoga of non-apprehension, nor attain the realizations of final departure through perfection?" To this, the Bhagavan says: "O Bhagavan, it is like this: form is not something to be grasped," and so forth. This is called the "accomplishment of non-grasping."

This accomplishment is shown in three ways: not grasping at phenomena, not grasping at signs <note>original: "nimitta"</note>, and not grasping at knowledge.

Zu gleicher Weise, wie alle Dinge viel schädlicher sind, die man nicht bekennet, denn die man bekennet, also ist auch diese Gefahr, darauf man nicht viel hält noch achtet, als, die Gespielschaft, Gesellschaft oder Lust in Creaturen. Wie nun der Hirsch von einem jeglichen Gejage erhitziget wird, und sein Durst je mehr dadurch zunimmt, also soll der Mensch von einer jeglichen Bekörung mehr erhitziget werden nach göttlicher Liebe zu unserm Herrn, und in wahrem Durst gereizt oder gedrungen werden von jeglicher Anfechtung, je mehr und mehr in Gott zu laufen, wo er nichts findet, denn Wahrheit, Freude, Gerechtigkeit und Trost. *)

greatly, it must rot from this wound. The same happens to the person; when he defends himself against sins and has overcome them, the little hounds come, against which he does not intend to guard himself; these are the playmates, or the company, or the trinkets, or the entertainment of people, and the kindness of men; they tear him here and there, and mangle his heart and his inwardness, so that he must necessarily rot in all divine life and in divine seriousness, and he does not feel God's grace and devotion. This small temptation is often much more harmful to the person than the great afflictions, for the person guards himself against the latter with diligence and considers them wrong; but the person does not want to notice these small failings, nor consider them wrong. In the same way that all things are much more harmful that one does not confess than those one does confess, so is this danger also, which one does not hold or regard as much, such as companionship, society, or pleasure in creatures. As the deer is heated by every hunt, and its thirst increases all the more thereby, so the person should be heated by every temptation toward divine love for our Lord, and be incited or compelled by every affliction into a true thirst, to run more and more into God, where he finds nothing but truth, joy, justice, and comfort. *)

Now, sometimes hunters do this: when the deer is too tired and too thirsty, they feed the hounds a little, and they are thus held back; when they are sure of the deer in the animal park, they let the deer rest a little so that it is strengthened somewhat, so that it may then endure the hunting all the better. Our Lord does the same for the person; when he sees that the hunting is becoming too much for him and the affliction too great, he holds them back a little, and then a drop comes into the mouth of the person’s heart, that is, a sweet taste of the sweetness of divine things; these strengthen him so much that all things taste bitter and contrary to him that are not God, and then he thinks he has overcome all his need completely and entirely.

---

*) Ed. 1543.

english:
<meta>This page continues Augustine’s response to the philosopher Porphyry. Having previously cited pagan oracles that spoke well of Christ as a "pious man," Augustine now addresses Porphyry’s claim that Christians are in error for rejecting the worship of other spiritual beings or "demons."</meta>

### XIX

...warns concerning God and commands that he be worshipped everywhere. But the unlearned and those of such a nature to whom fate <term>fatum: In this context, Augustine is critiquing the Neoplatonic idea that some souls are destined to remain in ignorance, contrasted with Christian grace.</term> did not truly proceed from the Lord to obtain his gifts, nor to have a notion of the immortal Jupiter—not listening to either gods or divine men—have indeed rejected all gods. Yet, they have chosen not only to follow the forbidden demons with no hatred, but even to revere them. While pretending to worship God, they do not perform those things through which alone God is adored. For God indeed, as the father of all, needs nothing; but it is well for us when we adore him through justice, chastity, and other virtues, making our very life a prayer to him through imitation and instruction concerning him. "For instruction," he says, "purifies; imitation deifies by working the affection toward him." He [the oracle or philosopher] indeed preached well concerning God the Father and said by what morals he is to be worshipped. The prophetic books of the Hebrews are full of these precepts, whether the life of the holy ones is being praised or censured. But regarding the Christians, they err so much—or rather, he slanders them as much as the demons (whom he thinks are gods) desire—as if it were difficult for anyone to recall what filthy and disgraceful things were performed in service to the gods in theaters and temples <note>Augustine often contrasts the "obscenity" of Roman stage plays (which were part of religious festivals) with the moral sobriety of Christian worship.</note>, and to notice what is read, said, and heard in the churches, or what is offered to the true God; and from this to understand where the building up of morals lies and where their ruin. But who said this to him or inspired such a vain and obvious lie—that Christians revere rather than hate the demons whose worship was forbidden by the Hebrews—except a diabolical spirit? But that God whom the wise men of the Hebrews worshipped, and the holy heavenly angels and powers of God (whom we venerate and love as most blessed fellow-citizens in this our mortal pilgrimage), forbids sacrifice to be made to any other. He thundered this in his law which he gave to his Hebrew people, and he introduced it very threateningly, saying: *He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out.* <note>original: "Sacrificans diis eradicabitur" — Reference to Exodus 22:20.</note> And lest anyone should think it was commanded that sacrifice not be made to the worst demons and earthly spirits, whom that man [Porphyry] calls the least or lesser ones (who are themselves called "gods" in the holy scriptures, though not the gods of the Hebrews...

<column-break/>

...but of the Gentiles), the Seventy interpreters <note>Seventy interpreters: A reference to the Septuagint, the influential Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible used by the early Church.</note> clearly placed this in the Psalm, saying: *For all the gods of the Gentiles are demons.* <note>original: "Quoniam omnes dii gentium demonia" — Psalm 96:5 (LXX 95:5).</note> Therefore, lest anyone should think that while it was forbidden to sacrifice to these demons, it was permitted to sacrifice to either all or some of the heavenly beings, he immediately added: *except to the Lord only*; that is, to the Lord alone. This is to prevent someone from believing that because he said "to the Lord alone," one should think there is only one God to whom sacrifice is due <note>Augustine is clarifying that "the Lord" refers to the specific God of the Bible, not a generic monotheistic concept.</note>. That it should be understood this way is very easily found in the Greek scriptures. Therefore, the God of the Hebrews, to whom even this great philosopher provides such great testimony, gave a law to his Hebrew people, written in the Hebrew language; not obscure and unknown, but now spread abroad among all nations. In this law it is written: *He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, except to the Lord only.* What need is there to search out many things in his law and his prophets concerning this matter? Rather, there is no need to search, for they are not hidden or erased; it is easy to collect frequent and plain passages and place them in this discussion of mine, through which it appears clearer than light that the true and supreme God willed that sacrifice be offered to no one at all except to himself. Behold, let this one thing, spoken briefly—or rather grandly, threateningly, but truly—by that God whom the most learned of the pagans preach as so excellent, be heard: let it be feared; let it be fulfilled, lest the "rooting out" follow those who are disobedient. *He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out,* he says, *except to the Lord only.* Not because he has need of anything, but because it is beneficial for us that we should be his property. For to him it is sung in the sacred letters of the Hebrews: *I have said to the Lord, you are my God, for you have no need of my goods.* <note>original: "Dixi domino deus meus es tu: quoniam bonorum meorum non eges" — Psalm 16:2.</note> Moreover, we ourselves are his most noble and best sacrifice. This is his City <note>This is a foundational statement for the book's title: the "City of God" is not a physical place, but the community of the faithful who offer themselves to God.</note>, the mystery of which we celebrate with our offerings, which are known to the faithful, as we have discussed in the preceding books. For the oracles thundered through the Hebrew prophets that the animal sacrifices which the Jews offered as a "shadow of things to come" would cease, and that the nations from the rising of the sun to its setting would offer one single sacrifice, just as we now see being done.

<summary>Augustine argues that even pagan philosophers acknowledge the God of the Hebrews, yet they falsely claim Christians revere demons. He cites the Mosaic law to prove that sacrifice is reserved for the one true God alone, culminating in the idea that the Christian community itself is the ultimate sacrifice.</summary>
<keywords>Porphyry, demons, sacrifice, Hebrew Law, Exodus 22:20, City of God, Septuagint, worship, moral ruin vs building</keywords>

with some light medicine. And one must treat the ulcer either with bloody <note>remedies designed for wounds</note> dressings that are soaked, or with <term>polyophthalmia</term> <gloss>a plant with many buds/leaves</gloss>, or with those things with which fractured bones in the head are treated. 6 And one must not apply anything very cold. The first joints <note>fingers/toes</note> are therefore the least dangerous. 7 But those still higher are more dangerous. One must replace them on the same day or the day after. 8 On the third or fourth day, least of all. For being on the fourth day, they indicate the greatest possibility of relapses. 9 Therefore, for those in whom the replacement does not happen immediately, one must exceed these mentioned days. 10 Whoever replaces them within ten days, everything is within control. 11 If, however, a convulsion should befall one who has been replaced, one must quickly dislocate the joint. And soak it as often as possible with warm [substances], and keep the whole body warm, oily, and soft, especially around the joints. 12 The whole body should be bent rather than extended. One must expect, however, that the joints of the fingers which are being replaced will be prone to abscess. For most things happen this way, if even any inflammation should arise. 13 So that, if the doctor were not going to be blamed due to the ignorance of the common people, there would be no need to replace them at all. Therefore, bones protruding around the joints are dangerous if replaced, as has been said.

### LXXIX.
As many things as are cut off completely at the joints of the fingers, these for the most part are harmless, unless one is harmed by fainting during the very wounding. 2 And ordinary treatment will suffice for such ulcers. Moreover, even those that are not at the joints, but at another...

<column-break/>

with some light [medicine]. But one must treat the ulcer, either with bloody plasters which are soaked, or with the leaves of <term>polyophthalmos</term> or <term>buphthalmos</term> <gloss>ox-eye daisy</gloss> applied, or with those [remedies] with which bones in the head that are fractured are treated. 6 Do not apply anything very cold. The first joints are therefore the least dangerous. 7 But the higher ones are more dangerous. It is necessary to replace them on the same day or the day after: 8 On the third or fourth day, least of all. For on the fourth day they are accustomed to recrudesce <note>flare up</note> the most. 9 In those, however, for whom they have not been replaced immediately, one must pass beyond these mentioned days. For whatever has been replaced within ten days, all of that is contained. 10 If, however, a convulsion approaches a replaced bone, one must quickly eject the joint. And soak it as often as possible with warm [liquids], and treat the whole body, and especially around the joints, warmly and gently and softly. 11 Verily, the whole body ought to be bent rather than extended. One must expect, however, that the joints around the fingers which are replaced will abscess. For it usually happens in this way, if even any inflammation underlies it. 12 Wherefore, if a doctor were not to fear accusation on account of the ignorance of the masses, it would be necessary to replace none at all. english:
arising, and when they do not appear, there is no ceasing; even if it becomes one, there is no decrease, and even if it becomes many, there is no increase; and there is not the slightest affliction or purification in them. Likewise, because conceptually constructed essences are utterly non-existent, they have no arising or ceasing, and no increase, decrease, affliction, or purification. 

Enlightenment is also the thoroughly established essence. Since it is utterly solitary <note>empty of dualistic constructs</note>, transcending all conceptualization, and like space, it has no arising and no ceasing. It has no increase and no decrease. Because it is perfectly pure, it has no affliction. Because it is pure by nature, it has no purification. "Why is that?" This is shown by phrases such as: "Form is like an illusion, feeling is like an illusion," and so forth. This is shown in two ways: that the illusion does not exist, and that the consciousness apprehending the illusion does not exist. 

The statement that an illusion is merely a name and "does not reside in an object, nor does it reside in a direction" shows that because an illusion is conceptually constructed, it does not exist. The statement "Seeing an illusion is an error; it does not exist" shows that the consciousness <note>that perceives the illusion as real</note> does not exist. By "not residing in an object," it shows that an illusion does not have the characteristics of matter, because material phenomena do not fail to reside in an object. By "not residing in a direction," it shows that it does not have the characteristics of the formless. Although the formless phenomena like consciousness and so forth do not reside in an object, they are conventionally designated as residing in the direction of the eyes and so forth; thus they reside in a direction. The term "error" shows that it is not true. By "it does not exist," the characteristic of the non-existence of a thing is shown.

bent modi rebus per sanitate ingrenda ubi exocissimi

english: ...you shall recite it faithfully and act securely in the help of God. However, certain superstitious people and children of this world, wishing to heap error upon error, strive to defend themselves beyond the understanding and intention of Scotus and the canonists with these arguments: Because natural things have certain occult virtues whose cause cannot be assigned by man, such as the magnet attracting iron. And many other things which Augustine enumerates in Book 21 of The City of God. Therefore, these modes should be admitted for obtaining health where exorcisms and natural medicines fail; it will not be illicit if one sees it as vain. But if it were done where one wishes to procure health for oneself or another through images that are not necromantic or astrological, or through rings and such things. Also, he argues: Just as natural bodies are subject to celestial bodies, so also artificial bodies, such as images, acquire certain occult virtues, pursuing hope from the impression of celestial bodies; therefore, artificial bodies, such as images, also acquire some occult virtues from celestial bodies to cause certain effects; therefore, to use them and other such things is not illicit. Furthermore, demons can transmute bodies in many ways, as Augustine says in Book 3 of De Trinitate, and it is evident in the bewitched; therefore, it is licit to use even their power to remove those things. But, in truth, the words of all the holy doctors are to the contrary, and it has been shown here and there. Wherefore, to the first, it is said that if natural things are simply applied to produce some effects for which they are thought to have a natural virtue, it is not illicit. But if they add any characters or any other unknown and vain observations that clearly have no natural efficacy for this, it will be superstitious and illicit, as Thomas Aquinas treats in the Summa Theologica, Part 2-2, Question 96, Article 2, at the end of the question.

جمع گشته بر سرای شاه خلق
از شتاب او فحش اجتهاد
آن یکی دو دست بر افروزنان
از نفیر و فتنه و خوف و نکال
هر کسی فالی همی زد از قیاس
راه جست و راه داد شاه زود
هر که می پرسید حالی زان ترش
وهم می فروزد این فرهنگ او
کرد اشارت دلقک تا شاه کرم
تا که باز آید بس عقل دم دمی
بعد یک ساعت که شه از وهم ظن
کوندیده بود دلقک را چنین
دائماً دستان و لاغ افراشتی

که ز زور خنده خوی کردی تنش

وهم در وهم و خیال اندر خیال
که دل شه با غم و پرهیز بود
بس شهان آن طرف را کشته بود
این شه تر مداز در وهم بود
گفت زوتر باز گو تا حال چیست
گفت من در ده شنیدم انکه شاه
که کسی خواهم که تاز در سه روز
کنج ها بستم و را اندر عوض
من شتابیدم برو بهر آن
اینچنین پستی نیاید از چومن

شورش در و هم آن سلطان فاد
تا چه تشویش و بلا حادث شدست
یا بلای ملکی از غیب خاست
چند اسب تازی از در راه کشت
تا چرا آمد چنین اشتاب لق
غلغل و تشویش در تر مد فاد
وان دگر از وهم و اویلا کنان
هر دلی رفته به صد گونه خیال
تا چه آتش افتاد اندر پلاس

جمله در تشویش گشته دنگ او
یکدمی بگزار تا من دم زنم
که فتادم در عجایب عالمی
تلخ گشتش هم گلو و هم دهن
که از خوشتر نبودش همنشین
شاه را او شاد و خندان داشتی
که گرفتی شه شکم را باد و بست
رو در افتادی زخنده کردنش
دست بر لب میزند کای شه خموش
شاه را تا خود چه آید از نکال
زانکه خوارزم شاه بس خونریز بود
یا حمیله یا بسطوت آن عنود
وز فن دلقک خود آن وهم فزود
اینچنین آشوب و شور تو زکیست
زد منادی بر سر هر شاه راه
تا سمرقند و دو هم و اگر هنوز
چون شود حاصل ز پیغام غرض
تا بگویم من ندارم آن توان
تار این امید را بر من متن

دو شدی فترت جمله دیوانه هم

کلدی دلقک سرعت اوزره پیچ پیچ

اکه یول ویردی حضور چونکه شاه
حالی لندن کیم صورور سه پر تلاش

دلقک اشارت ایتدی ای شاه کرم

کجدی بر ساعتکه شاهی و هم و ظن

خنده خوی ایتدی ایدکچه سخن

وهم و هم اوزره خیال اوزره خیال

اول کیاچوق شاهی ایتدی بی وجود

دیدی بن کویده ایتدم اید شاه
کیم بر آدم استرم اوچ کونده تا
کنجلر ویروب اکا ایدیم عوض
بن شتاب ایتدم انک ایچون همان

مورث و هم اولکد اول سلطانه هم
کیم نه تشویش و بلا ایتدی ظهور
غیبدن یا کلدی بر مملکت بلا
یولده بوجه اسب تازی اولدی هیچ
نچون ایتدی سرعتی تصغیر دلق
ترمدی ایتدی مشوش چساب
اول بر و اویل کوی و موی کن
دو شد هر بر قابه یوز دور لو خیال
دیر لایدی تشه دو شد پلاس
اوپدی یر دیدی مدیر پیغام راه
دست بر لب بر اید خاموش باش
جلدی تشویش ایتد دنگ و لال
باکه رخصت ویر نفس ایلیم
بر عجایب حالمه دو شد دمان
تلخ ایدوب خشک ایدے کیم ایله من
اندن علا یوق ایدے بر شوخ و شنگ
شاه اکله شاد و خنده رو ایدی
کیم اولوردی دستی اطینده دو تا
شه یوکر اوزره دو شد خنده دن
دست بر لب ایلیه یعنی خموش
شاه ایرات ایلیرمی انفعال
باعثی خوارزم شه خونریز ایدی
قهر ایله یا حمیله ایله اول عنود
وضع دلقک ویره افزون همناک
کیمدن آشوب که بوشور و ملال
ایلمش امر ندابی اشتباه
اول سمرقنده واره آلسون عطا
پس خبر دن حاصل اولدقه غرض
کیم دیم یوق بنده اول تا به توان
بندن امید ایلیه بو خدمتی

english:
The proclamation of the Sayyid of the Malak of Tirmidh, that whoever goes to Samarkand in three or four days, for a certain task, [will receive] a robe, horse, slave, and slave girl, and several [pieces of] gold and silver; and the hearing of this proclamation by the clown in the village, and the buffoon coming to the King, saying: "I can go; this task is not [for me]."

The Sayyid of Tirmidh, who was the king there,
Had a task and important business in Samarkand,
He made a proclamation: "Whoever [can get there] in five days,"
The clown in the village heard that,
Two mounts died on that road,
Then he ran and saw [it] from the struggle.

The jester, he was an aware clown,
He searched for a city to become that oppression,
I brought news from there, treasures together,
He sat and ran until he was weary,
From [the] two, the horse became [spent] from that path,
At an untimely time, he sought the road and the king's court.

The Sayyid of Tirmidh, who was the king there,
Until the interior of Samarkand fell into confusion,
He found, he made a cry: "Five days,"
The clown in the village heard this order,
He made two mounts perish on that road,
He entered, crazy with the dust of the road.

The buffoonery of the clown was aware,
He sought a place, he was that oppressed one,
From there he brings news, I will be kind,
He made an effort and clamor on the road,
With the speed of travel, that shore remained,
The king at an untimely hour intended to arrive.

Ὡς ὁ μὲν Ἰνδῴοιο παρὰ ῥάχιν εὔβοτον ὕλης
Ἔζεε Βάκχος ὅμιλος ἐρημάδος ἀστὸς ἐρείκης,
Ἀμβολίῃ πολέμοιο· φόβῳ δ᾽ ἐλελίζετο Γάγγης,
<margin>5</margin>Οἰκτείρων ἑὰ τέκνα· νεοφθιμένων δ᾽ ἐπὶ πότμῳ

Ἤδη γὰρ κλύε πάντα· τὸ δὲ πλέον ὄμματι λοξῷ
<margin>10</margin>Ἄχνυτο παπταίνων ὅτι θέσκελον εἶδος ἀμείψας.
Οἴνῳ κυματόεντι μέλας κελάρυζεν Ὑδάσπης·
Καί θι καὶ εὐῤῥέεος ἑὸν πόδα νωθρὸν ἐλίσσων·
Καὶ πυρὸς ἀχλυόεσσαν ἔχων ἀλαωπὸν ὁμίχλην
Ξανθινῷ λυσιπόνοιο μέθης ἐῤῥαίνεν ἐέρσην
<margin>15</margin>Ὄμμασι κολλητῆσιν· ἀρυομένῳ δὲ προσώπῳ
Οἰνωπὰς ῥαθάμιγγας ἀνῴχθησαν ὀπωπαί·
Τερπμένους δὲ πόδεσσι, γέρων ἐχόρευε λιγαίνων
Ἰκμάδα φοινίσσουσαν ἀλεξικάκου ποταμοῖο·
Χερσὶ δ᾽ ἡγηλαίῃσι ῥέον νεφεληδὸν ἀφύσσων,
<margin>20</margin>Πορφυρέης ἔπλησε μέθης εὐώδεας ἀσκούς,
Καὶ Διῒ βωμὸν ἅνψε καὶ οἰνοχύτῳ Διονύσῳ·
Ληθήσας Φαέθοντος ἀήθεος ὄψιμον αἴγλην,
Καὶ κώας οἰνωθέντας ἐπ᾽ ἤϊσι κοῦρος ἐάσας,
Λαρὸν ὕδωρ λάπτοντας ἐρευθομένῳ ποταμοῖο·

Ἀγάλλον γλυκὺ χεῦμα μεθυσφαλίος ποταμοῖο·
Ἤδη οἱ ἀμπελόεσσα δι᾽ ἄστεος ἔτρεχεν ὀδμή,
Καὶ λιγυροῖς ἀνέμοισιν ὅλας ἐμέθυσεν ἀγυιάς·
<margin>30</margin>Νικίῳ ἱδροφόνοιο περισκαίρουσα Λυαίῳ·

Δειδιότες μὴ τεῖχος ἐμιτρώσαντο βοείαις

So that I may kill with a wise spear the remnants of the Indians;
for Bacchus sat there, near the fertile ridge of the Indian forest,
a citizen of the desert wilderness,
in the delay of war. And Ganges trembled with fear,
<margin>5</margin> pitying his own children; and upon the fate of those recently perished,
the whole city was shaken; and the streets resounded
with the mournful clatter of the lamenting women.
And fear and amazement and shame shook Deriades;
for he had already heard everything; and he was distressed
<margin>10</margin> looking with a sidelong eye because he had changed a divine form.
The black Hydaspes murmured with wine-like waves;
And there, rolling his own sluggish foot of the flowing river,
And having the gloomy mist of fire,
he sprinkled the yellow dew of the drunkenness that releases pains
<margin>15</margin> with sticky eyes. And with the drawing countenance,
wine-like drops were opened in his eyes;
and delighting with his feet, the old man danced, singing
of the reddening moisture of the evil-averting river.
And with his old hands, drawing the stream like clouds,
<margin>20</margin> he filled the sweet-smelling skins with purple drunkenness,
and he lit an altar to Zeus and to the wine-pouring Dionysus;
forgetting the late radiance of unaccustomed Phaethon,
and leaving the wine-drunk sheep on the shores, the youth
lapping the sweet water of the reddening river.
<margin>25</margin> A hunter, a companion of the mountain-dwelling Archeress <note>Diana/Artemis</note>,
bent his path into the city to the disobedient Deriades,
rejoicing in the sweet stream of the wine-erring river.
Already the vineyard-scent was running through the city,
and in the clear winds, it intoxicated the whole town,
<margin>30</margin> dancing around Lyaeus <note>Dionysus</note>, who brings the victory of the Indian-slaughter.
And the citizens were dwelling in the high towers,
fearing lest the guards of the high-crested city
might have girded the wall with ox-hides, and towards the hills...

<summary>Dionysus transforms the river Hydaspes into wine, causing confusion among the Indian inhabitants and signaling his impending victory.</summary>

english:
836. "If you do not desire such a jewel as this,
a woman desired by many kings,
what do you say of your view of life,
and your becoming?" 2.

837. "There is no 'this is what I say' for him,"
said the Blessed One, Māgandiya,
"concerning things firmly held;
seeing that there is no attachment to views,
I sought inner peace and saw nothing." 3.

838. "Those determinations which are imagined,
thus Māgandiya spoke,
you call those things attachments,
as for this 'inner peace,'
how is it explained by the wise?" 4.

839. "Not by view, not by what is heard, not by knowledge,"
said the Blessed One, Māgandiya,
"nor by virtuous conduct and rites does one claim purity.
Without view, without hearing, without knowledge,
without virtuous conduct, without rites, and not even by that,
having set these aside, without attachment,
the peaceful one does not long for existence." 5.

840. "If indeed you do not say purity comes from view, hearing, or knowledge,"
thus Māgandiya spoke,
"nor from virtuous conduct and rites,
without view, without hearing, without knowledge,
without virtuous conduct, without rites, and not even by that,
I think this is a delusion,
others think purity comes from view." 6.

because the path is neither entity nor non-entity, the result, Buddha, is also not an entity; that is the characteristic of the exhaustion of all afflictions without exception. "That itself" refers to the Buddha. "Nor is it the manner of a non-entity" refers to the Truth Body itself, which is the nature of the perfectly pure primordial wisdom of one taste. "The aspect of faces and hands" refers to the Enjoyment and Emanation bodies. From what does the formless arise? It is the "holy bliss," meaning it is even through enjoying the "bliss of the Dharma" of the Truth Body. Because of that, the result is neither entity nor non-entity. Therefore, all beings are co-emergent joy; that co-emergent joy is connected to the co-emergence of Buddhahood itself. "All beings" refers to all sentient beings. If one wonders why it is called the "co-emergence of Buddhahood itself," it is said: **Co-emergent**, and so forth. "Nature" <note>original: "prakṛti"</note> and "essence" <note>original: "svabhāva"</note> are synonyms for the word "co-emergent" <term>sahaja</term>. This refers to the principal Truth Body of Buddhahood. Regarding that, it is said: **perfectly pure**, and so forth. "Perfectly pure" is the very nature of stainless luminosity. The mind is that which possesses its aspect. Because its nature is its essence, it is spoken of in that way. That very nature is Nirvana; it is the perfectly pure nature and it is also the mind. Since it is ultimately pure and in Nirvana, it is not an entity. Since the mind itself is the perfectly pure nature, it is also not a non-entity; this is the intended meaning. By this, it is taught that through the mind being luminous by nature, the seed of Buddhahood is established from beginningless time. "Well then, at that time the Complete Enjoyment Body would be without a seed, because an ordinary body belongs to that very body and is of a discordant type," if one thinks this, it is said: **The deity's**, and so forth. Here too, the word "deity's form" refers to its very seed.

<summary>The author argues that the result of the path, Buddhahood, transcends the duality of entity and non-entity. He identifies the mind's luminous nature as the beginningless seed of Buddha-nature (Tathāgatagarbha) present in all beings.</summary>
<keywords>entity, non-entity, Truth Body, co-emergent, luminosity, Nirvana, seed of Buddhahood</keywords>

△答中有三謂舉數辨相總結
答曰是因緣有八種云何為八
△辨相中初一是總後七是別所以爾者總通兼正

一者因緣總相所謂為令眾生離一切苦得究竟樂

english:
A question arises: What causes and conditions led to the creation of this treatise?
△ In the answer, there are three parts: listing the number, distinguishing the characteristics, and providing a summary.
The answer is: These causes and conditions are of eight types. What are these eight?
△ Regarding the distinction of characteristics, the first is the general one, and the subsequent seven are specific. The reason for this is that the general one encompasses and clarifies the primary purpose, while the specific ones are intended for the recipients of the teaching; therefore, it must be so.
First, the general cause and condition is the desire to enable sentient beings to leave behind all suffering and attain the ultimate happiness. Leaving behind all suffering in the general sense means enabling sentient beings to depart from the three types of suffering and the two types of death. Attaining the ultimate happiness means enabling them to attain supreme enlightenment, the happiness of great <term>nirvana</term> <gloss>extinction of suffering/transmigration</gloss>, and so forth, rather than seeking worldly fame and profit. This has two interpretations. First, it is not to encourage them to seek the profit and happiness of humans and gods in future lives.

When his flesh rotted, an enemy to his own enemy, it flowed out heavily and in great quantity, so that neither the discharge nor the audacity of the physician could hide the sickly, swirling corruption. Constantly slipping and rushing, it consumed his whole body, from which he was given over to madness and rage, until the spirit, up to the very vitals, was torn apart by the spreading of the disease. Not even thus was Clearchus <note>referring to the previous tyrant</note> cleared of the punishments he was perceived by those who saw him to be announcing, which he had lawlessly inflicted upon the citizens. For they often say that in his sickness, death came upon him, but it did not, and for seven days he was consumed by the bitter and heavy disease. Thus, the curse slipped away, and the six years which the tyranny held passed. Agesilaus was king of the Lacedaemonians at that time. This Timotheus, having received the rule, adjusted it toward a gentler and more democratic form, so that he was no longer called a tyrant, but a benefactor by those things he did. He resolved the debts for the men, and for those who needed [funds] for trade and other life, he assisted without hesitation. And he was not only a deliverer of those in prison, but also an accurate judge for those who were unworthy <note>of their status or legal standing</note>, and he was kind. In other matters, he was useful and did not turn away from petitions. He treated his brother Dionysius <note>also referred to as Dionusios</note> in these matters bitterly, but he held him as a partner in the rule, though not as a successor. तमुपनिधिं राज्ञा दैवेनोदकादिना तस्करैर्वापहृतं नष्टं न दाप्योऽसौ यस्मिन्नुपहितं । धनिन एव तद्द्रव्यं नष्टं यदि जिह्मकारितं न भवति । यथाह **नारदः**— 'ग्रहीतुः सह योऽर्थेन नष्टो नष्टः स दायिनः । दैवराजकृते तद्वन्न चेत्तज्जिह्मकारितम् ॥' इति ॥

अस्यापवादमाह—

### भ्रेषश्चेन्मार्गितेऽदत्ते दाप्यो दण्डं च तत्समम् ॥ ६६ ॥

स्वामिना मार्गिते याचिते यदि न ददाति तदा तदुत्तरकालं यद्यपि राजादिभिर्भ्रेषो नाशः संजातस्तथापि तद्द्रव्यं मूल्यकल्पनया धनिने ग्रहीता दाप्यो राज्ञे च तत्समं दण्डम् ॥ ६६ ॥

भोक्तारं प्रति दण्डमाह—

### आजीवन्स्वेच्छया दण्ड्यो दाप्यस्तं चापि सोदयम् ।

यः स्वेच्छया स्वाम्यननुज्ञयोपनिहितं द्रव्यमाजीवन्मुपभुङ्क्ते व्यवहरति वा प्रयोगादिना लाभार्थमसावुपभोगानुसारेण लाभानुसारेण च दण्ड्यस्तं चोपनिधिं सोदयमुपभोगे सवृद्धिकं व्यवहारे सलाभं धनिने दाप्यः । वृद्धप्रमाणं च **कात्यायनेनोक्तम्**— 'निक्षेपं वृद्धिशेषं च क्रयं विक्रयमेव च । याच्यमानो न चेद्दद्याद्वर्धते पञ्चकं शतम् ॥' इति । एतच्च भक्षिते द्रष्टव्यम् । उपेक्षाज्ञाननष्टे तु तेनैव विशेषो दर्शितः— 'भक्षितं सोदयं दाप्यः समं दाप्य उपेक्षितम् । किंचिन्न्यूनं प्रदाप्यः स्याद्द्रव्यमज्ञाननाशितम् ॥' इति । किंचिन्न्यूनमिति चतुर्थांशहीनम् ॥

उपनिधेर्धर्मान्याचितादिष्वतिदिशति—

### याचितान्वाहितन्यासनिपेक्षादिष्वयं विधिः ॥ ६७ ॥

विवाहाद्युत्सवेषु वस्त्रांलंकारादि याचित्वानीतं **याचितम्** । यदेकस्य हस्ते निहितं द्रव्यं तेनाप्यनु पश्चादन्यहस्ते स्वामिने देहीति निहितं तद**न्वाहितम्** । **न्यासो** नाम गृहस्वामिनेऽदर्शयित्वा तत्परोक्षमेव गृहजनहस्ते प्रक्षेपो गृहस्वामिने समर्पणीयमिति । समक्षं तु समर्पणं **निक्षेपः** । आदिशब्देन सुवर्णकारादिहस्ते कटकादिनिर्माणाय न्यस्तस्य सुवर्णादेः, प्रतिन्यासस्य च परस्परप्रयोजनापेक्षया त्वयेदं मदीयं रक्षणीं मयेदं त्वदीयं रक्ष्यते इति न्यस्तस्य ग्रहणम् । यथाह **नारदः**— 'एष एव विधिर्दृष्टो याचितान्वाहितादिषु । शिल्पेषूपनिधौ न्यासे प्रतिन्यासे तथैव च ॥' इति । एतेषु याचितान्वाहितादिष्वयं विधिः उपनिधेर्यः प्रतिदानादिविधिः स एव वेदितव्यः ॥ ६७ ॥

<header>Section on Deposits 4 ] with the Mitakshara Commentary.</header>
<sig>Yājñavalkya 17</sig>

If that deposit is seized or lost by the King, by an act of God such as water, or by thieves, the person with whom it was deposited shall not be made to pay. The loss of that wealth belongs to the owner himself, provided it was not caused by the holder's deceit <term>jihma</term>. As **Narada** says: "That which is lost along with the property of the receiver is the loss of the giver. It is the same if caused by an act of God or the King, unless it was caused by deceit." 

He states an exception to this:

### If there is a loss after it has been demanded but not given, he shall be made to pay its value and an equal fine. 66.

If the holder does not return it when it has been "demanded"—requested by the owner—and if a loss <term>bhreṣa</term> occurs after that time through the King or similar causes, the receiver must be made to pay the value of the wealth to the owner, and a fine of equal value to the King. 66.

He states the punishment for one who uses the deposit:

### If he lives off it by his own will, he should be fined and made to pay it back with interest.

One who, by his own will and without the owner's permission, "lives off it"—meaning he enjoys the deposited wealth or deals with it through lending or similar means for profit—should be fined according to the degree of enjoyment or the amount of profit. He must also be made to pay that deposit to the owner along with the "increase" <term>udaya</term>—with interest in the case of enjoyment, and with profit in the case of business dealings. 

The standard for interest was stated by **Katyayana**: 
> "If one does not give a bailment <term>nikṣepa</term>, the remainder of interest, a purchase, or a sale when it is being demanded, it increases at five percent." 

This should be understood to apply when the object has been consumed <term>bhakṣita</term>. But in the case of loss due to negligence or ignorance, the same author shows a distinction: 
> "For what is consumed, he should be made to pay with interest; for what is neglected, he pays the same amount <term>samam</term>. For property lost through ignorance, he should be made to pay slightly less." 

"Slightly less" means reduced by one-fourth. 

He extends the rules of deposits to "borrowed items" <term>yācita</term> and the like:

### This is the rule for items borrowed, items handed over, trusts, and bailments. 67.

An item requested and brought for a festival like a wedding, such as clothing or ornaments, is "borrowed" <term>yācitam</term>. Wealth placed in one person's hand, which is then placed by him into another's hand with the instruction "give this to the owner," is "handed over" <term>anvāhitam</term>. A "trust" <term>nyāsa</term> is the act of dropping something into the hands of the household members in the absence of the master of the house, without showing it to him, so that it may be handed to him later. But handing it over in his presence is a "bailment" <term>nikṣepa</term>. 

By the word "and the like" <term>ādi</term>, this includes gold or similar material placed in the hands of a goldsmith for the manufacture of bracelets, and "mutual trusts" <term>pratinyāsa</term>—where, for mutual benefit, one says "protect this of mine and I shall protect this of yours." 

As **Narada** says: "This very rule is seen for borrowed items, handed-over items, and the like; for artisan's work, deposits, trusts, and mutual trusts likewise." In these cases—borrowed items, handed-over items, etc.—this very rule of deposits regarding returning the item and so on should be understood. 67.

<meta>This page continues the biography of Sisinnius, the Novatian bishop of Constantinople, known for his wit and urbanity. It follows the discussion of the omens and political shifts following the exile of John Chrysostom.</meta>

### SOCRATES SCHOLASTICUS, BOOK VI

...it frequently happened that he avoided the [trap of] cleverness in debate. Regarding his lifestyle, he was not simple <note>original: "λιτός" — referring to an ascetic or plain way of living</note>, but he practiced luxury with extreme self-control. He delighted in wearing **white clothing**, and he continued the habit of bathing twice a day in the public baths. Once, when someone asked him why he, as a bishop, bathed twice a day, he replied, "Because I do not have time for a third."

On another occasion, while seeing **Sergius** the bishop <note>likely the Novatian bishop of another see</note>, he was asked by one of those in the circle of **Arsacius** <note>The bishop who replaced John Chrysostom</note> why he wore clothing unsuitable for a bishop, and where it was written that a priest should dress in white. He said, "You tell me first where it is written that a bishop must wear black clothing." When the questioner was at a loss for an answer, **Sisinnius** followed up his counter-question: "You would not be able to show that a priest must dress in black. But **Solomon** advised me, saying, 'Let your garments be white' <note>Ecclesiastes 9:8</note>. And the Savior in the Gospels is shown wearing white clothing. Furthermore, he showed **Moses** and **Elijah** to the Apostles wearing white." Having said these things and many others quite readily, he was greatly admired by those present.

When **Leontius**, the bishop of **Ancyra** in **Galatia**, was seizing a church from the **Novatians** <note>The Novatians were a rigorist Christian sect who believed those who fell into serious sin after baptism could not be readmitted to communion</note> and happened to be visiting **Constantinople**, **Sisinnius** went to him and urged him to return the church. **Leontius** answered him warmly <note>meaning with heat or anger</note> and said to him, "You **Novatians** ought not to have churches, for you do away with repentance and shut out the mercy of God." As **Leontius** said these things and more against the **Novatians**, **Sisinnius** replied, "Indeed, no one has ever repented as much as I have." When **Leontius** asked him again, "How have you repented?" **Sisinnius** replied, "That I ever came to see you!"

On another occasion, when **John** <note>John Chrysostom</note> the bishop was accusing him of something and saying that a city could not have two bishops, **Sisinnius** said, "It does not." When **John** grew angry and said, "Do you see that you admit I am the only bishop in your opinion?" **Sisinnius** replied, "I do not say that; rather, I mean that I am not a bishop to you alone, though I am a bishop to the ears [of my own people]." **John**, becoming indignant at this remark, said, "I will stop you from speaking, for you are a heretic." To this, **Sisinnius** wittily replied, "I would even pay you a reward if you would relieve me of such great labor!" **John**, softened by this response, said, "I will not stop you from your freedom of speech if speaking is so painful to you." 

Such was the readiness and wit of **Sisinnius** in his replies. To write down and record all the things he said would be a long task. Therefore, through these few examples, I have shown what kind of man he was when he took up leadership. I say this: everyone knows him for his education, and because of this, all the bishops in succession loved and honored him. Not only that, but all the distinguished members of the Senate loved and admired him. Many books have been written by him, but he uses a specific style in them, mixing in poetic vocabulary. He was admired more when speaking than when being read, for there was such grace in him—in his face, his voice, his posture, his look, and the whole movement of his body. He was loved for these reasons by all religions, and especially by Bishop **Atticus**. These are the matters concerning **Sisinnius**.

# पराभिध्यानात्तु तिरोहितं ततो ह्यस्य बन्धविपर्ययौ ।। 3.2.5 ।।

।। 3.2.5 ।।

अथापि स्यात् -- परस्यैव तावदात्मनोंऽशः जीवः -- अग्नेरिव विस्फुलिङ्गः; तत्रैवं सति यथा अग्निविस्फुलिङ्गयोः समाने दहनप्रकाशनशक्ती भवतः, एवं जीवेश्वरयोरपि ज्ञानैश्वर्यशक्ती; ततश्च जीवस्य ज्ञानैश्वर्यवशात् सांकल्पिकी स्वप्ने रथादिसृष्टिर्भविष्यतीति। अत्रोच्यते -- सत्यपि जीवेश्वरयोरंशांशिभावे प्रत्यक्षमेव जीवस्येश्वरविपरीतधर्मत्वम्। किं पुनर्जीवस्य ईश्वरसमानधर्मत्वं नास्त्येव? न नास्त्येव; विद्यमानमपि तत् तिरोहितम् अविद्यादिव्यवधानात्। तत्पुनस्तिरोहितं सत् परमेश्वरमभिध्यायतो यतमानसय जन्तोर्विधूतध्वान्तस्य -- तिमिरतिरस्कृतेव दृक्शक्तिः औषधवीर्यात् -- ईश्वरप्रसादात् संसिद्धस्य कस्यचिदेवाविर्भवति, न स्वभावत एव, सर्वेषां जन्तूनाम्; कुतः? ततो हि ईश्वराद्धेतोः, अस्य जीवस्य, बन्धमोक्षौ भवतः -- ईश्वरस्वरूपापरिज्ञानात् बन्धः, तत्स्वरूपपरिज्ञानात्तु मोक्षः। तथा च श्रुतिः -- 'ज्ञात्वा देवं सर्वपाशापहानिः क्षीणैः क्लेशैर्जन्ममृत्युप्रहाणिः। तस्याभिध्यानात्तृतीयं देहभेदे विश्वैश्वर्यं केवल आप्तकामः' इत्येवमाद्या ।।

# देहयोगाद्वा सोऽपि ।। 3.2.6 ।।

।। 3.2.6 ।।

कस्मात्पुनर्जीवः परमात्मांश एव सन् तिरस्कृतज्ञानैश्वर्यो भवति? युक्तं तु ज्ञानैश्वर्ययोरातिरस्कृतत्वम्, विस्फुलिङ्गस्येव दहनप्रकाशनयोः -- इति। उच्यते -- सत्यमेवैतत्; सोऽपि तु जीवस्य ज्ञानैश्वर्यतिरोभावः, देहयोगात् देहेन्द्रियमनोबुद्धिविषयवेदनादियोगात् भवति। अस्ति च अत्रोपमा -- यथा अग्नेर्दहनप्रकाशनसंपन्नस्याप्यरणिगतस्य दहनप्रकाशने तिरोहिते भवतः, यथा वा भस्मच्छन्नस्य -- एवमविद्याप्रत्युपस्थापितनामरूपकृतदेहपाधियोगात् तद्विवेकभ्रमकृतो जीवस्य ज्ञानैश्वर्यतिरोभावः। वा-शब्दो जीवस्य ईश्वरात् अन्यत्वशङ्काव्यावृत्त्यर्थः। नन्वन्य एव जीवः ईश्वरादस्तु, तिरस्कृतज्ञानैश्वर्यत्वात्; किं देहयोगकल्पनया? नेत्युच्यते -- न हि अन्यत्वं जीवस्य ईश्वरादुपपद्यते -- 'सेयं देवतैक्षत' इत्युपक्रम्य 'अनेन जीवेनात्मनानुप्रविश्य' इत्यात्मशब्देन जीवस्य परामर्शात्; 'तत् सत्यं स आत्मा तत्त्वमसि श्वेतकेतो' इति च जीवाय उपदिशति ईश्वरत्वम्; अतः अनन्य एव ईश्वराञ्जीवः सन् देहयोगात्तिरोहितज्ञानैश्वर्यो भवति। अतश्च न सांकल्पिकी जीवस्य स्वप्ने रथादिसृष्टिर्घटते; यदि च सांकल्पिकी स्वप्ने रथादिसृष्टिः स्यात्, नैवानिष्टं कश्चित्स्वप्नं पश्येत्, न हि कश्चिदृनिष्टं संकल्पयते। यत्पुनरुक्तम् -- जागरितदेशश्रुतिः स्वप्नस्य सत्यत्वं ख्यापयतीति, न तत्साम्यवचनं सत्यत्वाभिप्रायम्, स्वयंज्योतिष्ट्वविरोधात्, श्रुत्यैव च स्वप्ने रथाद्यभावस्य दर्शितत्वात्; जागरितप्रभववासनानिमित्तत्वात् स्वप्नस्य तत्तुल्यनिर्भासत्वाभिप्रायं तत्। तस्मादुपपन्नं स्वप्नस्य मायामात्रत्वम् ।।

# तदभावो नाडीषु तच्छ्रुतेरात्मनि च ।। 3.2.7 ।।

तदभावाधिकरणम् ।। 3.2.7 ।।

स्वप्नावस्था परीक्षिता; सुषुप्तावस्थेदानीं परीक्ष्यते। तत्रैताः सुषुप्तविषयाः श्रुतयो भवन्ति; क्वचिच्छूयते -- 'तद्यत्रैतत्सुप्तः समस्तः संप्रसन्नः स्वप्नं न विजानात्यासु तदा नाडीषु सुप्तो भवति' इति; अन्यत्र तु नाडीरेवानुक्रम्य श्रूयते -- 'ताभिः प्रत्यवसृप्य पुरीतति शेते' इति; तथान्यत्र नाडीरेवानुक्रम्य -- 'तासु तदा भवति यदा सुप्तः स्वप्नं न कंचन पश्यत्यथास्मिन्प्राण एवैकधा भवति' इति; तथान्यत्र -- 'य एषोऽन्तर्हृदय आकाशस्तस्मिञ्छेते' इति; तथान्यत्र -- 'सतासोम्य तदा संपन्नो भवति स्वमपीतो भवति' इति; तथा -- 'प्राज्ञेनात्मना संपरिष्वक्तो न बाह्यं किंचन वेद नान्तरम्' इति च ।।

तत्र संशयः -- किमेतानि नाड्यादीनि परस्परनिरपेक्षतया भिन्नानि सुषुप्तिस्थानानि, आहोस्वित्परस्परसापेक्षतया एकं सुषुप्तिस्थानमिति। किं तावत्प्राप्तम्? भिन्नानीति; कुतः? एकार्थत्वात् -- न हि एकार्थानां क्वचित्परस्परसापेक्षत्वं

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the dream state (svapna) and the nature of the individual soul in relation to the Supreme Lord. Having previously argued that dreams are not objective realities like the waking world, the text now addresses why the soul, though divine in essence, lacks the creative power of God during sleep, eventually transitioning to the study of deep sleep (sushupti).</meta>

# But by meditating on the Supreme, that which is hidden is revealed; for from Him come bondage and its opposite. [3.2.5]

Now, an objection might be raised: The individual soul <term>Jiva: the individual living being or soul</term> is a part of the Supreme Self—just as a spark is a part of a fire. This being the case, just as a spark shares the qualities of heat and light with the fire, the soul should share the qualities of knowledge and power with the Lord <term>Ishwara: the Supreme Lord or Creator</term>. Therefore, by the sheer force of its own will, the soul should be able to create chariots and other objects during a dream.

In response, we say: Although the soul and the Lord stand in the relation of a part to the whole, it is a matter of direct experience that the soul possesses qualities opposite to those of the Lord. 

Does this mean the soul has no qualities in common with the Lord? No, that is not the case. Although these divine qualities exist within the soul, they are hidden <note>original: "tirohitam"</note> by the veil of ignorance and other limitations. 

However, for a seeker who strives by meditating on the Supreme Lord, this hidden nature is revealed. Through the grace of the Lord, the darkness of ignorance is dispelled—much as a person’s sight, though clouded by a cataract <note>original: "timira"</note>, is restored by the power of a potent medicine. This revelation happens only to some who have attained perfection through divine grace, not naturally to all living beings. 

Why is this? Because from Him—that is, from the Lord—come both bondage and liberation for the soul. Bondage <note>original: "bandha"</note> results from not knowing the true nature of the Lord, while liberation <note>original: "moksha"</note> results from realizing that nature. As the scripture <note>Shvetashvatara Upanishad 1.11</note> says: "By knowing the Divine, all fetters fall away; with the exhaustion of sufferings, birth and death cease. By meditating upon Him, there is a third state—at the dissolution of the body, universal lordship, where one is absolute and all desires are fulfilled."

# And that concealment results from connection with the body. [3.2.6]

But why is it that the individual soul, being a part of the Supreme Self, has its knowledge and power hidden? It would seem more logical for these qualities to be manifest, just as the heat and light of a spark are manifest.

We reply: This is true; however, the concealment of the soul's knowledge and power occurs because of its connection to the body—specifically its attachment to the physical frame, the senses, the mind, the intellect, and the experience of objects and pain. 

There is an analogy for this: Just as the heat and light inherent in fire are hidden when the fire is latent within a piece of wood <note>original: "arani": wooden sticks used to kindle fire by friction</note>, or when fire is covered by ashes, so too the soul's knowledge and power are hidden. This concealment is caused by the soul's identification with the body and its limitations <term>Upadhis: limiting adjuncts or "overlays" that make the infinite appear finite</term>, which are products of Name and Form conjured by ignorance. This leads to the illusion that the soul is distinct from the Lord. 

The word "or" <note>original: "va"</note> in the sutra is used to dismiss the doubt that the soul might be entirely different from the Lord. 

One might ask: "Why not simply say the soul is different from the Lord because its knowledge is hidden? Why invent this idea of connection with the body?" 

We say: No, it is not possible for the soul to be fundamentally different from the Lord. Scripture begins with, "That Divinity thought..." and continues with "entering by means of this living soul," using the word "soul" <note>original: "atmana"</note> to refer to the Lord's own Self. Furthermore, the teaching "That is the Truth, that is the Self, That Art Thou, O Shvetaketu" instructs the soul on its identity with the Lord. 

Therefore, the soul is non-different from the Lord, but its powers are hidden by its connection to the body. Consequently, the soul cannot create chariots in a dream by mere will. If the soul could create by will, no one would ever see an unpleasant dream, for no one wills something unpleasant for themselves. 

As for the argument that scripture compares the dream state to the waking state to suggest they are equally real: that comparison is not intended to prove the reality of dreams. Such a view would contradict the teaching that the soul is "self-luminous" in dreams <note>because it creates without external light</note>, and scripture itself explicitly denies the existence of chariots in the dream state. The comparison only serves to show that dreams appear like the waking world because they are triggered by the impressions <note>original: "vasana"</note> left by waking experiences. Therefore, it is established that the dream state is mere illusion <note>original: "maya-matram"</note>.

# The absence of dreams takes place in the nerves and the Self, according to scripture. [3.2.7]

## The Section on the Absence of Dreams

We have examined the dream state; now the state of deep sleep <term>Sushupti: the state of dreamless sleep</term> is examined. Regarding deep sleep, there are several scriptural passages. 

In one place it says: "When a man is so asleep that he is completely calm and knows no dream, he then sleeps in these nerves <note>original: "nadis": subtle channels in the body</note>." [Chandogya Upanishad 8.6.3] 

Elsewhere, after describing the nerves, it says: "Having moved through them, he rests in the pericardium <note>original: "puritat": a sac surrounding the heart</note>." [Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.1.19] 

In another place, again referring to the nerves: "He is in them when he is asleep and sees no dream; then he becomes one with the breath <note>Prana</note> alone." 

In another: "He sleeps in the space within the heart." 

In yet another: "Then, my dear, he is united with the Existent <note>Sat: Pure Being/Brahman</note>, he has entered into his own Self." [Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.1] 

And: "Embraced by the conscious Self <note>Prajna-Atman</note>, he knows nothing without and nothing within." [Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.3.21]

Here a doubt arises: Are these various locations—the nerves, etc.—different places for deep sleep that are independent of one another, or do they collectively form a single place of sleep by working together? 

What is the first view? That they are separate and independent. Why? Because they all serve the same purpose. When things serve the same purpose...

<summary>Shankara explains that the soul's divine powers are hidden due to its identification with the body and ignorance, meaning dream creations are illusory rather than real acts of will. The text then transitions to discussing the scriptural locations of deep sleep (the nerves, the heart, and Brahman).</summary>

"Means and wisdom" refer to the body of self-cognition and one's own body. "Not binding" means untainted. If one asks why, it is said: "Means..." and so forth. "Continuous arising" is the arising. Through the power of the two accumulations, for the sake of wandering beings, the mind that appears as the body and so forth through compassion arises continuously and uninterruptedly, equal to the realm of space; this is "means." 

Therefore, why would the perfect fruit of meditation through means ever perish? "Perishing" is non-perception; because individual appearances are false, it shows an appearance as a body like the moon in water or a star. That itself is perishing, which is "wisdom." Therefore, this is the "end of existence," making an end to the existence rooted in conceptual attachment to objects; it brings it to an end. For that reason, there is no perishing in this, and there is also no birth, because there is no perishing. Furthermore, in reality there is no perishing, so there is no birth; because one knows that this body of <term>Mahāmudrā</term> appears falsely as false to itself, those too appear in reality, so there is no birth itself. 

If one thinks that even mundane people are in <term>saṃsāra</term> <gloss>cyclic existence</gloss>, it is said: "Perished..." and so forth. The meaning of this is: among those who have achieved the accomplishment of <term>Mahāmudrā</term>, if there is no one who conceptually clings to their own body as something that will perish, who is there to be exhausted? For there is no perishing. There is no corruption; it should be known thus. Again, for Brahma and so forth, although there is no true thing in the body, there is conceptual attachment to it as a thing; therefore there is arising, and from arising there is perishing. The accomplishment of <term>Mahāmudrā</term> is not like that, for there is no conceptual attachment to it as a thing. CHAPTER TWENTY-ONE.
It declares how, although God answers what is asked of Him at times, He does not like them to use such a term. And it proves how, although He condescends and answers, He is often angry.

<note>A woodcut depicts a decorative initial letter A with floral and scrollwork motifs.</note>
SINCE, as we have said, some spiritual people are secure and do not pay much heed to the curiosity they sometimes use in trying to know certain things through supernatural means, thinking that because God sometimes answers their requests, it is a good term and that God likes it: however true it may be that He answers them, it is neither a good term, nor does God like it; rather, He dislikes it. And not only that, but He is often angry and feels it deeply. The reason for this is that it is not appropriate for any creature to go outside the terms that God has ordered for its government. He placed rational terms upon man for his government; therefore, wanting to go outside them, and wanting to ascertain and reach things through supernatural means, is to go outside one's terms. Therefore, it is not a holy or convenient thing; therefore, God does not like it. You will say: "If it is true that God does not like it, why does He sometimes answer?" I reply that sometimes the devil answers. But when God answers, I say it is because of the weakness of the soul, which wants to go along that path, so that it does not become discouraged and turn back, or so that it does not think that God is displeased with it, and thus be tempted too much, or for other ends that God knows are founded in the weakness of that soul, for which He sees that it is appropriate to answer and condescend along that path.

ནི་མངོན་པར་བརྗོད། །མེ་མ་དང་ནི་ཡིད་བཟང་མ། །གཉིས་པོ་གྷསྨ་རཱིར་ཤེས་སོ། །གསུམ་འཇུག་མ་དང་འདོད་ལྡན་མ། །གཉིས་པོ་ས་སྤྱོད་མར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཁྱིམ་མ་གཏུམ་མོ་བདུད་འཇོམས་མ། །གསུམ་པོ་མཁའ་སྤྱོད་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་བས་ན་རྣལ་འབྱོར་མ་བཅོ་ལྔ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་རྩ་
ཐམས་ཅད་བསྡུས་པའོ། །དེ་ལྟར་ཡང་སྔགས་དང་ཕྱག་རྒྱ་ཐམས་ཅད་བསྡུས་པའི་དོན་གྱི་ལེའུ་ལས་འཆད་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ་རིགས་ཀྱི་ལེའུ་ལས་རྩ་རྣམས་གང་། བཅུ་དྲུག་གཉིས་ཀྱི་བདག་ཉིད་གསུངས། །རྣལ་འབྱོར་མ་ནི་རེ་རེ་ཞིང་། །རྩ་ནི་གཉིས་གཉིས་རིམ་བཞིན་འདོད། །ལ་ལ་ནཱ་དང་ར་ས་ནཱ། །
ཨ་བ་དྷཱུ་ཏཱི་བདག་མེད་མ། །ཞེས་པ་དང་། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་ནི་ཟླ་བར་གྱུར། །བཅོ་ལྔ་ཆ་ཡི་བདག་ཉིད་ཅན། །ཨཱ་ལིའི་གཟུགས་ཅན་བདེ་བ་ཆེ། །རྣལ་འབྱོར་མ་རྣམས་དེ་ཡི་ཆ། །ཞེས་སོ། །འདིར་ནི་ཇི་ལྟར་དང་པོའི་བདག་མེད་རྣལ་འབྱོར་མ་རྩ་གསུམ་ཡིན་པ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཐ་མའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་མ་
མཁའ་སྤྱོད་མ་ཡང་རྩ་གསུམ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་དོན་གྱིས་གསུངས་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། གཞན་དུ་ན་རྩ་གཉིས་ཤིང་རྣལ་འབྱོར་མ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་བསྡུས་པར་འདོད་པ་མི་འགྲུབ་ལ། བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་སེམས་ཀྱང་སུམ་ཅུ་རྩ་གཉིས་འབབ་པ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པས་སོ། །རྣལ་འབྱོར་མའི་རྒྱུད་ལས་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་སེམས་
སུམ་ཅུ་རྩ་གཉིས་སུ་ཕྱེ་བས་དེ་རྣམས་བདེ་བ་ཆེན་པོའི་འཁོར་ལོ་ཉིད་ལ་གནས་སོ། །དེ་ཡང་སོ་སོར་རྩ་སུམ་ཅུ་རྩ་གཉིས་ལས་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་སེམས་བདེ་བ་ཆེན་པོའི་འཁོར་ལོ་ལས་འབབ་བོ། །དེ་བས་ན་དེ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་གནས་གང་དང་གང་ན་གཙོར་གནས་པ་དང་འབབ་པ་བཤད་པར་བྱའོ། །རྣལ་འབྱོར་
མའི་རང་བཞིན་དེ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་དབྱེ་བ་ནི་རྒྱུད་ཀྱི་དབྱེ་བས་དབྱེ་བར་བྱ་སྟེ་རྒྱུ་ཐམས་ཅད་མཐུན་པ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །རྩ་བྲན་ཀུན་དུ་རྒྱུ་ཞིང་ཕན་ཚུན་རྗེས་སུ་འགྲོ་བ་ཡང་གནས་དང་ལས་ཇི་ལྟར་བསྟན་པ་ལས་རིག་པར་བྱའོ། །ཁ་སྦྱོར་ལས། སྐྱེ་གནས་དབུས་སུ་རྩ་གཉིས་ནི། །གཡོན་དང་དེ་བཞིན་གཡས་
པ་ལས། །གཡོན་ནས་ཁུ་བ་ཤེས་པར་བྱ། །གཡས་པ་ལས་ནི་ཁྲག་ཉིད་དོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །ཡང་ཁ་སྦྱོར་དང་རྡོ་རྗེ་མཁའ་འགྲོ་ལས་གསུངས་པ། རྐན་ནས་བརྩམས་ཏེ་གཡོན་པ་ནས། །རྩ་ནི་ལོངས་སྤྱོད་སྐུ་དང་ལྡན། །ལྟེ་བའི་དབུས་སུ་ངལ་སོ་བ། །འོག་ཏུ་བལྟས་ཏེ་མྱོས་པ་

Fire-Maker <term>Ghasmari</term> and Good-Minded <term>Sumati</term>—these two are known as Ghasmari.
Three-Entrants <term>Triveni</term> and Desire-Possessor <term>Kamini</term>—these two become the Earth-Walker <term>Bhumicari</term>.
House-Mother <term>Grhadharma</term>, Fierce One <term>Candika</term>, and Demon-Subduer <term>Marasundari</term>—these three are the Sky-Walker <term>Khecari</term>.

Therefore, all channels are included within the fifteen yoginis. This will also be explained in the Chapter on the Collection of All Mantras and Seals. In the Chapter on the Families, it is said:
"The nature of the sixteen doubled <note>thirty-two</note> is taught.
For each yogini,
Two channels are assigned in order.
Lalana, Rasana,
And Avadhuti are Nairatmya."
And:
"The mind of enlightenment becomes the moon,
Possessing fifteen parts.
The nature of the vowels <term>ali</term> is Great Bliss;
The yoginis are its parts."

Here, just as the first Nairatmya has three channels, the final yogini Khecari also has three channels; this is the implied meaning. Otherwise, the claim that two channels are included for each yogini would not hold, especially since it is said that "thirty-two [channels] of the mind of enlightenment flow."

In the Yogini Tantras, the mind of enlightenment is divided into thirty-two, and these abide in the Wheel of Great Bliss. Furthermore, from each of the thirty-two channels, the mind of enlightenment flows from the Wheel of Great Bliss. Thus, we shall explain where their primary locations and flows are.

The divisions of these yogini-natures should be distinguished according to the divisions of the tantras, as all causes are not identical. The minor channels that circulate everywhere and follow one another should be understood according to how their locations and functions are taught.

From the *Union of the Kiss* <term>Samputa</term>:
"In the center of the birth-place are two channels,
To the left and likewise to the right.
From the left, the semen <note>white drop</note> is known;
From the right is the blood <note>red drop</note>."

<summary>This page continues the mapping of subtle body channels to the yoginis of the Hevajra mandala, specifically identifying Lalana, Rasana, and Avadhuti. it discusses the flow of white and red drops (semen and blood) from the palate to the navel and the symbolic numbering of thirty-two channels.</summary>
