Dico adunque che nel primo modo, che è quella festiua narratione, non è bisogno arte alcuna, per che la natura medesima crea, & forma glihuomini atti à narrare piaceuolmente, & da loro il volto, i gesti, la voce, & le parole appropriate ad imitar cio che vogliono. Nell'altro delle argutie, che può far l'arte: conciofiacosa che quel falso detto dee esser uscito, & hauer dato in brocca, prima che paia, che colui, che lo dice: v'habbia potuto pensare, altrimenti è freddo, & non ha del buono. Però estimo ch'el tutto sia opera dell'ingegno, & della natura. Rispose allhor le parole M. Pietro Bembo: & disse, il S. Prefetto non vi nega quello, che voi dite, cioè che la natura, & lo ingegno non habbiano le prime parti, massimamente circa la inuentione, ma certo è che nell'animo di ciascuno, sia pur l'huomo di quanto buono ingegno puo essere, nascono de i concetti buoni, & mali: & piu, & meno, ma il giudicio poi, & l'arte li lima, & corregge: & fa elettione de i buoni: & rifiuta i mali. Però lasciando quello che s'appartiene allo ingegno, dechiarateci quello che consiste nell'arte, cioè delle facetie, & de i motti, che inducono à ridere, quai son conuenienti al Cortegiano: & quai nò, & in qual tempo, & modo si debbano usare, che questo è quello ch'el S. Prefetto v'addimanda. Allhor M. In the other sort, of subtleties, what can art do, seeing that this witty remark must have been uttered and hit the mark before it appears that the one who says it could have thought about it? Otherwise, it is cold and lacks goodness. Therefore, I deem that the whole thing is a work of wit and nature." Then Master Pietro Bembo <note>original: "M. Pietro Bembo"</note> replied and said, "The Prefect does not deny what you say, namely that nature and wit have the primary roles, especially regarding invention <note>original: "inuentione"</note>. But it is certain that in the mind of everyone, even if a man is of the best wit he can be, good and bad concepts are born, some more and some less; but judgment <note>original: "giudicio"</note> then and art file and correct them, and make a selection of the good and reject the bad. Therefore, leaving aside what pertains to wit, clarify for us what consists in the art—that is, regarding the witticisms <note>original: "facetie"</note> and jests <note>original: "motti"</note> that induce laughter—which are convenient for the Courtier <note>original: "Cortegiano"</note> and which are not, and in what time and manner they should be used, for this is what the Prefect asks of you." Fede."</note>, also laughing, said, "There is no one here among us to whom I do not yield in everything, and especially in being witty, except perhaps if the foolishness that often makes others laugh, more than fine sayings, were itself accepted as witticisms." This is because it protects the unsurpassed bliss of the nature of the condensed essence. It is there that "I" reside.

In order to symbolize all phenomena as being one within the form of Great Bliss, it says: "The form of the shape of the letter E." The Buddhahood itself is the jewel. Its casket <gloss>precious container</gloss> is the place where it is set. Now, to show the greatness of such a self, it says "I am the teacher" and so forth. This means one who explains such teachings as the *Hevajra Tantra*. "The listener" refers to the student who possesses good qualities. "The object to be accomplished is I" refers to what was previously shown. Its accomplisher is also the self.

"The teacher of the wanderers" refers to the two <term>Sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>Enjoyment Bodies</gloss>, which are the self. Regarding the phrase "the world and the transcendent world," that which arises from the elaboration of both is the "world." The "transcendent world" is the seminal fluid of <term>bodhicitta</term> <gloss>enlightened mind/essence</gloss> which acts as the cause for those two. Because this is necessary for the world and is the very essence of the <term>Sambhogakaya</term>, it is the self.

If you ask: "If you are primarily the essence of Great Bliss, what is that like?" it says "of the Sahaja-joy" <gloss>co-emergent joy</gloss> and so forth. If you ask what the specific quality of that co-emergent joy is, it says "the end of the supreme" and so forth. The truth is lost because the hearts of the common people are more inclined toward superstitions, and thus the reports became confused. Then, another calamity came from the direction of the heretics (<term>Zanadiqa</term>), the followers of <term>Mani</term>, such as Ibn al-Muqaffa', 'Abd al-Karim ibn Abi al-'Awja', and their likes. They cast doubt in the minds of the weak-willed regarding the "First One" through the concepts of modification and possibility, drawing them toward dualism and adorning the life of Mani in their eyes until they grasped his rope. He was a man not content with the ignorance of his own doctrine, but spoke of the structure of the world with deceptions that became widespread in speech. Added to this were the previous Jewish intrigues, so it became a view attributed to Islam—God is far above such a thing. Whoever opposes it and holds to the truth that conforms to the Qur'an is labeled an infidel and an atheist, with their blood judged as lawful to be spilled, and they are not permitted to have their speech heard. And this is worse than what is heard from the speech of Pharaoh: "I am your lord most high" <note>Qur'an 79:24</note>, "and I know of no other god for you besides me" <note>Qur'an 28:38</note>. Fanaticism may lead us away from the ideal path due to excessive zeal, but God will make firm the steps of the one who intends Him and intends the truth. As for the Indians, their religious books and the informational <term>Puranas</term> all speak on the structure of the world in a way that contradicts the truth evident to their own astronomers. However, the people are compelled by the necessity of performing their rituals and leading the vast majority of the public to follow them toward astrological calculations and judicial predictions. Thus, they show inclination toward them, speak of their virtues, seek blessing in meeting them, and declare with certainty that they are among the people of Paradise and that none of them will enter Hell. Their astronomers reciprocate by confirming and matching what they are upon, even if most of it contradicts the truth, and they support them...

<summary>Al-Biruni discusses the corruption of historical and geographical knowledge through political and religious factionalism, specifically critiquing how Indian astrological traditions are compromised by religious and social necessity.</summary>
<keywords>heretics, Mani, Ibn al-Muqaffa', Islam, idolatry, Puranas, astrological calculations</keywords>

**Jiaona**

Scholar Kong, a descendant of the Sage <note>Confucius</note>, was a refined person skilled in poetry. He had a close friend in Tiantai who sent a letter inviting him to visit. The scholar went, but just as he arrived, his friend passed away. Stranded and unable to return, he took up residence at Putuo Temple, working as a copyist for the monks. About a hundred paces west of the temple, there was the residence of Master Dan. The Master was a former nobleman; due to a major lawsuit, his household was in decline, and with few family members left, they moved to the countryside, leaving the mansion empty. One day, during a heavy snowfall, the roads were silent and deserted. As he happened to pass by the gate, a youth came out, his appearance remarkably refined. Seeing the scholar, he approached and paid his respects, offered warm greetings, and immediately invited him inside. The scholar was delighted and readily followed him. The rooms were not very spacious, but everywhere hung silk curtains. On the walls were many paintings and calligraphy by the ancients, and on the desk lay a volume titled *Langhuan Suo* <gloss>Trifles from the Hall of Immortality</gloss>.

<summary>Scholar Kong, a refined man and descendant of Confucius, finds himself stranded and working at a temple, eventually meeting a young man who invites him into the nearby, supposedly empty Dan mansion.</summary>

knowing the past, future, and present minds of oneself and others. Regarding "The higher realms and the human world" and so forth, "single form" means having a single nature. The meaning of "the parts of self and others" and so forth has already been shown.

To show the distinguished <term>Hevajra</term> <gloss>Joyous Vajra</gloss> from other scriptures, "Knowing all the Vedas" and so forth was spoken. The "Vedas" are the Rig Veda, Atharva Veda, Sama Veda, and Yajur Veda <note>original: "nges brjod, srid srung, snyan dngags, mchod sbyin"</note>. "Philosophical tenets" refers to the views of the non-Buddhists such as the Jainas <note>original: "rnying ba"</note> and so forth, and the sutras of the Shravaka <gloss>Hearer</gloss> pitakas and so forth, because one acts as the end of rebirth through these. "Extensive rituals" refers to the Action Tantras and so forth. The accomplishment characterized as explained in these does not exist. 

If it is asked "Does it exist in the Paramitayana <gloss>Perfection Vehicle</gloss> or not?", "Existence will be purified" and so forth was spoken. "Purified" means it exhausts the obscurations of mental afflictions and the knowable; it is the path characterized by the six perfections. Through that purification, enlightenment will be obtained; however, "at the end of existence" means after three immeasurable eons, passing from one birth to another.

If it is asked "If obtaining enlightenment in this life is also spoken of in the Yoga Tantras, what makes this superior?", "Even without that" and so forth was spoken. If "that"—the co-emergent characterized by self-awareness—is absent, it is not spoken that there is accomplishment in this life or in other lives. 

"Then what is the difference between that and this?", "He who does not know Hevajra" and so forth was spoken. This is because other tantras merely teach the co-emergent, while this Hevajra speaks of the fully clear aspect. Therefore, it is very clearly shown that for whoever does not know Hevajra, the hardship of hearing, reflecting, and meditating becomes meaningless.

others similarly. It is necessary, therefore, that the soul have one essence, another power, and another activity; and one who wishes to grasp and contemplate the whole of it must speak about all of these. There will be, then, three primary chapters regarding the <term>psychogonia</term> <gloss>generation of the soul</gloss>: one concerning its essence, one concerning its power, and one concerning its activity; for this is a complete examination of the subjects proposed. But we see the psychic essence as threefold. For its own <term>hyparxis</term> <gloss>subsistence/existence</gloss> is one thing, and the harmony within it is another, according to which its essential multitude is held together—being neither a single essence, as is the Intellect, nor divided into infinites, as is the body that comes after it, but rather into essential parts that are more than one, yet finite in number. It is impossible for there to be more parts of the soul than these, as the parts themselves are not further divisible into others, as will be clear as we proceed. Another thing is its <term>eidos</term> <gloss>form/species</gloss>, which is perfected from these; so that the essence of the soul is both one and threefold. For it is fitting for it to have both the monad and the triad, since we also divide the entire soul into three. Therefore, the essence is both one and triple. For existence is one thing, harmony another, and form another; the first defining existence alone, the second harmonizing the essential multitude, and the third holding together the <margin>C</margin> <note>marginal note: C</note> identity of the whole system. And all these are within one another. For existence has the harmonized multitude with itself; for it is not without multitude, nor does it have only multitude without harmony. And this harmony is also essential, connective, and formative of the essence; from which it is also shown how the soul is harmony and how it is not, and that Plato is consistent with himself here in positing it as harmony, while in the <term>Phaedo</term> <gloss>a dialogue of Plato</gloss> he refutes those who say these things. For it was one thing for a harmony to be of itself and of others, and another to be of another alone. The latter creates harmony in a subject, inseparable from the things harmonized and based upon an alien seat, but the former is separable, existing of itself, and turned toward itself. And indeed, the form of the harmonic ratios is comprehensive and contains the existence of the soul; for according to this, the identity of the soul is most defined, and the single <term>logos</term> <gloss>ratio/principle</gloss> according to which it is what it is. All these things, therefore, are in one another (the existence, the harmony, the form), and the essence is one and threefold, since it consists of three genera: essence, the same, and the other. <margin>D</margin> <note>marginal note: D</note> And again, existence is according to...

By "devoid of essence," it shows the lack of an essence. A Bodhisattva is said to be one who "observes as being like an illusion." This is shown by saying that when a Bodhisattva Mahasattva practices the Perfection of Wisdom in this way, "he does not correctly perceive the arising of any phenomenon," and so forth. In this regard, for the conceptually constructed, there is neither arising nor ceasing; they are merely appearance and non-appearance. For the dependent <term>paratantra</term> <gloss>the dependent nature</gloss>, there is neither increase nor decrease; they are merely conceptual constructions. For the thoroughly established, there is neither affliction nor purification; they are merely pure by nature. 

Although all phenomena thus lack essence, in order to clear away further doubt, the reason is asked "Why is that?" and the text says: "Because names are artificial." This means that the names and signs of the aggregates and so forth, such as "form," "feeling," and "perception," are artificial and do not exist by essence. Therefore, one should know all phenomena to be without essence, because an essence is not something artificial. 

The artificiality itself is shown by "those phenomena which are dependently originated are imputed," and so forth. The meaning is that those phenomena which depend on conceptual causes and conceptual conditions are called "dependently arising" because they are imputed in such and such ways. This shows the following: if something depends on another, it arises through the power of that other and not through its own power. How could that be an essence? Therefore, since it lacks its own thingness and becomes the thingness of another, it is established that all phenomena lack essence. Thus, the meaning of "lacking essence" is the meaning of "dependent origination." Following that, the conventional expression of names arises from the causes of conceptually constructed names.

Among them is <term>Soma</term>, because it is auspicious, and auspicious [planets] are called <term>Soma-kara</term> <gloss>moon-doer/auspicious-doer</gloss>, while the malefics are called <term>Papa-kara</term> <gloss>evil-doer</gloss>. Among them is <term>Nishisha</term> <gloss>Lord of the Night</gloss>, <term>Nakshatrana</term> <gloss>Lord of the Mansions</gloss>, <term>Dvija-ishvara</term> <gloss>Lord of the Twice-Born</gloss>, and <term>Shitanshu</term> <gloss>Cold-Ray</gloss>, because its sphere is changing, and in it is tranquility. When the ray falls upon it, it cools with its coolness and reflects, thus illuminating the darkness and cooling the night, and extinguishing what the sun has corrupted with burning. For this reason, it is also called <term>Chandra</term> <gloss>Moon</gloss>, and it is the left eye of <term>Narayana</term>, just as the sun is his right eye. I have entrusted to this table the suns of the months and the defect of the disagreement among them, similar to what preceded in the determination of the earths.

236                                     *Glory of the World.*

they ought to take, there they took pyrite, sulfur, salt, metal, and various other materials, in which there is no operation, and yet from workshops they are expensive things, but in the work they are of absolutely no value. But our material is not bought from any workshop, yet it is found in it daily, and merchants throw it into the streets. It is enough therefore that it be found by grace: But the material of our stone is compared to all those things with which artisans labor: For our stone is our salt, our Mercury, verdigris, halonitrum, sal ammoniac, Mars (iron), sulfur, and countless other things of that kind, not however dug out from wooded and open mountains with hammers and other instruments: But our stone is extracted only from our mountains and springs: in our Salt-spring our Salt is found: from our earth our metal, Mercury, and sulfur are produced, and not from wooded, foreign, and open mountains; all of which artisans do not understand, nor can they believe, nor comprehend; for the Lord has obscured and stopped up their senses, for which reason they used these things otherwise than they ought to be done, and aimed least at the goal, nevertheless they persisted in that contrary sense, and obeyed their stubborn heads; as for instance, when they ought to distill gently, there they sublimated with a strong fire, they burned strong waters, and immediately burned the operation of nature and its substances, and reduced them to nothing. While also they ought to dissolve, there they coagulated, and again, as unskilled in things, they also unskillfully handled the matter, and fell into doubt, and with lying words declared the art to be not true, but false, in which, however, they themselves deservedly lie: for their own ignorance shamefully deceived them, which is to be imputed to their own obscure, dark cunning, while, according to their obscure understanding, they interpreted words otherwise than they sounded. For example, when Philosophers spoke of calcination (which they call grinding), then those unskilled philosophasters understood it as burning, and reduced the things entirely to ashes, so that nothing could be made from them. english: So it is with poetry in relation to philosophy; for poetry is another philosophy. In time, it is ancient; in harmony, it is metrical; in thought, it is mythological. And philosophy is another, ethical; in time, it is newer; in harmony, it is more discordant; in thought, it is clearer. Why, then, if they are busy with time and are carried along together, how should one train the difference in those things which each says about the divine, both the diverse [poets] and the philosophers? Or let the examination be like this: just as someone who has considered medicine, which he has first now, in relation to the new one and the one directed at diseases, would examine which of the two is better or worse; for Asclepius would [not] say to him: "Those who do not change simple arts, the times do not change them." For of those things whose need is simple, the works are also simple. But the medical [art], if it were to follow the head of the body's affairs, would not exist; nor would it be consistent. But because of the change and shift of the food [the body] currently has, it finds healing things that are sufficient for it, others appropriate at different times for the current food. Do not, therefore, consider this: he who cuts the ulcers with a knife, and the one suffering from gout, it was not then necessary to heal them [in the same way] as the one who applied himself to the art later. And these wise and varied cures of the keen-witted; but when the art, communing with bodies, is not therapeutic nor varied, nor completely dissolved, it handles them easily. And for them, the work is simple. But now, healing bodies that are becoming more varied and have an evil temperament, [the art] became varied itself, and changed from its former simplicity to a varied one. Therefore, let both the poet and the philosopher answer about the practices of Asclepius. This one [the philosopher] even gets angry at the sufferers; if someone ignored Homer and Hesiod, or Orpheus, or another who said the same things, or [who claimed] to be wiser than Aristotle...

भांति मल निकालकर बिठादे कफ और वायुके व्रणोंके मलको चतुर वैद्य कईवार सूंत सूंत कर निकाले ॥ ३९ ॥ व्रणको नीचेसे दबाकर रोमगतिके अनुसार स्रावित करे (रिसावे) और सब गूढ बंधों (जोडों) को तथा संधियोंको अच्छे प्रकारसे मिलादे ॥ ४० ॥ होठके जोडनेमें यथायोग्य जैसे पहले कह आये हैं वैसे करे तथा जोडोंका जाननेवाला वैद्य हड्डीके जोडनेमें भी अपनी बुद्धिसि विचार कर यथोक्त बंध लगावे ॥ ४१ ॥

उत्तिष्ठनो निपण्णस्य शयनं चापि गच्छतः ॥ गच्छतो विविधाद्यैनैर्नस्य दुष्यति सै व्रणः ॥४२॥ संध्यस्थिकोष्ठप्राप्ताश्च शिरा-स्नायुगतास्तथौ ॥ तथैवगाढगंभीराः सर्वतो विषमस्थिताः ॥ नैते साधयितुं शक्या ऋते वन्धैर्भवंति हि ॥ ४३ ॥

इति सुश्रुतसंहितायां सूत्रस्थानेऽष्टादशोऽध्यायः ॥ १८ ॥

उठते हुए बैठते हुए शयनको प्राप्त होते हुए चलते हुए सवारी करते हुए मनुष्योंका व्रण (यथोक्त बन्ध लगे पीछे) पीडा नहीं देता ॥ ४२ ॥ संधि और हड्डी तथा कोष्ठमें प्राप्त हुए व्रण, शिरा और स्नायुके व्रण, गाढे और गंभीर व्रण तथा जो सब ओरसे विषम हो गये हों ऐसे व्रण यथोक्त बन्धके बिना साधन नहीं किये जासकते ॥ ४३ ॥

इति पण्डितमुरलीधरशर्मभि० सुश्रुतस० भा० टी० सूत्रस्थानेऽष्टादशोऽध्यायः ॥ १८ ॥

### एकोनविंशोऽध्यायः १९.

अथातो व्रणितोपासनीयमध्यायं व्याख्यास्यामः ।

अत्र यहांसे व्रणितोपासनीय (व्रणोंके बरतावकी विधिनामक) अध्यायका व्याख्यान करते हैं ।

व्रणिनः प्रथममेवागारमन्विच्छेत्तच्चागारं प्रशस्तवास्वादिकं कार्यम् ॥ १ ॥ प्रशस्तवास्तुनि गृहे शुचौवातपवर्जिते ॥ निवाते ने च रोगाः स्युः शारीरागन्तुमानसाः ॥ १ ॥ तस्मिञ्छयनमसंबाधं स्वास्तीर्णं मनोज्ञं प्राक्छिरस्कं सशस्त्रं कुर्वीत ॥ ३ ॥ सुखचेष्टाप्रचारः स्यात्स्वास्तीर्णे शयने व्रणी ॥ प्राच्यां दिशि स्थितां देवास्तत्पूर्वाधं नैतं शिरः ॥ ४ ॥

(सूत्र ४२) वधयुक्त व्रण ।

<header>Sūtrasthāna, Chapter 19</header>

(143)

When the patient is standing, sitting, lying down, or moving about, the wound <note>if bandaged according to the prescribed method</note> will not be afflicted by pain. (42) Wounds involving joints, bones, <term>koṣṭha</term> <gloss>viscera/internal cavities</gloss>, veins, and ligaments, as well as those that are deep-seated or severely irregular, cannot be healed without the application of proper bandages. (43)

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter of the Sūtrasthāna in the Suśruta Saṃhitā. (18)

### Chapter Nineteen

We shall now explain the chapter titled <term>Vraṇitopāsanīyam</term> <gloss>Treatment and Conduct for the Wounded</gloss>.

Here, we begin the exposition of the chapter regarding the conduct for those suffering from wounds.

The physician should first seek out a dwelling for the wounded person, and such a dwelling should be well-constructed and suitable. (1) In a house with a favorable orientation, which is clean, free from exposure to the sun, and protected from drafts, the patient will not be afflicted by physical, external, or mental diseases. (2) In that place, one should prepare a bed that is spacious, well-appointed, pleasant, oriented with the head to the east, and furnished with a protective weapon. (3) On a comfortable bed, the patient can move freely; since the gods reside in the east, the head should be directed toward that quarter for the sake of honoring them. (4)

<note>(Verse 42) This describes the stability provided by correct bandaging during physical activity.</note>

Just as those who speak of the <term>Alaya-vijnana</term> <gloss>All-ground consciousness</gloss> assert that the all-ground consciousness is what holds the seeds of all wandering beings, so too is <term>mahasukha</term> <gloss>great bliss</gloss> realized through the empowerment of the wisdom of primordial awareness. The nature of the emptiness of all phenomena is also praised in the Great Vehicle Secret Mantra <note>Mahayana Vajrayana</note> as being the very foundation of all phenomena.

To achieve that very realization, the text says "dark bliss" and so forth. "Union" refers to the meditative equipoise of <term>upaya</term> <gloss>skillful means</gloss> and <term>prajna</term> <gloss>wisdom</gloss>. "Entity" refers to the nature of the five Buddhas. "Non-entity" refers to the state of being free from conceptual elaboration regarding those very Buddhas.

If one asks how the nature of bliss arises within the mandala of the glorious Hevajra, which is the nature of skillful means and wisdom, the text says "Vajrasattva" and so forth. From the union of the sun and moon, which are the nature of skillful means and wisdom, a seed syllable arises. From that seed arises the hand-symbol, the <term>vajra</term> <gloss>scepter or diamond</gloss>. The seed syllable residing in the center of that is the <term>sattva</term> <gloss>being</gloss>. The being together with the vajra is Vajrasattva. That very state is described as bliss.

Regarding the phrase "Vajragarbha requested," what was the purpose of his request? Because the Blessed One praised the reality of the generation stage as being the essence of bliss, the text says "perfection" and so forth. "Meditation" refers to the meditation on the deity itself. "What is the need for a non-existent generation?" means there is no need. The intention is as follows: what is the need for this effort in meditating on the mandala cycle if one is devoted to great bliss? If one asks whether the desired goal can be accomplished by great bliss alone, the text says "degenerated through the force of faith" to show respect. This means that one who possesses respect for the generation stage and yet "degenerates" is one who actually abandons the generation stage. "The non-entity of the body" refers to that very generation stage <unclear>one or two words illegible</unclear>.

<summary>This page explains the philosophical foundation of Great Bliss by comparing it to the All-ground consciousness and details the symbolic emergence of Vajrasattva from the union of wisdom and means. It addresses the relationship between the generation stage of meditation and the ultimate realization of Bliss within the Hevajra tradition.</summary>

# ON MORAL PHILOSOPHY

Christ teaches that one must do good to all, that even enemies must be loved, that one must give freely without expecting a return, that vengeance should not be taken against anyone, and that one should give to every requester. On the contrary, the philosophers say one should only give to those who compensate a benefit with a benefit; otherwise, it is permissible to be angry, to hate, to contend, to wage war, and to charge interest. Furthermore, they have given us, with their free will and the dictates of right reason and the light of nature, the Pelagian heretics. Moreover, all of moral philosophy (as Lactantius witnesses) is false and empty, neither instructing in the duties of justice nor confirming the office of man and his reasons. Finally, it is entirely repugnant to divine law and to Christ himself, so that its glory is owed to no one other than Satan.

# ON POLITICS
### Chapter LV

Politics also pertains to philosophy, which is the art of administering the Republic. There are three species of it, namely: Monarchy, which is the rule of one; Aristocracy, which is the rule of a few, but of nobles,

<column-break/>
rich men, or wise men; and Democracy, which is the rule of the people. And related to all these are tyrannies, oligarchies, and anarchies. But all these things must be referred to that which comes to each person. For although the philosophers wish to define which is best, they follow diverse opinions. Some admit that Monarchy is the truer form of good government, just as there is one God in heaven, one head in the members, and one leader among the bees. Likewise, others contend that Aristocracy or Democracy is the form of government that is equal and by which liberty is preserved. Above others, however, are Plato, Aristotle, Apuleius, and others, who are not only from our own traditions but also from the barbarians. Those who have written about these say nothing except about matters pertaining to external administration, to peace, to the tranquility of public affairs, and to consultation, and not to the soul, nor to salvation, nor to eternal aids; indeed, they look only to those things which are to be performed in this world. # HERODOTUS IV 288

These are the things the cities report, but I know what happened to the Metapontines in Italy four hundred and forty years after the second disappearance of Aristeas, as I discovered by comparing accounts in Proconnesus and Metapontum. The Metapontines say that Aristeas appeared to them in their land and commanded them to set up an altar to Apollo and to place beside it a statue bearing the name of Aristeas the Proconnesian. They claim that Apollo had come to them, the only Italians to be visited by him, and that the current Aristeas was following him; at that time, when he followed the god, he was a raven. Having said this, he disappeared. The Metapontines say they sent to Delphi to ask the god what the apparition of the man meant. The Pythian priestess commanded them to obey the apparition, stating that it would go better for them if they did. They accepted this and carried it out. And now a statue bearing the name of Aristeas stands beside the image of Apollo itself, and laurel trees stand around it; the statue is set up in the marketplace. Let this be sufficient regarding Aristeas.

<margin>16</margin> Concerning the land, about which this story is set in motion to be told, no one knows accurately what lies above it, for I have been unable to learn anything from anyone claiming to be an eyewitness. Not even Aristeas, whom I mentioned a little while ago, claimed in his own verses that he had traveled further than the Issedones; rather, he spoke of the regions above by hearsay, claiming that the Issedones were the ones who told him these things. But everything we have been able to reach with certainty by hearsay will be told.

Regarding **"That itself is selfless,"** if one asks what its reality is, it is said: **"having the nature of the sphere of phenomena <term>dharmadhatu</term>."** This is the answer to the five questions. When it says **"Vajragarbha petitioned,"** what did he petition? It is the meaning of the summary <term>samvara</term>. **"Remaining in the center of the yogini's body,"** and so forth was spoken. The "center of the body" is the navel. **"The form of the letter E"** is the first vowel. **"Abiding"** means always residing there.

To show the meaning of the summary, **"Just as externally"** and so forth was spoken. The meaning is: just as the external Nairatmya is meditated upon, so it is here. The meaning is that it is not inferior to that. The intent is that because it is gathered into the body, it is a "summary." Furthermore, here, just like the mandala of Nairatmya, so too is the letter **A** residing in the navel. Just as the letter **A** residing in the navel is the summary of Nairatmya, so too is the letter **HUM** in the "Vajra Sense-Base." The intent is that by the method itself, it is the summary residing in the heart of the Method, Hevajra.

If one asks what happens by that, **"Vajra bliss"** and so forth was spoken. The intent is that the bliss of those two letters reaching the "Vajra Tip" is the cause of accomplishing the body of Mahamudra; therefore it is called **"Mahamudra."** Regarding **"By this"** and so forth, the **"secret union"** is the meditative union of the inner self. If one asks if there is an example for this, **"The two of the two external ones"** was spoken, which refers to the union of Nairatmya and Heruka. Regarding **"The three bodies"** and so forth, the "three bodies of the Buddhas" are the three kayas. It should be said that they reside within the body of the yogini. The full knowledge of the three is the "Essence Body" <term>Svabhavikakaya</term>, which is the nature of the knowledge of equality. It is the "Wheel of Great Bliss." This means the form of the summary of the three bodies is shown in the form of the Wheel of Great Bliss.

ཉིད་ཀྱིས་དགྲའི་སྒོ་ལོགས་ལ་བསྐུས་ནས་ཁྱིམ་གྱི་སྒོར་སྟོང་ཕྲག་བརྒྱད་བཟླས་ན་སྐྲོད་པར་བྱེད་དོ། །ཕྱེ་མ་དེ་དང་དུར་ཁྲོད་ཀྱིས་དགྲ་བོའི་སྒོ་རྩར་བཅད་ཅིང་སྦས་ན་དགྲ་བོའི་རིགས་རྣམས་འཇོམས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཡང་ན་དགྲ་བོའི་རིགས་སྐྲོད་པར་འདོད་ན། ཙྪུ་ཙྪུནྡ་རའི་པགས་པ་བླངས་ལ་སྟོང་
ཕྲག་བརྒྱད་ཡོངས་སུ་བཟླས་ནས་གཅིན་ཤུལ་གྱི་སས་བཀང་ནས་སྐུད་པ་སྔོན་པོས་བཅིངས་ཏེ་ནམ་མཁར་བཏགས་ན་གཅིན་འགགས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །བཀྲོལ་ན་ཐར་རོ། །ཙྪུ་ཙྪུནྡ་རའི་པགས་པ་ཕྱེ་མར་བཏགས་ནས་ལྷ་ཆེན་པོའི་མདུན་དུ་སྟོང་ཕྲག་བརྒྱད་བཟླས་ལ། ཡང་དྲི་དང་མེ་ཏོག་
དང་བདུག་སྤོས་དང་། གཏོར་མ་བཏང་སྟེ། སླར་ཡང་སྟོང་ཕྲག་བརྒྱད་བཟླས་ན་དེ་ནས་འགྲུབ་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཕྱེ་མ་དེ་སྣའི་རྩེ་མོར་བསྐུས་ན་སྐྱེ་འགྲོ་ཐམས་ཅད་སྡུད་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །མགོ་བོར་བཞག་ན་དགྲ་ཐམས་ཅད་དང་འགྱེད་པའི་ལེན་ཐེབས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཕྱེ་མ་དེ་ཉིད་རང་
གི་སྙིང་གར་བསྐུས་ནས་གལ་ཏེ་དགྲ་ལ་བསྟན་ན་སྙིང་ངན་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །སཱ་ལུའི་ཕྱེ་མ་ལས་གཟུགས་བྱས་ནས་ཕྱེ་མ་དེས་བསྐུས་ན་དགྲ་བོ་དེ་རེངས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །སཱ་ལུའི་ཕྱེ་མ་ལས་གཟུགས་བྱས་ཏེ་ཕྱེ་མ་དེས་བསྐུས་ན་མཛེས་ཐེབས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དུར་ཁྲོད་ཀྱི་ཐལ་བ་དང་
བཅས་པས་དགྲའི་ཚོགས་ལ་གཏོར་ན་གང་གིས་མནན་པ་དང་མཐོང་བ་དེ་དག་ནད་ཀྱིས་ཐེབས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཕྱེ་མ་དེ་ལ་ལན་སྟོང་བཟླས་ན་གང་གང་གི་མགོ་བོར་བླུགས་པ་དེ་དབང་དུ་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཕྱེ་མ་དེ་ཐོད་པ་དང་ལྷན་ཅིག་ཏུ་སྒོ་གླེགས་སུ་བཞག་ན་དགྲ་བོ་དབྱེ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །
ཕྱེ་མ་དེས་བུད་མེད་ཀྱི་ལག་པ་ལ་བསྐུས་ན་བུད་མེད་དེ་འཆི་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཕྱེ་མ་དེ་གང་གི་སྒོར་སྦས་ན་སྐྲོད་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཕྱེ་མ་དེ་དང་ཤ་ཆེན་པོ་བསྲེས་ནས་གང་གི་བཏུང་བར་བྱིན་ན། ཉི་མ་བདུན་ན་འཆིའོ། །ཕྱེ་མ་དེ་དག་བཤང་བ་དང་བསྲེས་ནས་དགྲ་ལ་བྱིན་ན། དགྲ་བོ་བཀྲེས་པ་

### ACCOUNT OF THE REVOLT OF THE SHERIF JALAL AL-DIN IN THE LAND OF MA’BAR AND THE CONNECTED EVENTS CONCERNING THE KILLING OF THE VIZIER'S NEPHEW

The Sultan had appointed the Sherif Jalal al-Din Ahsan Shah as commander over the land of Ma’bar <note>original: "Ma'bar"</note> <gloss>the crossing, referring to the southeastern coast of the Indian peninsula</gloss>, which lies at a distance of six months' travel from Delhi. He rebelled, claimed the kingship for himself, killed the Sultan’s deputies and agents, and minted gold and silver coins in his own name. On one side of the dinar, he had inscribed: "The descendant of Taha and Yasin <note>These are the titles of the 20th and 36th chapters of the Quran, used here as epithets for the Prophet Muhammad</note>, the father of the poor and the destitute, Jalal al-Dunya wa al-Din." And on the other face: "He who trusts in the support of the Merciful, Ahsan Shah the Sultan."

<summary>Ibn Battuta describes the mountaineers' tribute and begins the account of the revolt of Sherif Jalal al-Din Ahsan Shah in the province of Ma'bar.</summary>

at that time, that manner which dwells in its own inexpressible, non-conceptual nature is called "<term>dharmata</term> form." It is called "essenceless" because it lacks the imagined essence. It is called "selflessness of phenomena" because it lacks the manner of a phenomenal self. "Suchness" <term>tathata</term> refers to the non-erroneous manner. "Ultimate reality" <term>bhutakoti</term> refers to the finality of such a manner. The same should be applied to feeling and so forth. 

"Maitreya, whatever is imagined form should be viewed as non-substantial" means it is completely non-existent. "Whatever is conceptualized form should be viewed as substantial, because conceptualization is substantial" means it exists because it exists conventionally. It is a substance in the sense that it perishes in the manner of conditioned things and exists as form; therefore, the meaning is that it is explained as existing conceptualization and being a substance. "It does not function independently" was said because it is the other-dependent essence. "Whatever is <term>dharmata</term> form is neither non-substantial nor substantial." "<term>Dharmata</term> form" is that which is distinguished by the ultimate. Because it exists in an inexpressible nature, it is not suitable to say it does not exist; therefore, it is not non-substantial. Because it does not exist in the manner of a conceptualized entity, it is not suitable to say it exists; therefore, it is not substantial. Thus, having abandoned the two extremes, the Middle Way is shown. "Distinguished by the ultimate" means the essence of the ultimate. The word "distinguished" <note>original: rab tu phye ba</note> means the sense of the "essence." The same should be applied up to the limit of the qualities of a Buddha.

## ततो मनोजवित्वं विकरण-
## भावः प्रधानजयश्च ॥ ४८ ॥

कायस्यानुत्तमो गतिलाभो मनोजवित्वम् । विदेहाना-
मिन्द्रियाणामभिप्रेतदेशकालविषयापेक्षो वृत्तिलाभो विकरण-
भावः । सर्वप्रकृतिविकारवशित्वं प्रधानजय इत्येतास्तिस्रः
सिद्धयो मधुप्रतीका उच्यन्ते । एताश्च करणपञ्चरूपजयाद-
धिगम्यन्ते ॥ ४८ ॥

## सत्त्वपुरुषान्यताख्यातिमा-
## त्रस्य सर्वभावाधिष्ठातृत्वं
## सर्वज्ञातृत्वं च ॥ ४९ ॥

निर्धूतरजस्तमोमलस्य बुद्धिसत्त्वस्य परे वैशारद्ये परस्यां
वशीकारसंज्ञायां वर्तमानस्य सत्त्वपुरुषान्यताख्यातिमात्ररूपप्र-
तिष्ठस्य सर्वभावाधिष्ठातृत्वम् । सर्वात्मानो गुणा व्यवसायव्य-

---

पञ्चरूपेन्द्रियजयात्सिद्धीराह—**ततो मनोजवित्वं विकरणभावः प्रधानज-
यश्च ।** विदेहानामिन्द्रियाणां करणभावो विकरणभावः । देशः काश्मीरादिः ।
कालोऽतीतादिः । विषयः सूक्ष्मादिः । सोन्वयेन्द्रियजयात्सर्वप्रकृतिविकारवशित्वं
प्रधानजयः । ता एताः सिद्धयो मधुप्रतीका इत्युच्यन्ते योगशास्त्रनिष्णातैः ।
स्यादेतदिन्द्रियजयादिन्द्रियाणि सविषयाणि वश्यानि भवन्तु, प्रधानादीनां तत्कार-
णानां किमायातमित्यत आह—**एताश्चेति ।** करणानामिन्द्रियाणां पञ्च रूपाणि ग्रह-
णादीनि तेषां जयात् । एतदुक्तं भवति—नेन्द्रियमात्रजयस्यैताः सिद्धयोऽपि तु पञ्च-
रूपस्य तदन्तर्गतं च प्रधानादीति ॥ ४८ ॥

त एते ज्ञानक्रियारूपैश्वर्यहेतवः संयमाः साक्षात्पारम्पर्येण च स्वसिद्धयुपसंहार-
संपादितश्रद्धाद्वारेण यदर्थास्तस्याः सत्त्वपुरुषान्यताख्यातेरवान्तरविभूतीर्दर्शयति—
**सत्त्वपुरुषान्यताख्यातिमात्रस्य सर्वभावाधिष्ठातृत्वं सर्वज्ञातृत्वं च ।** निर्धूतर-
जस्तमोमलतया वैशारद्यं ततः परा वशीकारसंज्ञा रजस्तमोभ्यामुपप्लुतं हि चित्तसत्त्वम-
वश्यमासीत्तदुपशमे तु तद्वश्यं योगिनो वशिनस्तस्मिन्वश्ये योगिनः सत्त्वपुरुषान्यता-
ख्यातिमात्ररूपप्रतिष्ठस्य सर्वभावाधिष्ठातृत्वम् । एतदेव विवृणोति—**सर्वात्मान इति ।**

## From that comes speed of mind, independence of the senses <note>original: "vikaraṇa-bhāva"</note>, and mastery over the primal source. ॥ 48 ॥

Speed of mind is the attainment of incomparable movement for the body. Independence of the senses is the attainment of the activity of the senses, whether they are separated from the body <note>original: "videha"</note> or not, dependent upon the desired place, time, and object. Mastery over the primal source is the control over all the modifications of the primary matter <term>prakṛti</term> <gloss>the fundamental creative force</gloss>. These three accomplishments are called "honey-like" <note>original: "madhu-pratīkā"</note>. They are attained through the mastery of the five forms of the sense-organs. ॥ 48 ॥

## For one established only in the discernment between the pure intellect <term>sattva</term> and the Self <term>puruṣa</term>, there arises lordship over all states and omniscience. ॥ 49 ॥

For one who is abiding in the highest clarity of the pure intellect <term>buddhi-sattva</term>, cleansed of the impurities of activity <term>rajas</term> and inertia <term>tamas</term>, and who is currently in the state known as the "highest mastery," there arises lordship over all states, established solely in the discernment between the pure intellect and the Self. All beings are qualities <term>guṇas</term>, which are essentially business and...

---

He speaks of the accomplishments arising from the mastery of the five forms of the senses: **"From that comes speed of mind, independence of the senses, and mastery over the primal source."** The sense-organ's condition when separated from the body is the "independence of the senses." "Place" means places like Kashmir. "Time" means past time and the rest. "Object" means subtle objects and the rest. Following that, mastery over the primal source is control over all modifications of the primary matter. These accomplishments are called "honey-like" by those learned in the science of yoga. 

One might ask: even if the senses with their objects are mastered through mastery of the senses, what is the consequence regarding the primary source <term>pradhāna</term> and its causes? To this, he says: **"And these..."** Through mastery of the five forms of the sense-organs, such as apprehension. This means: these accomplishments are not merely from mastery of the sense-organ itself, but of its five forms, and included within that is the primary source and its derivatives. ॥ 48 ॥

He shows the secondary powers <term>vibhūti</term> of that discernment between the pure intellect and the Self—which is the goal of those <term>saṃyamas</term> that are the causes of power in the form of knowledge and action—by showing it to be the fruit of the faith accomplished by one's own mastery: **"For one established only in the discernment between the pure intellect and the Self, there arises lordship over all states and omniscience."** "Clarity" comes from the removal of the impurities of activity and inertia. From that comes the "highest state of mastery." For the mind-stuff <term>citta-sattva</term> was certainly subservient when clouded by activity and inertia. But upon their cessation, when it is subservient to the yogi who has mastery, there arises in that yogi, who is established solely in the discernment between the pure intellect and the Self, lordship over all states. He clarifies this: **"All beings are..."**

van die spaensche/ als Vygen/ Granaten/ Limoenē/ Citroenē/ Orangen/ Meloenē/ Boonen/ Erwitten en Suycker rieden/ alle seer smackelijck/ jae beter dā in spaengien/ en voor-waer om het menschelijcke levē met vreuchde te passeren/ als die schandale oneenicheden en oorloge daer niet en ware/ is voorseker dese plaetse een van die schoonste van die geheele werelt: want die landtschap daer ontret so getepere/ dat het geheele jaer over geen excessive hitte ofte schadelijcke koude daer is/ oock heeft men nopt gesien dat daer honger ofte pest/ ofte eenige regen ofte donderflagen/ ofte blixem vanden Hemel 

<margin>
Waer voor de Coningen kade haren naem vercregen heeft/ en is ghebout int jaer 1535.
</margin>
geslagen: maer ter contrarie altoos eē helder/ klare en schoone Hemel/ is gesticht van de Admirael Don Francisco Pizarro, int jaer 1535. is genaēt der Coningē stadt/ om dat het volck op drie Coningen dagh/ daer in gebracht zijn/ aenlangēde listrocht/ behalven die visch/ die zy uyt die Zee ende Reviere in grooter overvloet hebbe/ als oock vleysch en vruchte der boomen en der aerde/ gelijck gesept is/ niet minder isser vor overvloedich Terwe en greyn/ en die vier maende alst in spaengiē somer is/ so ist aldaer winter/ ende een wepnich kouder als op ander tijt. In dese 4. winters maende valt alle daghe voor dē middagh eē kleyne dou ofte mist ghelpck nevel/ doch niet als by ons ongesont: wat die welcke pyne int hooft hebbe/ haer hier mede wasschende/ krygen verlichtinghe. Is seer apparent/ dat dese stadt Lima dagelijcks meer toe neme sal van volck en rijckdō/ hoe wel daer voor veel jaren over die 500. huysen gheweest 

<margin>
De breede en lenghte der huysen van Lima.
</margin>
hebben/ en die stadt is seer wit ghebout/ datter wel 2000 staē mogen/ want die straten breedt zijn/ en dat merckt velt groot/ elck huys heeft 80. voete erfs/ en 160. voeten lengten. En om datter geen bequaem hout en is om solders af te maken: want wort binnen 2. ofte 3. jarē vā die wormen veretelt/ so huysen niet dan van eene verdiepinge gebout/ noch tās zeer 

<margin>
Ghedaente vande huysen
</margin>
kostelijck en magnifijck met vele cameren/ salē en faletten/ bequaem om te woone/ en vreemde gasten te herbergen: Die wanden zijn gemaect van eenige materialen die zy aen malkanderen backe seer dick/ en vullē die met aerde. Op decken hare huysen met gheschilderde matten/ oft geschildert lijnwaet/ ronds omme en bovē

<column-break/>

op die wanden make zy prieelkens van riepen daer zy in schuylen voor die Sonne. Voor den regen doze zy niet sorgē: wat ten regent daer niet. Dese stadt heeft onder haer alle dese stede daer Bisschoppen woonen/ Quito, Cusco, Guamanga, Arequipa, Pax, Plata, Trugillo, Guanuco, Chachapoia, Portus vetus, Guayaquil, Popaian, Catchi, S. Michael, S. Francisco. Hier bevorens is gesept dat Peru afgedeelt wordt in drierley landtschappen. In plat lādt aen die Zee in bergen ofte berghachtich landt midden door Peru loopende/ en in landt over die gheberchten. Van het platte landt/ aen die oever des Meers hebben wp tot noch gehandelt/ beginnende vā die Linea eñ die C. Passao tot hier toe/ so is noch te weten/ dat van Tumbes af niet alleen tot Lima: maer noch veel verder die Zee Cust zupden op zeer drooch ende vol groote woeste sandt plaetsen is/ daer 't op 10. mylen weghes die stadt dondert/ bliremt noch regent: maer over die 10. myle wel/ ofte so veel mūn ofte meer alst gheberchte van die Zee lept: Daer zijn oock in dit platte landt geen fonteynen ofte putte: maer wel 4. ofte 5. staende wateren die brack zijn/ om dat zp nae bp die Zee ligghen. Die Inwoonders onderhouden haer met het water uyt die Reviere/ die van die geberchte comen/ die door de sneeu en regē die in de bergē vallen oorspronck nemē/ niet uyt fonteynen die wepnich int gheberchte zijn. Die distantie deser Revieren zijn eensdeels hier te bevores beschrevē/ liggē 7. 8. 10. 12. 15. en 20. mplē vande anderē/ doch meest 7. ofte 8. waer na die repsende lupde haer regulerē/ om dat zp geē ander water elders vindē. Ten bepde zpdē vā dese revierē/ een mple weeghs breet/ ofte ooc luyder/ somtyts meer/ somtyts min/ nae die gelegentheyt vant landt/ zijn differente vrucht-bare boome en coren landen die vant volck gebouwt en besaept werden/ 'twelck zp het gheheele jaer over doen moghen; Oock wassen ontrent dese revierē veellerlep wilde boome/ Cotton/ Riet/ Distelen/ Biesen eñ Lis/ etc. En nae dat die Spaengiaerden het landt inghenomen hebbe/ saepen ooc Terwe/ die landt vocht makende door eenighe Canalen die zp uyt dese Revieren leyden/ Welcke om dat zp van hooghe bergen snel af loopen/ datmen qualijck sonder hulpe over varen mach/ en veel daer inne ver-droncken. Die langs het platte land hare repse doen/ houden gemeenlijck so dichte aen die Zee kant/ dat zp die altoos int gesichte hebbe. Alst winter int geberchte is en veel regent/ so ist periculooz daer te reysen/ om 't aenloopen der revieren die men passeren moet/ ofte met seeckere vloten die zp daer toe hebben/ ofte met een net dat zp met Cauwaerden dichte vullen/ daer op die repsende man uptegestreckt moet liggen/ en eender van die Indianen swemt voren/ dat net ofte die blote met een coorde voort treckende/ en een ander vā achter stuerēde. Het volck vant platte landt woonē onder hutten van mepē gemaeckt. Die mans dragen hemde en doecken op die knien en daer over streckēde/ eñ opperste kleet gelijck eē mantel. Die vrouwē ee Cours vā Cottoen nae die lengte des lijfs/ en hoe wel 't fatsoē van die cleedinge vast over al eenderlep is/ so isser nochtans eenich onderschept int pareelsel des hoofts: wat sommighe enckele coodekē/ sommighe gevlochte/ eenige vā eederlep/ andere van verschepden coleuren die dragē/ en niemant isser ofte hy draecht pet op t hooft/ en alle onderschepdē/ na gewoonhept des landts.

<meta>This page continues the description of the Peruvian coast, moving from the travel route to a detailed account of Lima, the colonial capital, its architecture, climate, and the surrounding geography of the "Llanos" (flat lands).</meta>

# Description of Lima, City of the Kings.

<margin>
The appearance of the city of Lima.
</margin>
In this city, there are good houses, some of which are very beautiful with small towers and galleries. The market square is large, and the streets are wide, all leading directly to the market, from where one may also see into every corner; on both sides lies the open field. Through most of the houses run canals, bringing fresh water from the river, providing great convenience and comfort for the citizens, who can thereby water all their orchards and herb gardens, which they keep beautiful and pleasant. Also,

<margin>
Many watermills, with which they grind their grain.
</margin>
in this river lie many watermills after our own country’s fashion <note>The author compares them to Dutch-style mills</note>, where they grind their grain. In short, very wealthy citizens live here, some of whom possess 150,000 ducats. From this city, ships sometimes depart carrying cargo worth 800,000 ducats, and some even worth a million. On the east side, above the city, is a high mountain upon which stands a crucifix. On another side outside the city, the citizens have their dwellings and places where they keep their livestock, as well as their dovecotes and their vineyards—though the grapes are not good due to the nature of the soil. They have beautiful gardens, filled not only with all kinds of fruits of that land, but also

<margin>
Description of the fertility of the land.
</margin>
with those from Spain, such as figs, pomegranates, lemons, citrons, oranges, melons, beans, peas, and sugarcanes, all very tasty—indeed, better than in Spain. Truly, for passing a human life with joy—were it not for the scandalous discords and wars—this place is certainly one of the most beautiful in the whole world. For the landscape there is so temperate that throughout the entire year there is no excessive heat or harmful cold. Moreover, it has never been seen that hunger or plague occurred there, nor any rain, thunderclaps, or lightning from Heaven

<margin>
Why the City of the Kings obtained its name, and was built in the year 1535.
</margin>
striking the earth. On the contrary, there is always a clear, bright, and beautiful sky. It was founded by the Admiral Don Francisco Pizarro in the year 1535 and is named the City of the Kings because the people were brought into it on Epiphany <note>original: *drie Coningen dagh*; literally "Three Kings' Day," January 6th</note>. Regarding provisions, besides the fish which they have in great abundance from the sea and the river, as well as meat and the fruits of the trees and the earth, as has been said, there is no less an abundance of wheat and grain. During the four months when it is summer in Spain, it is winter there, being a little colder than at other times. In these four winter months, a small dew or mist like a fog falls every day before noon, yet it is not unhealthy like ours; those who have a pain in the head find relief by washing themselves with it. It is very apparent that this city of Lima will daily increase in population and wealth, although for many years there have been over 500 houses,

<margin>
The width and length of the houses of Lima.
</margin>
and the city is built so white that it might well contain 2,000, for the streets are wide and the market square large. Each house has a lot 80 feet wide and 160 feet long. And because there is no suitable wood to make upper floors—for within two or three years it is consumed by worms <note>Likely termites or wood-boring beetles</note>—the houses are built with only one story. Nevertheless, they are very

<margin>
Appearance of the houses.
</margin>
costly and magnificent, with many rooms, halls, and galleries <note>original: *faletten*; likely refers to architectural features like loggias or balconies</note>, suitable for living and for lodging foreign guests. The walls are made of certain materials that they bake together very thickly and fill with earth. They cover their houses with painted mats or painted linen; all around and above

<column-break/>

on the walls, they make small arbors of hoops <note>original: *prieelkens van riepen*</note> where they take shelter from the sun. They do not need to worry about rain, for it does not rain there. This city has jurisdiction over all these cities where Bishops reside: Quito, Cusco, Guamanga, Arequipa, Pax, Plata, Trujillo, Guanuco, Chachapoia, Portus Vetus, Guayaquil, Popayan, Catchi, St. Michael, and St. Francisco. It was mentioned previously that Peru is divided into three types of landscapes: the flat land by the sea, the mountains or mountainous land running through the middle of Peru, and the land beyond the mountains. Of the flat land on the shore of the sea, we have dealt until now, starting from the Equator <note>original: *Linea*</note> and Cape Passao to this point. It should also be known that from Tumbes not only to Lima, but much further south, the sea coast is very dry and full of large, desolate sandy places. Within ten miles of the city, it never thunders, lightens, nor rains; but beyond those ten miles—or as far as the mountains lie from the sea—it does. There are also no springs or wells in this flat land, but rather four or five standing waters that are brackish because they lie near the sea. The inhabitants support themselves with water from the rivers that come from the mountains, which originate from the snow and rain that fall in the mountains, not from springs, of which there are few in the mountains. The distances between these rivers were partly described before; they lie 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, and 20 miles from each other, but mostly 7 or 8, by which travelers regulate their journey because they find no other water elsewhere. On both sides of these rivers, for a mile’s breadth or sometimes more, sometimes less, depending on the layout of the land, there are various fruitful trees and grain fields which are cultivated and sown by the people; this they may do throughout the entire year. Also, many types of wild trees grow around these rivers: cotton, reeds, thistles, rushes, and irises, etc. And since the Spaniards took the land, they also sow wheat, making the land moist through certain canals <note>The *acequias* or irrigation channels inherited from the Incas and expanded by Spaniards</note> which they lead out of these rivers. Because these rivers run swiftly down from high mountains, one can hardly cross them without help, and many have drowned in them. Those who make their journey along the flat land generally keep so close to the seaside that they always have it in sight. When it is winter in the mountains and rains heavily, it is perilous to travel there because of the rising of the rivers that one must pass, either by certain floats they have for that purpose, or with a net that they fill tightly with gourds <note>original: *Cauwaerden*; calabashes used as flotation devices</note>, upon which the traveler must lie stretched out; one of the Indians swims in front, pulling the net or float with a cord, and another steers from behind. The people of the flat land live in huts made of branches. The men wear shirts and cloths reaching to the knees, and over that an upper garment like a mantle. The women wear a gown of cotton the length of the body; and although the fashion of the clothing is almost the same everywhere, there is nonetheless some distinction in the head-dressing: for some wear a single small cord, some braided, some of one color, others of various colors, and there is no one who does not wear something on the head, all distinguished according to the custom of the land.

english: They do not mean "excessively long" or "excessively broad." Regarding the explanation of past actions, "by liberating those to be killed, providing food and drink, performing service for life, and practicing the abandonment of taking life": by liberating those who were to be killed from a short life, they remain in an ordinary lifespan, but it does not mean they suddenly become long-lived. Similarly, by giving the necessities of life, one prevents a short life, but does not suddenly make it long. Likewise, here also, the "long" fingers and heels simply mean they are not short; it does not mean they are excessively long. "Towering seven cubits high" means being taller than the body of an ordinary person; it refers to the measure of the ordinary body. Because the crown of his head <note>original: "ushnisha"</note> cannot be seen, the exact measure of the Blessed One's form body <note>original: "rupakaya"</note> cannot be determined. Abandoning the taking of life corresponds to a straight body because there is no crookedness in the actions of the body. "Feet without protruding joints" refers to the bones of the knee joints and ankle joints; if they are prominent, they are called "bumpy." When they are not like that but are very clear yet well-set and recessed, it is called "feet without protruding joints." In others, because those two bones are large, the feet and calves are unattractive. Because they are not supple, walking is uncomfortable and the gait becomes unattractive. Because the Blessed One's joints are not protruding, his calves are beautiful. Because they are supple, his gait is attractive. Others say that in ordinary people, the ankle bones appear on the back of the foot; therefore, their feet are like they have been pierced with nails, and because they are not supple, they cannot be moved freely, and the soles do not appear when walking. Whoever becomes a sower of greed,
With greed, how can the eye and heart become bright?
Before his eyes, the fantasy of status and gold,
Is just like a hair in the sight.
Except for the intoxicated one who is filled with the Truth,
Even if he is in a corner, he is the master of the treasure.
Whoever becomes graced with the vision,
This world becomes carrion in his eyes.
That Sufi was far from intoxication,
Inevitably, he was night-blind in his greed.
He hears a hundred stories but his intellect is full of greed,
The point does not enter the ear of greed.

**The Proclamation by the Judge's Town Criers to the bankrupt man in the city**

There was a bankrupt man, homeless,
Remaining in prison and bondage, without reprieve.
He ate the prisoners' bread excessively,
Because of greed, he was like Mount Qaf upon the hearts of the people.
No one had the courage to eat a morsel of bread,
Because that morsel of bread would be snatched by his greed.
Whoever is far from the invitation of the Merciful,
He is a beggar, even if he is a Sultan.
He has placed his hope in that profit,
He has made a prison of hell out of that profit.
If you do something for the hope of comfort,
From that side, an affliction will also arrive.
There is no treasure that is not without a snare,
There is no rest except in the sanctuary of the Truth.
The corner of the prison of this world is inevitable,
It is not without the wages of the suffering of the mat.
By God, if you go into a mouse hole,
You will become the victim of a cat's claw.
The son of Adam has an imagination,
That his imagination is a master of beauty.
Consolation is in the imagination,
If the imaginations are of beautiful aspect.
In his imagination, he shows unpleasantness,
The candle from fire, the moth from fire.
Amidst snakes and scorpions, if you have
God with beautiful imaginations.
Snakes and scorpions will be your companions,
Because that imagination of yours was the alchemy of copper.
Sweet patience is from a beautiful imagination,
Because those imaginations are the relief that has come.
That relief comes from faith in the conscience,
Weakness of faith is hopelessness and affliction.
Patience is the foundation of faith,
"Where there is no patience, there is no faith."
The Prophet said God did not give faith,
To anyone who has no patience in his nature.
That one in your eyes is like a snake,
But it is a jewel in the eyes of another.
Because in the eyes, imagination is disbelief,
And that imagination of the believer is in the eyes of a friend.
Disbelief is underneath the imagination of the eye,
Sometimes it is a fishing hook, sometimes it is the moon.
In one person, two forms are evident,
Half of him is greed, and half is the description of the patient.
Half of him is a believer, half is his arrogance,
Half of him is greed-bringing, half is his patience.
Half of him is a believer, half is the mark of an unbeliever,
Half of him is greed, half is the description of the patient.
Your Lord said, "Among you is a believer,"
"And among you is an unbeliever," ancient arrogance.

english: ...at once. **EV.** What birds do I see here? **CA.** It is the patriarch of the college. Do not withdraw; they have already finished drinking; sit down for a little while; when he has departed, we shall converse in our usual manner. **EV.** Come, I will ask of you what you were unwilling to tell me. Now that we are alone, tell me the whole story, for I would rather learn it from you. **CA.** Of so many friends, whom I thought to be the most steadfast, I now perceive there was not one who gave me more prudent and mature counsel than you, the youngest of all. **EV.** But how did you overcome the affection of your parents? **CA.** First, by the wicked exhortations of the monks and nuns; then also by my own: my mother’s spirit was weakened by prayers and blandishments; my father could by no means be persuaded. At last, with every engine brought to bear, he was conquered and overwhelmed, rather than consenting. It was done between drinks: they threatened horrible evil and ruin if he denied his daughter to Christ. **EV.** O the wickedness of fools! What happened then? **CA.** I was kept secretly at home for three days; meanwhile, certain women of that college, whom they call *Conversae*, were always present, adding spirit with their exhortations, that I should persist in the holy purpose, and anxiously guarding that none of my kinswomen or companions should approach me who might seem likely to change my mind. In the meantime, my clothes and other things pertaining to the banquet were being prepared. **EV.** What were your feelings during this time? Did you waver? **CA.** No, but I suffered something so horrendous that I would rather die ten times over than endure it again. **EV.** I beseech you, what is that? **CA.** I cannot speak it. **EV.** What you say to me, you say to your friend. **CA.** Do you promise silence? **EV.** I would have guaranteed that, even if you had stipulated nothing. As if you did not know me yet.

And I ask for my livelihood, like some wandering servant,
having a rough head, with a miserable garment.
And much he
struck the royal house of the Atreidae with evil words,
appearing as an enemy to the commanders.
May he perish, may he perish utterly,
before he sets foot in the land of the Phrygians.
Semi. But fear of Odysseus, or not, holds me.
For Hector will blame us, the guards.
Semi. Who is calling? Semi. Odysseus.
Semi. What are you doing? Why are you trembling?
Semi. To set fire among us. Semi. Which of the men
Semi. These who came by night to the Phrygian army.
Oh, alas. The heavy fate of the spirit. Alas, alas.
Semi. Behold. Silence, everyone.
Semi. Are you afraid? For perhaps someone is coming into the net.
Oh, alas, heavy misfortune of the Thracian allies.
Semi. Who is listening?
Oh, alas. I am of Odysseus, and you, king of the Thracians.
O most wretched one, having looked upon Troy,
what end of life has taken you?
Chor. Who are you among the allies? In the night
my eyes are dim, and I do not know you at all.
Oh, where are the Trojan guards?
Where is Hector
who sleeps under the shield?
To whom do I signal the army of the two kings?
What we have suffered. What someone
has made us disappear, gone, clearly
the Thracian army suffering much.

In this way, the eighth theorem converts with the fourth. For the one states that equal sides and angles subtend equal bases, while the other states that equal sides lying on equal bases contain equal angles. Of these, the one regarding equal bases was the conclusion of the former, while the one regarding "equal sides lying" was one of the hypotheses previously assumed in that same theorem. Since there are these two types of conversion, the primary one is uniform and defined, while the other is varied and proceeds into a large number of theorems, converting not in one case, but in many, due to the number of hypotheses in compound theorems. Often, we also perform a conversion with a theorem starting from two <note>or more</note> hypotheses, when the hypotheses are not all defined, but some are indefinite.

One must also observe in these cases that many conversions turn out to be false and are not strictly conversions; for instance, "every hexagonal number is a triangular number," but it is no longer true that "every triangular number is a hexagonal number." The reason is that the one is more common, while the other is more particular, and it is only said of the one that it is the other. In cases where the attribute belongs primarily and is taken according to that which it is <note>the essential nature</note>, conversion also follows. This has not escaped the notice of the mathematicians around Menaechmus and Amphinomus.

<summary>Proclus explores the mechanics of geometric conversion, noting that false conversions often arise when one term is more general than the other, and asserts that valid conversion requires an essential relationship between the concepts.</summary>
<keywords>conversion, logic, hexagonal numbers, triangular numbers, Menaechmus, Amphinomus, mathematical definitions</keywords>

Since there is no loyalty in any whole, why do you go toward every whole?
All trust is placed in You, for You are the pillar and the mainstay.

If they cut their hands <note>referring to the story of the women who cut their hands upon seeing Joseph's beauty</note> at the face of Joseph,
You have cut two hundred Josephs of the soul with your heart and intellect.

From filth and from goodness, You fashion a form,
From the scent of which the foul-smelling flees for two leagues.

Before the earthy food that becomes pure greenery,
It escapes from impurity when You breathe the spirit into it.

Come, O heart, go to the sky, go to the pasture of God;
You have grazed enough in the pasture of beasts.

Place all your greed on that for which you have no hope;
For from your first despair, you arrived at this side.

Be silent, so that the Lord who grants speech may speak;
For He built the door and the lock, and He also made the key.

---

<meta>This page continues Proclus’s examination of how the Soul acts as a mediating force between the eternal Intellect and the physical world. While the previous page focused on whether Forms exist for base things, this section explores the mathematical "Harmony" and "Numbers" that structure the Soul, and how the Soul uses these to govern the "Vehicle" (ochêma) and the celestial bodies.</meta>

# Commentary on Plato's Timaeus
## Book II: The Harmony of the Soul and the Cosmic Order

<page-num>272</page-num>

...to hold together, for every imposition of form from Being, after it is self-sufficient, acts as a **holding force** <term>Holding force: 'Synektikên', the power that keeps the universe from dissolving into chaos.</term> for the entire cosmos. This is not even the case with the figure itself, for **Forms** and **figures** are partial. But certain cosmic things do not possess all these powers. Just as with natural powers, those beyond reason or technical skill; by art they have power, but the majority in the whole will make the stars that are being formed. Why does the unity of souls remain? Not even there is there a power of the whole, nor in those is there a certain active quality because they are active; but all contribute their own particular qualities, by virtue of having them uniquely; participating in these powers. He fashions them, but not into the same things. He studied something uniquely, even their own psychic strengths. They are not the cause of the body, as we previously assumed; thus also those things that come into being, though they are the same, lack offspring. And from that sacrifice of creation there, why is it that in this way especially the things of the heavens and the numbers of sensible things follow the **Harmony** <term>Harmony: 'Harmonia', here referring to the mathematical ratios used by the Demiurge to weave the soul.</term> which creates **Reason** <term>Reason: 'Logos', often meaning mathematical proportion or ratio in this context.</term> within them? And the greatest things in the middle, toward the center, choose both the harmony of the soul and the sensible number, which are the underlying subjects. For just as the same harmony exists in souls, it does not exist in things that have been harmonized. For indeed, in the greatest intervals, it possesses its own "self-harmony," which does not exist when the soul-elements are safely settled as things harmonized within these. 

This alone is the Reason which is Harmony, as if it had the Form of harmony within itself; from which its works are also beautiful. Just as both remain through the harmony of the soul, for the <unclear>alpha</unclear> itself is harmonized, for through these they transmit it. For they transmit the harmony to certain divisions; and this same thing is well-being. Especially within his sight, he did not weave his own harmony and number from that of beings, but rather showed the sensible harmonies of itself. But the sensible harmony, as they say, has its numbers from its own particular nature. But that which is according to actions—for it is not this one—where the soul possesses harmony; because it might be carried along, even though it stands apart from harmony and the underlying things. But the harmony in **Form** <note>original: "en eidei"</note> is not truly from itself, but rather the things of the soul's **vehicle** <term>Vehicle: 'Ochêma', the subtle, celestial "chariot" or body that the soul inhabits before and after physical incarnation.</term>. And through each, again, the things directed toward the works are brought into harmony with the soul. And because it is the middle, the greatest harmony of number—whether in the earth or the ether—altogether perhaps has straight causes. He says he calls it this; he says it is something evil; for where it is failed, it must be a path, or soul, or mind. For things do not instill Form; this is not the appearance of the Form, for it is either the middle or the extremes.

<column-break/>

<page-num>273</page-num>

...a storehouse it shall have, the last of the private, the most identical, and the first. The order of the **Intellect** <term>Intellect: 'Nous', the divine mind containing the eternal Forms.</term>, increasing within the whole, does not bar this one, but holds equal things from the **Essence** <note>original: 'ousia', the fundamental nature of the soul.</note>. And there is a correction if you should destroy anything in the mind; they are ready for the Forms by not being in the divisible things, the self-same without the essence. But that which is mixed according to each season leads the way according to desire; and again, a preparation for souls, that of the Intellect from the beginning. For when they were studying in that place—among which there is also a certain greater soul, analogous to that which is with the Intellect. Some would be greater, and others would exist from the cause of division; for being placed as the cause of the even, and when the work is in the generation of Being, their parts were composed. The tongue of the thought and the matters of the essence were a concern. For the particular things, all being divided, are active in the forms of the senses; calling those things seen in the multitude. To make the whole from an excess; for he himself is also a power of being, and to God he is harmonized. Indeed, these things do not come from the superior to be understood; for they are similar. This soul established the chance occurrence, holding it together by this cause; and being thus by nature, it rightly sings of both these powers. But the things directed toward the ends in their forms are toward the power; or even the noble mixture, because it holds the power of these. 

Whence follow the things of power. They might speak of the meeting of the extremes with hope, but not by any means; as if to say the same thing of the second life, which is the explanation for the ordering. The cosmic power uses division in that which becomes an attribute of the indivisible—just as with living. For they become greater and similar, so that they are also divisible as if in potential; making it so that the soul may receive the Form. Just as the choice of the superior; for the whole is of each form; so that they are psychic powers of the stronger. He himself made these things best according to the soul; through which they might hold power themselves; where again they might only hold power. But the essence is in this way; whence it indeed seems to set apart—when the Intellect stands still in the greater vision of life; by such causes which, even if one sees such things, they would hold power. Just as the soul of the universe holds power; likewise to make her subordinate to itself, and to be. Not at all, the soul of the universe is of a greater cause; as many as are in their souls. For some are from the soul. The generation of these is eternal; these choose to hold power over the essence—they come into being. For after the sowing or the **demiurgy** <term>Demiurgy: 'Demiorgia', the act of cosmic creation or craftsmanship.</term> itself, the things from it will be established. The soul will make it with that which is from the **Demiurgic Mind**; with the straight power, since that which holds power is the same as those who might hold power. To use the straight path with the powers, this is the honor; the poetic things use the straight path. For these names, the soul...

ἐκείνῳ ἑαυτόν τε, τῆς δὲ ὑδραίας, διελέγετο δὲ ἐπ’ αὐτὸν τὸ ἑαυτοῦ εὐτελές· ἐσέπιπτε δὲ τις ἀκροατὴς τῶν διαλέξεων ὑπὸ τοῦ Δομετιανοῦ καθειμένος. ὁ δὲ χρῆμα ἀγαθὸν ἐδόκει, καὶ κινδυνεύειν τί ὡς ἔφασκε μέγα. γλῶττάν τε οὐκ ἀπαίδευτον εἶχεν, οἵαν τῶν συκοφαντικῶν οἱ ἐκωδωνίζοντο ἐπὶ ῥήματα, ἢ δίκας. ὁ δὲ Ἀπολλώνιος ἑαυτῷ τε ὅ τι τύχοι, διελέγετο ἃ μὴ ἐκείνῳ προὔβαινε. ταῦτα μὲν γὰρ πρὸς αὐτοὺς ἐμέμνητο καὶ ὀρῶν. καὶ θηρία δίψει, καὶ δένδρα· ὑφ’ ὧν, οἱ μὲν, εἴχοντο, οἵ δὲ ἐπέραινον· ὡς δὲ ἐπάγειν αὐτὸν ἐλοιδορίας τοῦ τυράννου ἐπειρᾶτο, ὦ τᾶν ἔφη, σὺ μὲν, ὅ, τι βάλῃ, λέγε. οὐ γὰρ διαβεβλήσῃ ὑπ’ ἐμοῦ· ἐγὼ δὲ, ὁπόσα μέμφομαι τὸν βασιλέα, πρὸς αὐτὸν λέξω. ἐγένετο καὶ ἕτερα ἐν τῷ δεσμωτηρίῳ τούτῳ ἐπεισόδια, τὰ μὲν, ἐπιβουλευόμενα, τὰ δὲ, ὡς ἐπίπαν οὕτω μεγάλα, ἃ οὐκ ἄξια ἐμοὶ ἀναγράφειν. ἐσπέρας δὲ ὁ μὲν ὑπὸ τῷ μὴ παραλελοιπέναι τί, αὐτῶν ἐπεμνήσθη· τὰ δὲ τοῦ λόγου ἐχόμενα, ἐστὶ μετὰ τὰς καθήκοντα δὲ ἡμέρας πέμπτην. παρελθὼν δέ τις ἐς τὸ δεσμωτήριον ἑλληνικὸς τῷ φωνῇ, ποῦ ἔφη ὁ τυανεύς; καὶ ἀπολαβὼν αὐτὸν, αὔριον ἔφη διαλέξεταί σοι ὁ βασιλεύς· Αἰλιανοῦ δὲ ταῦτα ἀκηκοέναι ἐδόκει. ἐχώρησε δὲ ἐς τὸ ἀπόῤῥητον. μόνον γὰρ δὴ ἐκείνου εἰδέναι αὐτὸ· περὶ μὲν καὶ τῷ ἐν τῷ δεσμωτηρίῳ προείρηται ἔφη πᾶν, ἐπὶ τέλοιο ἐπὶ τῇ δίκῃ σοι εἶναι. καλῶς μὲν ποιοῦντες ὑμᾶς εἶπεν ἐγὼ δὲ, καὶ ἐν οἷς ταῦτα βίον, καὶ ἐν οἷς ζῆν δὲ, ταυτὸν πράττω. διαλέξομαι μὲν ὑπὲρ τῶν παραπεπτωκότων, δέομαι δὲ ἐκείνου· ὧδε γὰρ ξυμβουλεύσειν ἔφη Ἀπολλώνιος, ὡς διαλέξῃ τῷ βασιλεῖ; νὴ Δί’ εἶπεν, εἰ μὴ κολάκουσι πείθοι. τί δέ με ὑπερορᾷ ἔφη, μηδὲ ὑπερφρονεῖν αὐτοῦ; ἄριστα εἶπε ξυμβουλεύεις, καὶ ὡς ἐμαυτὸν πέπεικα. ὑποδύων τῶν μὲν ἥκω ἔφη, καὶ χαίρω παρεσκευασμένος σοι ὁρῶν ξυμμίξας. διὰ δὲ τὸ πρὸς τὸ φθέγμα τοῦ βασιλέως παρεσκευάσθαι σε, καὶ πρὸς τὸ δύστροπον τοῦ προσώπου. φθέγγεται μὲν γὰρ βαρὺ, κἀν πράως διαλέγηται· ἡ δ’ ὀφρὺς, ἐπίκειται τῷ τῷ ὀφθαλμῷ ἤθη· μεστὴ δ’ ἡ παρειὰ χολῆς, ταυτὶ γὰρ μάλιστα ἐπιφαίνει· ταῦτα ὦ τυανεῦ, μὴ ἐκπλαττώμεθα. ἔστι γὰρ φύσεως μᾶλλον καὶ ἀεὶ ὅμοια. καὶ ὁ Ἀπολλώνιος, ὁ Ὀδυσσεὺς μὲν ἔφη παλαιὸς ἐς τὸ πολυφημον ᾄδων, καὶ μετὰ ὁπόσ’ ἐστὶ προακηκοὼς πρότερον, μηδὲ οἵα σιτεῖται, μηδ’ ὡς βροντᾷ ἡ φωνὴ, ἐθάῤῥησέ τε αὐτῷ, καίτοι σὲ ἀρχῇ δείσας, καὶ ἀπῆλθε τὸν αὐλὸν, ἀνὴρ δὲ ἐμοὶ ἐμοὶ δὲ βελτίων τε αὔταρκες, ἐμαυτόν τε σώσαντα, καὶ τοὺς ἑταίρους, ὑπὲρ ὧν κινδυνεύω. τοιαῦτα διαλεχθεὶς πρὸς τὸν ἥκοντα, καὶ ἀπαγγείλας αὐτὰ πρὸς τὸν δεῖ μεν, ἐκάθευδε. περὶ δὲ ὄρθρον, γραμματεύς τις ἥκων τῶν βασιλείων λικῶν, κελεύει σε ὁ βασιλεύς ἔφη ὦ Ἀπολλώνιε, περὶ πληθούσαν ἀγορὰν, ἐς πὼ αὐλὴν ἥκειν, οὔπω ἀπολογησόμενον, ἀλλ’ ἰδεῖν τέ σε ὅστις ὢν τυγχάνεις βούλεται, καὶ ξυγγενέσθαι μόνῳ. τί οὖν εἶπεν ὑπὲρ τούτων ἐμοὶ διαλέγῃ; οὐ γὰρ σὺ ἔφη Αἰλιανός; νὴ Δί’ εἶπεν ὁ τυανεύς. πρὸς τίνα οὖν ἔφη ταῦτα εἴπω; πρὸς τοὺς ἄξοντάς με εἶπω. χρὴ γὰρ που ὡς ἐκ δεσμωτηρίου φοιτᾶν. προστέτακται δὲ ἔφη πρὸς οἷς τοῖς ἐκείνοις ταῦτα· κάτω γὰρ ἀφίξομαι τοῦ καιροῦ. τινὶ δὲ παραγγέλων ἦλθον. ταυτὶ γὰρ μάλα ἑαυτῷ σε προστέτακται. ὁ μὲν, δὴ ἀπῆλθεν. ὁ δ’ Ἀπολλώνιος ἀναπαύσας ἑαυτὸν ἐπὶ τῆς κλίνης, ὕπνου ἔφη δέομαι· δεῖ με. χαλεπὴ γάρ μοι ἡ νὺξ γέγονεν, ἀναμνηθῆναι βουλομένῳ, ὧν Φραώτου ποτὲ ἤκουσα. κἀγὼ μὲν ἐγρηγορέναι τέ, εἴπερ ἐχρῶ μᾶλλον, καὶ ἑαυτῷ ἤδη ἑαυτὸν ἴσως παρηγγελμένον, μέγα οὕτως ὄν· καὶ πῶς ἂν ξυνταξαίμην ἔφη, μηδὲ τί ἐρήσεταί σε εἰδώς; οὐ γὰρ αἰάσεις οἷον εἰπεῖν ὑπὲρ τοῦ βίου; νὴ Δί’ ἔφη δέ με. αὐτὸ χρὴ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ χρῶμαι· ἀλλ’ ὅ γε αἰεὶ μνημονεύων οὗ φραώτου. βούλομαι διελθεῖν πρὸς σέ. χρηστὸν γάρ ἐστι τὸ παρὸν τὰ καὶ σοὶ δόξει· τοὺς λέοντας, οὓς τιθασεύουσιν οἱ ἄνθρωποι, κελεύει Φραώτης μήτε παίζειν, μνησικακεῖν γὰρ αὐτοὺς εἰ παίσοιντο, μήτε θεραπεύειν, ἀπερώχους γὰρ ἐκ φύσου γίγνεσθαι, ξυγκαλῇ δὲ μᾶλλον καταπλήττας, ἐς εὐάγωγα ἤδη ἄπειν. τοῦτο δὲ οὐχ ὑπὲρ θηρίων ἀγωγῆς ἐσπουδάζομεν, ἀλλ’ ἡνίκα ὠδὶ τοὺς τυράννους διδούς· ᾗ χρωμένους, οὐκ ἂν ἐκπέσειν ἐκεῖνο γὰρ ξυμμέσου. ἄριστα δὲ ἔφη ὁ λόγος οὗτος ἐς τυράννων ἤδη εἴρηται· ἀλλ’ ἔστι τις καὶ παρὰ τῷ Αἰσώπῳ λέων ὁ ἐν τῷ σπηλαίῳ. φησὶ δ’ αὐτὸν ὁ Αἴσωπος οὐ νοσεῖν μὲν, δοκεῖν δ’ οὖν τῶν θηρίων, ἃ ἐφοίτα παρ’ αὐτὸν ἀπ’ εὐθείας. πῶς δὲ ὁ Ἀλώνιππος οὐ τούτῳ χρώμεθα εἶπε, παρ’ οὗ μὴ δι’ αἰαλύαι τίς, μὴ δὲ λείπεται τί τῶν δεξιότητων ἔχοι;
