to that one himself, and of the water, he conversed about his own cheapness; and a listener of the discourses, settled by Domitian, fell in. And he seemed to be a good thing, and as he said, to be in danger of something great. He also had a tongue not uneducated, such as those of the informers who were ringing for words, or lawsuits. And Apollonius conversed with himself about whatever might happen, which did not proceed to that one. For he remembered these things to them, and seeing. And wild beasts with thirst, and trees; by which, some were held, others were ending; but when he tried to bring him to the abuse of the tyrant, O man, he said, you, whatever you cast, say. For you will not be slandered by me; but I, as much as I blame the king, will say to him. There were also other episodes in this prison, some being plotted, others mostly so great that they are not worth me writing down. And in the evening, he, because of not having left anything, remembered them; but the things held by the speech are after the fifth day that is due. And someone passed into the prison, Greek in voice, Where, he said, is the Tyanean? And having taken him, Tomorrow, he said, the king will converse with you; and it seemed that Aelianus had heard these things. But he went into the secret place. For only he seemed to know it; about indeed and the one in the prison, it has been told before, he said, all, to be at the end of the trial for you. Doing well, he said, for you; and I, in which these are life, and in which to live, I do the same. I will converse about those who have fallen, but I need him; for thus, Apollonius said, will you counsel, as you will converse with the king? By Zeus, he said, if he does not persuade the flatterers. But why does he despise me, he said, and not even disdain him? You counsel best, he said, and as I have persuaded myself. Going under, he said, I have come of some, and I rejoice having prepared to see you having joined. But because of the fact that you have been prepared for the voice of the king, and for the difficult face. For he speaks heavily, even if he speaks gently; and the eyebrow lies upon the nature of the eye; and the cheek is full of bile, for these show most; these, O Tyanean, let us not be struck. For it is more of nature and always similar. And Apollonius, Odysseus, he said, of old, singing to the much-famed, and after how much he had heard before, neither what he eats, nor how his voice thunders, he took courage to him, although fearing in the beginning, and departed the flute, but a man to me, and to me better, self-sufficient, both saving myself and the companions for whom I am in danger. Having conversed such things to the one who had come, and having announced them to the one who needed, he slept. And about dawn, a certain secretary of the kings, coming, says, The king orders you, O Apollonius, about the full market, to come to the court, not yet to apologize, but he wishes to see you, whoever you happen to be, and to be with you alone. Why then, he said, do you converse about these things to me? For are you not, he said, Aelianus? By Zeus, said the Tyanean. To whom then, he said, shall I say these things? To those who lead me, I shall say. For one must, I suppose, go out as from a prison. It has been ordered, he said, to those things, to those; for I will arrive at the time. To whom I am coming, ordering. For these things, indeed, it has been ordered to yourself. He, indeed, departed. But Apollonius, having rested himself on the bed, I need, he said, sleep; I must. For the night has become difficult for me, wishing to remember what I once heard from Phraotes. And I, indeed, to be awake, if one were to use more, and to himself already to himself perhaps having been ordered, being so great; and how, he said, could I compose, not even knowing what he will ask you? For will you not allow, as if to say about the life? By Zeus, he said, I must. I use it for him; but the one always remembering that Phraotes. I wish to go through to you. For it is good that the present also to you will seem; the lions, which people tame, Phraotes orders not to play, for they harbor grudges if they should play, nor to serve, for they become unruly by nature, but rather calls together, striking, to go into already yielding ways. And this we were not zealous about for the sake of the guidance of beasts, but when one gives the tyrants; by which using, one would not fall, for that is of the middle. This speech, he said, has already been spoken to tyrants; but there is also a lion in Aesop in the cave. And Aesop says that he is not sick, but seems to be, of the beasts that visited him from straight ahead. How then, he said, Apollonius, do we not use this, from which one does not, nor is left anything of the skills? And Apollonius, But I, he said, consider the fox wiser; but if having passed, it saw, not inside, but it went out of the cave, it wiped away its own tracks. Having said these things, he brought himself into sleep for a short time, and as much as it came upon the eyes; and when it became day, having prayed to the sun, as is expected in a prison, he conversed with those approaching, as much as they asked; and the market being full, the secretary arrived, and said to be at the doors to release, lest we be called more quickly. Et pacem gregis, quod significet quomodo cum discentibus seu Ecclesia, constat ex significatione pacis, quod sit quomodo se haberet, de qua mox supra n: 4712 ; & ex significatione gregis, quod sint illi qui discunt, pastor enim seu pascens est qui docet & ducit ad bonum charitatis, & grex qui discit & ducitur, de qua n: 343, ita quoque Ecclesia.

4714. Et reduc mihi verbum, quod significet cognitionem, constat ex significatione reducere verbum, quod sit referre quomodo se res haberet, ita cognitio.

4715. Et misit eum e valle Chebronis, quod significet ex Naturali & Sensuali Divino, constat ex significatione mitti, quod sit procedere & docere, de qua supra n: 4710 ; ex significatione vallis, quod sint illa quae infra sunt, de qua n: 1723. 3417 ; & ex significatione Chebronis, quod sit Ecclesia Domini quoad bonum, de qua n: 2909, ita per illa verba significatur quod doceret illa quae inferiora Ecclesiae sunt, & hoc ideo quia superiora non caperent ; qui enim fidem docet & non charitatem, is nusquam superiora seu interiora Ecclesiae appercipere potest, non enim habet quicquam quod ducit, & quod dictat num hoc fidei sit vel num hoc verum, at si docet charitatem, tunc habet bonum, hoc ei dictamen est, & eum ducit, nam omne verum est ex bono & agit de bono, seu quod idem, omne fidei est ex charitate & agit de charitate ; quod omne doctrinae spectet vitam, unusquisque ex solo lumine naturali scire potest. Quod per illa verba significetur ex Naturali & Sensuali Divino, est sensus superior ; quae enim inferiora Ecclesiae sunt, illa dicuntur esse ex Naturali & Sensuali Divino Domini, non quod in Domino haec sint inferiora, nam in Domino & in Ipsius Divino Humano omne est Infinitum, est enim Jehovah quoad utramque Essentiam n : 2156. 2329. 2921. 3023 ; sed quia ita est apud hominem ; qui enim sensuales homines sunt, sensualiter capiunt illa quae in Domino sunt & quae ex Domino, & qui naturales naturaliter ; ex qualitate illorum qui recipiunt, ita dicitur ; qui autem coelestes homines sunt, & inde vere rationales, illi interiora percipiunt, de illis dicitur quod doceantur ex Rationali Divino Domini ; hic est sensus superior, ut dictum, qui per illa verba significatur. <meta>This continues the interpretation of Joseph being sent from the vale of Hebron, contrasting the Natural/Sensual states with the Rational.</meta>

of the Lord is because Joseph represents the Lord as to the Divine Spiritual (n. 4669, 4708, 4710). Therefore, when it is said that Joseph was to go and see the peace of his brothers, it signifies His coming. A "coming" is said to occur when truth from the Word flows into the thought.

4713. "And the peace of the flock," which signifies how things were with those who are being taught, or the Church, is evident from the signification of "peace," which is how things are, as mentioned just above in n. 4712, and from the signification of "flock," which are those who are learning. For a pastor, or one who feeds, is one who teaches and leads to the good of charity, and the flock is the one that is taught and led (concerning which see n. 343), thus also the Church.

4714. "And bring me word again," which signifies knowledge, is evident from the signification of "bringing word back," which is to report how things are, thus knowledge.

4715. "And he sent him out of the vale of Hebron," which signifies from the Divine Natural and Sensual, is evident from the signification of "being sent," which is to proceed and to teach, as mentioned above in n. 4710; from the signification of a "vale," which refers to things that are lower (n. 1723, 3417); and from the signification of "Hebron," which is the Lord’s Church as to good (n. 2909). Thus, these words signify that He would teach the things that are lower in the Church. This is because higher things cannot be grasped; for whoever teaches faith and not charity cannot perceive the higher or interior things of the Church. He does not have anything that leads or dictates whether a thing belongs to faith or whether it is true. But if he teaches charity, then he has good, and this serves as a dictate to him and leads him, for every truth is from good and deals with good—or what is the same, everything of faith is from charity and deals with charity. That everything of doctrine should look to life, everyone can know from natural light alone. That these words signify "from the Divine Natural and Sensual" is the higher sense, for the lower things of the Church are said to be from the Lord’s Divine Natural and Sensual—not that these are "lower" in the Lord, for in the Lord and in His Divine Human everything is Infinite, as He is Jehovah as to both Essences (n. 2156, 2329, 2921, 3023). Rather, it is because this is how it is with man. For those who are sensual men perceive what is in the Lord and from the Lord sensually, and those who are natural perceive them naturally; it is described according to the quality of those who receive it. However, those who are celestial men, and therefore truly rational, perceive interior things; concerning them, it is said that they are taught from the Lord’s Divine Rational. This is the higher sense, as mentioned, which is signified by those words. That "valleys" are the lower things of the Church can be seen from other places in the Word; as in Isaiah: <note>original: "Propheticum vallis visionis; quid tibi hic, quod adscendisti omnis in tecta : dies tumultus, & conculcationis, & perplexitatis Domino Jehovih Zebaoth, in Valle visionis"</note> "The prophecy of the valley of vision; what is it to you here, that you have gone up to the rooftops? A day of tumult, of trampling, and of perplexity for the Lord Jehovah Zebaoth in the valley of vision" (Isaiah 22:1, 5). "Valley of vision" stands for fantasies about spiritual things derived from sensual things, thus from lower things. In the same prophet: "Your choice valleys were full of chariots, and the horsemen set themselves in array at the gate" (Isaiah 22:7). "Choice of valleys" stands for goods and truths in the natural or external man. In the same prophet: "The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare the way of Jehovah, make straight in the desert a path for our God, every valley shall be exalted" (Isaiah 40:3-4). Semianimis & exanguis formidine replebat intuentes: quid so-lutus & incolumis fecisset: Ioannes quidam ledesma hispalensis vaschi amicus & laboru focius: de tigride illo se comedisse fassus est. Bouina carne nihilo deteriorem esse mihi rettulit. Vnde tigridem esse dicant interrogati: qui nunc tigridem uiderunt: respondent a maculis: a feritate: a dexteritate: a signisq̃ aliis ab autoribꝫ datis tigrim arbitrari. Cum & pardos & pantheras maculatos ex ipsis plericq̃ se uidisse praedicent. Tigridi mare pes-rempto montes uersus uestigia illius fecuti antru coniugale ipsius domicilium adeunt.
Duos absente genitrice catulos uberibus adhuc matris indignos auferunt. Mutato consi-lio quo grandiusculos effectos in hispaniam posthec mitterent: ferreis catenis diligen-ter in colla compositis ad maternu antru paruulos reportant. Post paucos in de dies regressi ad speluncam catenis nil suo loco mutatis uacua reperere speluncam. Pu-tanta matre in frusta prae rabie dilaceratos ablatosq̃ ne quiscq̃ sise frueretur. Asseuerant naq̃ solui e catenis nullo pacto potuisse uiuos. Pellis perepti tigridis ad hispaniolam sic cis herbis & culmo farcta missa est ad admirattū & primores a quibus haec nouae terrae leges & auxilia expectant. Et qui a tigride incommoda passi sunt & qui pellem eius tractarunt haec mihi diseruerunt: quae dat accipimus. Ad pacram a quo fumus digreffi redeundu est. De fertos pacrae boios idest domos ingressus uaschus: pacram nititur attrahere. per legatos <margin>Redit pa chra</margin> eadem pacrae significat que caeteris significata memorauimꝫ. diu pacra renuit. Detrecta-ti minae superadduntur. venit tande tribus regulis comitatus. Deforme adeo sordiduq̃ scribit uaschus ac foedu esse pacram: ut turpius quicq̃ se uidisse nunq̃ fateatur. Humana <margin>Qualis sit pacra. p hercule habetur.</margin> tantum illi formam tribuisse naturam inquit: de caetero brutum animal agreste: mostro-sum. Mores inquit habitudini ac lineamentis pares. Quattuor vicinoru reguloru ui rap-tis filiabus abutebatur libidine detestanda. De obscenis pacrae moribus decq̃ ininitis alte-riusmodi multa per finitimos regulos coram uascho uti coram iudice praetorio uel her-cule ultore iactata sunt. ut de pacra suppliciu sumeretur. Belua immane cu <margin>quid cotra sceleratos.</margin> regulis ipsis tribus pacrae dicto parentibus iisdemq̃ morbis laborantibus in bellatorum canum fauces coiecit: illorumq̃ lacerata cadauera cremari iussit. De canibus cu quibus p-lia ineut mira referuntur. Ad indigenas armatos haud ferox insu: non ensibus aut fa-gittis uel tellis aliis opus fuisse ad profligandos hostes obuios: data quippe tessera canis-bus folutis peuntibus agmen torno molofforꝫ aspectu atq̃ infueto latratu perterriti hae <margin>mira de ca nibus.</margin> sitantes pugnas ordinesq̃ stupidi prodigioso inuento deferunt. Aliter tamen accidit qua-do cum caramairensibus & caribibus manus conferuntur: ferociores nanq̃ bellisq̃ gere-dis aptiores sunt: In ruentes canes citius fulgure icto uenenatas destinant fagittas: & mul-tos pimunt. Horum uero montiu incolae non fagittis bella gerunt: maccanis tantum id <margin>qbus armis bella gerut</margin> est ensibus ligneis latis oblongis & missilibus hastisq̃ pustis agunt in hostes. A uiuente pacra ubi nam aurum familiares eius colligerent nullis unq̃ bladiciis aut minis uel tor-mentis potuit extorqueri. Vnde aute illud haberet interrogat: ex eius quippe gazophi-latio libras auri triginta fuerant affecuti: respondit: mortuos esse familiares qui parenti- <margin>30 librafau ri a pacra</margin> fuoq̃ tempore aurum e montibus illis colligeret. Nil fuisse sibi curae ex quo excessit a pu-bertate de auro qritando. Diuelli ab hoc proposito instituto nuq̃ potuit. Ex hac in pacra feueritate finitimorum sibi regulorum animos conciliauit uaschꝫ. <margin>the tiger caught</margin>
animal. By necessity, a trick was finally invented by which it would pay the penalty for so much blood. The narrow paths through which it was accustomed to go out at night to its prey and the hideouts of its caves having been explored, the path was cut. Having dug a pit, they covered it with hurdles and earth, and dispersed the unnecessary part. A tiger, a male, came incautious, fell into the pit, and stuck in the sharp stakes fixed in the bottom of the pit. With its roar, it was deafening the whole neighborhood, and the mountains were resounding with that strident noise. It was killed by huge rocks and stakes thrown at it from the edges of the ditch. It was breaking the spears fixed into it into a thousand splinters and a thousand pieces with its right paw, and thrown from above. Half-dead and bloodless, it filled those watching with fear; what it would have done if released and unharmed! A certain Ioannes Ledesma, a Hispalian and Vasco's friend and companion in labors, confessed that he had eaten of that tiger. He reported to me that it was no worse than bovine meat. When asked whence they say it is a tiger—those who now saw the tiger—they respond that from the spots, from the ferocity, from the dexterity, and from other signs given by the authors, they judge it to be a tiger. Since most of them also declare that they have seen spotted leopards and panthers themselves. With the tiger destroyed, they followed its tracks toward the mountains and reached its den, its marital home. They take away two cubs, still unworthy of the mother's milk, while the mother is away. Having changed their plan to send them to Spain later when they were larger, they returned the little ones to the mother's den with iron chains carefully fastened around their necks. Returning to the cave a few days later, they found the cave empty, with the chains in nothing changed from their place. They think the mother, out of rage, tore them into pieces and carried them away so that no one might enjoy them. For they assert that they could by no means have been loosened from the chains alive. The skin of the destroyed tiger was sent to Hispaniola, stuffed with dry herbs and straw, to the admiral and the leading men from whom the laws and aid of these new lands are expected. And both those who suffered hardships from the tiger and those who handled its skin told me these things, which we accept as given. We must return to Pacra, from whom we departed. Vasco, having entered the villages of Pacra—that is, his houses—strives to attract Pacra. Through envoys, he signifies the same things to Pacra that we recorded were signified to the others. For a long time, Pacra refused. Threats are added to the refusal. Finally, he comes accompanied by three petty kings. Vasco writes that Pacra is so deformed, sordid, and foul that he confesses he never saw anything more shameful. He says that nature gave him only human form; as for the rest, a wild, monstrous brute animal. He says his morals were equal to his habits and features. He was abusing the daughters he had seized by force from four neighboring petty kings with detestable lust. Many things regarding the obscene morals of Pacra and the infinite things of another kind were cast before Vasco by the neighboring petty kings, as before a praetorian judge or Hercules the avenger, so that punishment might be inflicted upon Pacra. He threw the monstrous beast, along with the three petty kings themselves who obeyed Pacra's word and labored under the same diseases, into the jaws of the war dogs, and ordered their lacerated corpses to be burned. Miraculous things are reported about the dogs with which they enter into battle. They were not ferocious against the armed natives; there was no need for swords, arrows, or other weapons to rout the opposing enemies, for when the signal was given and the dogs were released, the troop was terrified by the sight and the unusual barking of the Molossian hounds, and they, stupid, abandon their ranks and the battle at the prodigious invention. It happened otherwise, however, when hands were joined with the Caramairians and Caribs; for they are more ferocious and more apt for waging wars. Rushing upon the dogs, they aim their poisoned arrows faster than a lightning strike, and kill many. The inhabitants of these mountains, however, do not wage war with arrows, but only with <term>maccanis</term> <gloss>wooden swords</gloss>, that is, broad, oblong wooden swords, and they act upon the enemies with missiles and fire-hardened spears. From the living Pacra, where his attendants were gathering gold could never be extorted by any entreaties, threats, or tortures. When asked, however, whence he had it—for from his treasury they had obtained thirty pounds of gold—he responded that his attendants who were gathering gold from those mountains in his father's time and his own were dead. That he had had no concern since he exceeded the age of puberty with searching for gold. He could never be pulled away from this stated purpose. བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་ཏེ། རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་ནི་དྲི་མ་མེད་པ་སྟེ། འོད་གསལ་བའི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་དོ། །དེའི་རྣམ་པ་ཅན་གྱི་སེམས་སུ་གང་གི་ཚེ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པར་གྱུར་པ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་དོན་ཏོ། །གལ་ཏེ་དངོས་པོ་དང་དངོས་པོ་མེད་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་འགྲོ་བ་སངས་
རྒྱས་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་ཉིད་ཡིན་ན། དེ་ལྟ་ན་ནི་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ལྷའི་རྣམ་པར་སྒོམ་པར་བྱེད་ཅེ་ན། དེ་ནི་བདེན་ན་ལྷའི་རྣམ་པའི་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གསུངས་ཏེ། བཞིན་ལག་ཁ་དོག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ནི་ཐ་མལ་པའི་ལུས་ཀྱི་ནི་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་དོན་ཏོ། །དེ་ལྟར་ན་ཡང་བསྒོམ་པ་དོན་མེད་

If you ask what the meaning of "co-emergent" is, it says: "Nature is called co-emergent." This is a synonym for saying it is born together with the nature of all phenomena. That itself is Nirvana. If you ask how it is made so, it says: "By the mind in the form of total purity" and so forth. "Total purity" means being stainless, the nature of Luminosity. The meaning is that when the mind takes that form, it becomes Nirvana.

If the world is the nature of Buddha because it is the essence of things and non-things, then why meditate on the form of a deity? It says: "That is true, but of the deity's form" and so forth. "The face, hands, and color" and so forth refers to the "ordinary body." If you then think that meditation is therefore useless, it says: "However," and so forth. The "habitual tendencies" of the distinct ordinary body refers to the "remnants." The intention is that one should meditate on the deity's body in order to abandon those and to expand the habitual tendencies of the uncontaminated aggregates.

Now, because it is to be established that the meditation on the body is itself the cause for non-abiding Nirvana, it establishes this through many examples. It says: "By that very one who knows the poison" and so forth. "To extract" means to overcome. Why was it called "wind" in the previous part? Because it is the cause of breath. How is it reversed? Because it is of the same class. Its examination is that very benefit. "Existence" is <term>Samsara</term> <gloss>cyclic existence</gloss>. "Purity" is total exhaustion.

The phrase "by existence itself" means that through the total transformation of the sun, moon, hand-symbols, and seed-syllables, there is "existence." The meaning is that through the very form of the deity, those <note>samsaric states</note> are exhausted. "Conceptual thought" is <term>Samsara</term>. The meaning is that through the conceptual thought of the deity's form, it will be exhausted. The phrase "Just as water enters the ear" is the example

<summary>This page argues that while all beings are naturally 'co-emergent' with Buddha-nature, deity meditation is necessary to clear away ordinary habitual tendencies. It uses the analogy of using poison to cure poison to show how conceptual meditation can exhaust samsaric concepts.</summary>
<keywords>Nirvana, Luminosity, Deity Meditation, Habitual tendencies, Samsara, Purity, Non-abiding Nirvana</keywords>

རང་གི་མཐུ་འབའ་ཞིག་གིས་སྐྱེ་བ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རྟེན་ཅིང་འབྲེལ་བར་འབྱུང་བ་ཁོ་ནའོ། །ཆོས་གཞན་ལ་#བརྟེན་ཏེ་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཆོས་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་དག་ནི་གཟུགས་སུ་རུང་བ་དང་། མྱོང་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་རང་བཞིན་ཡིན་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་། རྒྱུ་དང་རྐྱེན་ཚོགས་པ་ཉིད་ལས་སྐྱེ་བར་འགྱུར་
བས་ན་འདུས་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །འདུས་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་རང་གི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཅེས་བརྗོད་པར་ཇི་ལྟར་ནུས། དེ་བས་ན་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་གཞན་གྱི་དངོས་པོས་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རང་གི་དངོས་པོ་མེད་པས་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་མེད་པ་ཉིད་དོ། །རང་གི་དངོས་པོ་མེད་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་དངོས་པོ་
མེད་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཅེས་བྱའོ། །དེ་བས་ན་རབ་འབྱོར་འདུས་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་མེད་དེ། རྟེན་ཅིང་འབྲེལ་པར་འབྱུང་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་#གསུངས་སོ། །འདི་ཉིད་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་དངོས་པོ་མེད་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་དེ། དངོས་པོ་མེད་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ཅེས་བྱའོ། །
བཤད་པ་ཅིག་ཤོས་ནི། དངོས་པོ་ནི་དངོས་པོས་སྟོང་ངོ་། །དངོས་པོ་མེད་པ་ནི་དངོས་པོ་མེད་པས་སྟོང་ངོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྟེ། དངོས་པོ་དང་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ནི་དངོས་པོ་དང་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་དོ། །དངོས་པོ་དང་། ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་མེད་པ་ནི་དངོས་པོ་དང་། ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་མེད་པ་སྟེ། རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་པ་འདི་ལ་
དངོས་པོ་མེད་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་སྒྲས་ནི་དངོས་པོ་ཡོད་པ་མ་ཡིན་པར་རྟོགས་#པས་དངོས་པོ་དང་། དངོས་པོ་མེད་པ་ཡང་བཟུང་བ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་མེད་དོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་སྒྲས་ནི་རང་གི་དངོས་པོ་མ་ཡིན་པར་རྟོགས་པས་གཞན་གྱི་དངོས་པོ་དང་། རང་གི་དངོས་པོ་ཡང་བཟུང་བ་ཡིན་ཏེ། 
སྟོང་པ་བཞི་པོ་དེ་དག་ལ་དངོས་པོ་མེད་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ཅེས་བྱའོ། །དེ་ལས་བྱུང་བས་ན། དངོས་པོ་ཞེས་བྱ་སྟེ། དངོས་པོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་སྒྲ་ནི་འདུས་བྱས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ལ་བྱའོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་དངོས་པོ་ནི་དངོས་པོས་སྟོང་ངོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །དངོས་པོ་མེད་པའི་སྒྲས་#ནི་
english: ...by their own power alone; they arise by the power of causes and conditions. For example, when a seed produces a sprout, it does not produce it by its own power alone, but by the power of the collection of earth, water, and so forth. Similarly, all phenomena arise by the power of the assembly of causes and conditions. Because they do not arise by their own power alone, they are strictly dependently originated. Those phenomena that arise depending on other phenomena—even though they may possess the nature of being suitable as form, or being feeling, and so forth—are called "born from a collection" because they arise only from the assembly of causes and conditions. How can that which is "born from a collection" be called an "intrinsic nature"? Therefore, because all phenomena arise through the entities of others, they lack their own entity and thus lack intrinsic nature. Because they lack their own entity, it is called "the nature of non-entities." Therefore, it is said: "Subhuti, the nature of phenomena born from a collection does not exist, because they are dependently originated." This itself is the "nature of non-entities" of all phenomena, and it is called "the emptiness of the nature of non-entities." The other explanation is: "Entities are empty of entities; non-entities are empty of non-entities." Entities and intrinsic natures are "entities and intrinsic natures." The absence of entities and intrinsic natures is "non-entities and the absence of intrinsic nature." In this conceptualization, the term "non-entity" understands that entities do not exist, so both entities and non-entities are included. The term "no intrinsic nature" understands that it is not one's own entity, so both the entities of others and one's own entity are included. Those four emptinesses are called "the emptiness of the nature of non-entities." Because they arise from that, they are called "entities." The term "entity" refers to conditioned phenomena. Therefore, it is said "entities are empty of entities." By the term "non-entity"...

ཐོད་རྒལ་དུ་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པ་ལ་མཉམ་པར་བཞག་#ནས་སྙོམས་པར་འཇུག་པ་དེ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་གནས་པར་བྱེད་དོ། །བཅོ་ལྔ་པ་དག་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་དང་། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་དང་ལྡན་ཞིང་། ཡོངས་སུ་འདྲིས་པའི་ཤེས་པས་རྒྱུན་དུ་ཞུགས་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་
ལ་སོགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་ཤེས་པར་བྱས་ཀྱང་དེ་དག་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་མི་#བྱེད་པར་གཞན་དག་ཀྱང་ལམ་དང་འབྲས་བུ་དེ་དག་ལ་སོ་སོར་འགོད་དོ། །ཡོངས་སུ་དྲིས་#པའི་ཤེས་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ལ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་བཟོད་པ་དམ་པ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །བཅུ་དྲུག་པ་དག་ནི་བསྐལ་པ་བཟང་པོའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་
སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ཏེ། གང་བསྐལ་པ་འདི་ཉིད་ལ་མངོན་པར་རྫོགས་པར་སངས་རྒྱས་ཏེ། དེ་དག་རྣམ་པར་མི་རྟོག་པའི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་ལ་གནས་ནས་དགའ་ལྡན་གྱི་གནས་སྦྱོང་བར་བྱེད་དོ། །བཅུ་བདུན་པ་དག་ནི་སྐྱེ་བ་གཅིག་གིས་ཐོགས་པ་སྟེ། ཉན་ཐོས་དང་རང་

perfection of wisdom. In order to purify the Buddha-fields, they take birth from one Buddha-field to another.

The fourteenth type dwells in the non-conceptual perfection of wisdom. Having settled in meditative equipoise, they dwell in those absorptions by leaping over <note>a specific advanced meditative technique</note> the stages of absorption.

The fifteenth type possesses the factors of enlightenment and the Buddha-phenomena. Through their familiarized knowledge, although they fully understand the fruit of Stream-enterer and so forth, they do not manifest them personally. Instead, they establish others in those paths and fruits. This very familiarized knowledge is called the supreme "Bodhisattva's patience."

The sixteenth type are the Bodhisattvas of the Good Aeon. Those who manifest perfect enlightenment in this very aeon dwell in the six non-conceptual perfections and purify the Tuṣita abode.

The seventeenth type are those hindered by only one birth <term>eka-jāti-pratibaddha</term>. They possess all the qualities of Shravakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas, and through familiarized knowledge, they remain seeking the Noble Truths.

The eighteenth type, after having manifested perfect enlightenment over many hundreds of thousands of millions of countless aeons, remain dedicated to the welfare of sentient beings, such as the Noble Manjushri in the form of a youth.

The nineteenth type similarly strive for perfect enlightenment and remain teaching the Dharma to sentient beings.

The twentieth type similarly work for the benefit of sentient beings and dwell from Buddha-field to Buddha-field.

The twenty-first type dwell in the six perfections but specifically satisfy sentient beings through generosity and establish sentient beings in generosity itself.

པས་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཕྱག་རྒྱ་དེ་དང་ཕྱག་རྒྱས་བཏབ་པ་དག་དབྱེར་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བར་དགོངས་སོ། །གྲོང་ཁྱེར་ནི་པ་ཏ་ལི་པུ་ཏྲའོ། །ཧ་རི་ཀེ་ལའི་ཁྱད་པར་ནི་ལན་ཚྭ་རྒྱ་མཚོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའོ། །གསེར་དང་ལྡན་པ་ནི་གསེར་གླིང་ངོ་། །ཉེ་འཁོར་ནི་དེ་དང་ཉེ་བས་ན་ཉེ་འཁོར་རོ། །རྫིང་

If one wonders "how" with these grounds, "by these" means by the grounds of the sites and so forth. The mudras of the Ground of Practicing Devotion, the Joyous Ground, the Stainless Ground, and so forth, up to and including the Ground of Light, which are the grounds of primordial wisdom, are the sites and so forth as appropriate; such is the intention. "Others are inexpressible" means it is not because they are excluded from the sites and so forth; the intention is that the mudra and that which is sealed by the mudra are indivisible. "City" is Pāṭaliputra. The distinction of Harikela is the Salt Ocean and so forth. "Possessed of gold" is the Island of Gold <term>Suvarṇadvīpa</term>. "Proximity" means the vicinity of that. "Pond" refers to those staying in Narpa. "Hungry ghost" <term>Preta</term> "half-moon" means the end of the month. "Banner" is the graceful one. "Generating compassion" means thinking about the suffering of that very state. "By the wise" means by the learned. "Malicious" refers to those who hate the vehicle of mantra. "To make them enter" refers to the vehicle of mantra. "By that reason, all rituals" means all should be performed. "Principally" means by making them enter principally. Having spoken of compassion, wisdom <term>Prajñā</term> is also spoken: "In that..." and so forth. "Should be seen" means should be contemplated. Those two times are Hevajra and his Wisdom. Therefore, all actions gathered by that are virtuous. Other methods are spoken: "nothing not to be done..." and so forth. "In this" refers to the pride of Hevajra. Just as one is devoted to oneself, it is the same for sentient beings; therefore, for the sake of genuine gathering, "oneself also" is the meaning. 17. අථ වා පන උක්කණ්ඨිතො අනභිරතො සාමණෙරු ච විත්තුකාමො සික්ඛාපදං අක්ඛායමානො හරයමානො ජිගුච්ඡමානො ගිහිභාවං පත්ථයමානො --පෙ-- අසක්කසප්පතිභායමානො පත්ථයමානො ‘මාතා මෙ අත්ථි සා මං පොසෙස්සතී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘පිතා මෙ අත්ථි සො මං පොසෙස්සතී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘භාතා මෙ අත්ථි සො මං පොසෙස්සතී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘භගිනී මෙ අත්ථි සා මං පොසෙස්සතී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘පුත්තො මෙ අත්ථි සො මං පොසෙස්සතී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘ධීතා මෙ අත්ථි සා මං පොසෙස්සතී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, --- ‘පජාපතී මෙ අත්ථි සා මං පොසෙස්සතී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, ---‘ඤාතකා මෙ අත්ථි තෙ මං පොසෙස්සන්තී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘මිත්තා මෙ අත්ථි තෙ මං පොසෙස්සන්තී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති,-- ‘ගාමො මෙ අත්ථි තෙතාහං ජීවිස්සාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘නිගමො මෙ අත්ථි තෙතාහං ජීවිස්සාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘ඛෙත්තං මෙ අත්ථි තෙතාහං ජීවිස්සාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘වත්ථු මෙ අත්ථි තෙතාහං ජීවිස්සාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘හිරඤ්ඤං මෙ අත්ථි තෙතාහං ජීවිස්සාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, ---‘සුවණ්ණං මෙ අත්ථි තෙතාහං ජීවිස්සාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -පෙ- ‘සිප්පං මෙ අත්ථි තෙතාහං ජීවිස්සාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, එවම්පි සික්ඛාවෙ දුබ්බල්‍යාවිකම්මක්ඛෙව හොති සික්ඛා ච අපවචක්ඛාතා.

18. අථ වා පන උක්කණ්ඨිතො අනභිරතො සාමණෙරු ච විත්තුකාමො සික්ඛාපදං අක්ඛායමානො හරයමානො ජිගුච්ඡමානො ගිහිභාවං පත්ථයමානො --පෙ-- අසක්කසප්පතිභායමානො පත්ථයමානො ‘දුක්කර’න්ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති -- ‘කසුකර’න්ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, ‘දුබ්බර’න්ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘න සුවර’න්ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘න උස්සාහමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -- ‘න විස්සාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, --- ‘න රමාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, -පෙ- ‘න අභිරමාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, එවම්පි බො භික්ඛවෙ දුබ්බල්‍යාවිකම්මක්ඛෙව හොති සික්ඛා ච අපවචක්ඛාතා.

19. කථඤ්ච භික්ඛවෙ දුබ්බල්‍යාවිකම්මක්ඛෙව හොති සික්ඛා ච පවචක්ඛාතා? ඉධ භික්ඛවෙ භික්ඛු උක්කණ්ඨිතො අනභිරතො සාමණෙරු ච විත්තුකාමො සික්ඛාපදං අක්ඛායමානො හරයමානො ජිගුච්ඡමානො ගිහිභාවං පත්ථයමානො -පෙ- අසක්කසප්පතිභායමානො පත්ථයමානො ‘බුද්ධං පවචක්ඛාමී’ති වදති වික්ඛිපෙති, එවම්පි භික්ඛවෙ දුබ්බල්‍යාවිකම්මක්ඛෙව හොති සික්ඛා ච පවචක්ඛාතා.

<vocab>Pali, Vinaya Pitaka, Parajika Pali, Sikkhapada, Bhikkhu, Samaneru</vocab>
english:
17. Or, if he is dissatisfied, not liking the life, wishing to renounce the monkhood, failing to recite the training rule. Being humiliated, ashamed, disgusted, he desires the life of a householder—up to—and fearing that he is not a true follower of the Sakyans, he says, "I have a mother, she will support me," and he recites the training, "I have a father, he will support me," and he recites the training, "I have a brother, he will support me," and he recites the training, "I have a sister, she will support me," and he recites the training, "I have a son, he will support me," and he recites the training, "I have a daughter, she will support me," and he recites the training, "I have a wife, she will support me," and he recites the training, "I have relatives, they will support me," and he recites the training, "I have friends, they will support me," and he recites the training, "I have a village, I will live by it," and he recites the training, "I have a town, I will live by it," and he recites the training, "I have a field, I will live by it," and he recites the training, "I have an estate, I will live by it," and he recites the training, "I have gold, I will live by it," and he recites the training, "I have silver, I will live by it," and he recites the training—up to—"I have a craft, I will live by it," and he recites the training. In this way too, monks, the weakness is declared, and the training is renounced.

18. Or, if he is dissatisfied, not liking the life, wishing to renounce the monkhood, failing to recite the training rule. Being humiliated, ashamed, disgusted, he desires the life of a householder—up to—fearing that he is not a true follower of the Sakyans, he says, "It is difficult," and he recites the training, "It is very difficult," "It is unbearable," "It is not easy," "I do not have the energy," "I do not believe," "I do not delight,"—up to—"I do not find pleasure," and he recites the training. In this way too, monks, the weakness is declared, and the training is renounced.

19. And how, monks, is the weakness declared and the training renounced? Here, monks, a monk who is dissatisfied, not liking the life, wishing to renounce the monkhood, failing to recite the training rule, being humiliated, ashamed, disgusted, desiring the life of a householder—up to—fearing he is not a true follower of the Sakyans, says, "I renounce the Buddha," and he recites the training. In this way too, monks, the weakness is declared, and the training is renounced.

reversals.english: In this way too, monks, the weakness is declared, and the training is renounced.
the weakness is declared, and the training is renounced

defects: T8: §17/§18 refrains reversed to 'training is renounced'
T7: 'and he recites the training' repeated for each declaration; 'failing to recite the training rule'
mistranslation: 'fearing that he is not a true follower of the Sakyans' — patthayamāno means longing
T8: §17/§18 'the training is renounced' reverses 'apaccakkhātā'

و شهادت چه در دینی و چه در آخرت و مقصود با آن به
تحقیق و ظهور کمال اسما است که کمال جلا و استجلا است کمال
جلا یعنی ظهور او بحسب این اعتبارات و کمال یعنی استجلا
شود او را بحسب عین اعتبارات و این ظهور و شهود
عیانی عینی چون ظهور و مجمل مفصل بخلاف کمال ذاتی که ظهور
ذات است بنفس خود و از برای نفس خود بی اعتباری
و غیریت و این ظهور است علمی چون ظهور مفصل مجمل
و نمای مطلق لازم کمال آنیت و مغنی غنای مطلق است که
شئون و احوال اعتبارات ذات با احکامها و لوازمها
علی وجه کلی سبحانه که در جمله مراتب حقایق آلی و کونی
می نماید مر ذات را از بطنها و اندراج الکل فی وجدتها
شاهد و ثابت باشند بجمیع صورها و احکامها کما ظهرت ثبت

<meta>continues from previous page: world of the senses.</meta>
And witnessing, whether in religion or in the hereafter, and its purpose is the realization and manifestation of the perfection of the Names <note>original: "asma"</note>, which consists of the perfection of manifestation <gloss>jala</gloss> and the perfection of self-vision <gloss>istijla</gloss>. The perfection of manifestation <gloss>jala</gloss> refers to His appearance according to these conceptual considerations, and the perfection of self-vision <gloss>istijla</gloss> refers to His perception of Himself through these very considerations. This manifestation and vision is an ocular and concrete witnessing <note>original: "shuhud-i 'ayyani 'ayni"</note>, like the appearance of the detailed within the concise. This is in contrast to the Essential Perfection, which is the manifestation of the Essence to itself and for itself, without any consideration of otherness. This latter manifestation is intellectual <gloss>'ilmi</gloss>, like the appearance of the concise within the detailed. The Absolute Manifestation is a necessary consequence of the perfection of His I-ness <note>original: "aniyyat"</note> and His Absolute Independence <gloss>ghina</gloss>. All the modes, states, and considerations of the Essence, with their rulings and requirements, are expressed in a universal manner. Glory be to Him, who manifests Himself through all the levels of instruments and cosmic realities <note>original: "haqayiq-i ali va kouni"</note>, emerging from the inner depths and the inclusion of the whole within His Oneness. They are witnessed and established in all their forms and rulings, just as they appeared and were established.

T8: both similes swapped: 'detailed within the concise' for 'مجمل مفصل', 'concise within the detailed' for 'ظهور مفصل مجمل'

לכלות במתפט וסולל לקלוט לקדקם. ועל זה נאמר ויוי כי זקן יצחק
ותכהנה כלומר נס עליו נס על מדתו מדבר. ולפיכך ית' כסעת הדין הקטס
מרחם על עולמו וחוזר למעכי למעכי לעסקה כי חיך יתל' וזהו כסעת הדין הקטס
דוד כל חלה כדור קוים כל וזהו סוד כל הפך לכן טהור הוא. ועל דרך זה
סתכונן להין לפחד יצחק כח וממלה כטעם סתכתר כעליון מחיר פניו למט' לכי
לחולו הגדול מכסה חי לתק רחמיס כטעם סחיר פניו העליוני יתנלך מתכת
מכס. וזהו כויל וילד פניו ית' ויומך. והנני מחיר שיויך עוד כעס' לע
כי בכל מקוס סלתס מוכח חור פני' למעלה הוא קוד גדול והוא כי יוס סלס מלות
ועטרה פניס של יעם וכלס לדווקיס כפחד יצחק וכסמדת הכתר מחירה פניה
ומיוחסת לכל סל רמיס ונתפסת ונתפסת כלן לרמיס. וזהו סוד אל ירול ויתר
לכו. וזהו סדרו סעס ויועו תרועה וילד כחור פניך יסלכין. וכל' סתכונן סוד
יוסי כי יצחק יתקק ותכהנה עיניו מלחות. ולו תסיג סוד תקעו כסוד סופר כסוס
ליוס קננו. וסוד לטרי העס יודע תרועה וילד כחור פניך והלכין יתרחם מססוס
סופר סל חילו של יצחק. וכתקתכונן שכיניס כחור פניך והלכין יסוד סלכו לומריס

to finish in judgment and pave the way to receive their holiness. Regarding this, it is said: "And it came to pass, when Isaac was old, and his eyes were dim" <note>Genesis 27:1</note>. This means a miracle occurred regarding his attribute. Therefore, blessed be He, at the time of judgment, the Smallness <note>the lesser manifestation of the divine</note> has mercy on His world and returns to His deeds for the sake of the depths. This is the secret of the time of judgment: when everything is turned, then it is pure. 

In this way, contemplate how to understand the <term>Pachad Yitzchak</term> <gloss>Fear of Isaac</gloss> and the word according to its meaning. He is crowned in the Supreme, hiding His face below for His great soul, covering the attribute of Mercy <term>Rachamim</term>. As His face is turned, the Supernal is revealed through the covering. This is the secret of "he turned his face" and was hidden. 

I will now explain to you more concerning the "back." Know that wherever you find the "light of the face" above, it is a great secret. The day of three attributes and the crown of the face are all attached to the <term>Pachad Yitzchak</term> <gloss>Fear of Isaac</gloss>. When the attribute of the <term>Keter</term> <gloss>Crown</gloss> illuminates its face, it is attributed to the totality of Mercy and is grasped there as Mercy. This is the secret: "God is the Lord, and He has given us light" <note>Psalm 118:27</note>. 

This is the order: "Happy is the people that know the joyful sound; they shall walk, O Lord, in the light of Your countenance" <note>Psalm 89:16</note>. Contemplate the secret of: "when Isaac was old and his eyes were dim from seeing." You will then grasp the secret of the sounding of the <term>shofar</term> <gloss>ram's horn</gloss> on the day of our festival. The secret of "Happy is the people that know the joyful sound" is that they will walk in the light of the face through the merit of the ram of Isaac. 

When you contemplate "in the light of Your countenance they shall walk," you will find our foundation when we say "the Rememberer of forgotten things." Through the secret of the "Back of the Throne," you will understand the difference between the "Rememberer of forgotten things" and the "Recall of the Back of the Throne." The "Rememberer of forgotten things" comes from the Great Mercy above, in the secret of "God is the Lord, and He has given us light." The "Back of the Throne" comes from the attribute of <term>Elohim</term> <gloss>God/Judgment</gloss>, from the attribute of the darkness of which it is said "and darkness was upon the face of the deep" <note>Genesis 1:2</note>, which is the secret of the covering of Kindness <term>Chesed</term>. Therefore, the attribute of the Tetragrammaton illuminates below while being included in the attribute of <term>Elohim</term> <gloss>Judgment</gloss>, which is the place of the secret of the head. This is the secret of "He turned His face." 

Understand this well regarding these two attributes. Now I will inform you of the secret of the attribute of the Name, which is the mediator in the center. It connects and encompasses its perfection. These are the "nicknames" of the Name that stands in the middle, connecting the right side, which is <term>Chesed</term> <gloss>Kindness</gloss>, and the left side, which is <term>Din</term> <gloss>Judgment</gloss>. They are all included in the middle through Kindness and Judgment. These are called the "Attributes of Mercy," and their height in the middle of the emanation is the Mercy of the worlds.

I will now explain. Know that all the holy names, the nicknames, and the words, whether they are called Kindness, whether they are called Mercy, or whether they are called Judgment: there is not one among them that is pure Kindness or pure Judgment or pure Mercy without a mixture. This applies to everything from the first emanation and downward. But from Him and upward, all is Mercy and pure Kindness, simple and without mixture. 

Now, open your eyes and set your heart to these deep matters. They are like rules for the paths of the Chariot and the connection of the <term>Sefirot</term> <gloss>Divine Emanations</gloss>. When you see this, you will understand how the <term>Sefirot</term>, the Names, and the words are connected in the world. Regarding the Holy One, blessed be He, you will understand the secret of the "Root of the All." Know that the Names of the Supernal <term>Keter</term> <gloss>Crown</gloss> are all simple Names without any mixture. Like the known days of Mercy that are close to the name <term>Ehyeh</term> <gloss>I Will Be</gloss>, or the Kindness that is close to the name <term>Ehyeh</term>, they are all perfectly simple without mixture. This is the secret of what is said: "but with great mercies will I gather thee" <note>Isaiah 54:7</note>. What are these "great mercies"? They are...

# || Hitopadesha ||

->|| 140 ||<-

If war is imminent, O King, why not prepare for battle beforehand? Because: "He is neither a servant nor a minister who, at the very beginning, advises a King to rush into battle or abandon his own station without due consideration." Moreover: "One should never try to conquer enemies by war. It is not certain which of the two warring sides will be victorious." Furthermore: "One should try to overcome the enemy through <term>sama</term> <gloss>conciliation/peaceful means</gloss>, <term>dana</term> <gloss>gifts/bribery</gloss>, and <term>bheda</term> <gloss>dissension/creating discord</gloss>, either individually or all together; never by war." Moreover: "All people are heroes as long as they have not encountered a fight, have not seen the enemy's strength, and are full of pride." Furthermore: "War is not as easily provoked by living beings as it is terrible; the success of small means is not a small result. However, seeing that war is imminent, it should be treated with disdain." Because:

War is present. The <term>Chakravaka</term> says, "O King, war is not to be done first, because he is no servant and he is no minister who, at the beginning, advises the King to rush into war or to leave his own place without consideration. Furthermore, one should try to conquer the enemy by <term>sama</term> etc. [Conciliation, gifts, and discord], and never by war, because it is not certain who will win between two who are fighting. Furthermore, one should try to resolve the enemy by conciliation, gifts, or discord, separately or altogether, but never by war."

<summary>The King and his minister discuss the necessity of espionage, the importance of secrecy, and the philosophical preference for diplomacy over open warfare.</summary>

...a part out of one hundred and nine parts of a share. So you make the share one hundred and nine parts, and multiply the thirteen by one hundred and nine parts, and add to that eighty parts, and it becomes one thousand four hundred and ninety-seven, and the husband's portion is three hundred and twenty-seven.

If you leave two sisters and a wife, and bequeath to a man the equivalent of a sister's portion minus one-eighth of what remains of the <term>mal</term> after the legacy, the method for that is to set the distribution of the estate at twelve shares for each sister, a third of what remains of the <term>mal</term> after the legacy. You know that one-eighth of what remains with the legacy equals a sister's portion. So one-eighth of what remains is one-eighth of a <term>mal</term> minus one-eighth of a legacy. So one-eighth of a <term>mal</term> minus one-eighth of a legacy plus a legacy equals a sister's portion, which is one-eighth of a <term>mal</term> plus seven-eighths of a legacy. The whole <term>mal</term> equals three-eighths of a <term>mal</term> plus one-third of a legacy and five-eighths of a legacy. Subtract three-eighths from the <term>mal</term>, and there remains five-eighths of the <term>mal</term> equaling three legacies and five-eighths of a legacy. The whole <term>mal</term> equals five legacies and four-fifths of a legacy. The <term>mal</term> is twenty-nine, the legacy is five, and the portion is eight.

In another method of legacies, a man died and left four sons and bequeathed to a man the equivalent of the portion of one of his sons and to another a quarter of what remains of the third. Know that the legacy is only from the third.

english: ...to go a mile, go with him twain. Love your enemies, and do good to them which hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you and persecute you; that you may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for He maketh His sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust." You answer: "These things were not said to me. They were said to the apostles, they were said to the perfect." Have you not heard: "That you may be the children of your Father"? If you do not desire to be a child of God, the law does not pertain to you. Although, not even a good man is one who is unwilling to be perfect. Take this also: if you do not desire the reward, the command is nothing to you; for it follows: "For if you love them which love you, what reward have you?" As if he were to say: "None." For there is no virtue in doing this; but not doing it is a crime. Nothing is owed to either when equal has been returned for equal. Hear Paul, the great consultant and interpreter of Christian laws. Bless them which persecute you: bless, and curse not. Recompense to no man evil for evil. If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men. Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord. But if your enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing you shall heap coals of fire on his head. Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good. What, then, is to happen, you ask, if I nurture another's insolence with my gentleness, and by bearing an old injury, invite a new one? If you can either avoid or repel evil without your own evil, no one forbids you to do so; but if not, take care not to say, "It is more honorable to do harm than to suffer it." If you can, amend it, either by overwhelming them with benefits or by overcoming them with meekness. If otherwise, it is better for the other to perish than for both to do so; it is better for you to grow rich in the profit of patience than for both to become evil by mutual retaliation of evil. Therefore, let it be a Christian decree: to contend with all in love, meekness, and beneficence; and to willingly yield, even to the lowest, in contention, detraction, insults, and injury. "But he is unworthy," they say, "to whom a benefit should be done, to whom a concession should be made." But you are worthy to do it, Christ is worthy, for whose grace it is done. "I do not wish to harm anyone," they say, "nor will I suffer myself to be harmed." Rather, you, having been harmed, remit the injury from your heart, taking care lest there be anything that anyone remits to you.

བསམ་གཏན་གྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བཞི་བཅུ་བརྒྱད་པའོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་ན་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བཞི་བཅུ་དགུ་པའོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་ན་བརྩོན་འགྲུས་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་གནས་ཤིང་སྦྱིན་པའི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ལྔ་བཅུ་པའོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་
ན་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ལྔ་བཅུ་གཅིག་པའོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་ན་བཟོད་པའི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ལྔ་བཅུ་གཉིས་པའོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་ན་བསམ་གཏན་གྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ལྔ་བཅུ་གསུམ་པའོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་ན་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་

And Tsur Y. the Prince, when he sees Zekhophiel Y. the Prince—who is appointed to write the merits of Israel which they perform before the Throne of Glory—would remove the crown of glory from atop his head and fall upon his face. And Zekhophiel Y. the Prince, when he sees Anaphiel Y. the Prince—who guards the entrances of the palaces of Arabot of the firmament—would remove the crown of glory from atop his head and fall upon his face. And why is his name called Anaphiel? Because the branch [*anaph*] of his majesty, his splendor, his crown, his radiance, and his brilliance covers all the chambers of Arabot of the uppermost firmament, like the Creator of the world. Just as of the Uppermost Creator it is written: "His majesty covered the heavens, and the earth was full of His praise," so too does Anaphiel Y. the Prince cover with his majesty and splendor all the chambers of the uppermost Arabot. 

And Anaphiel Y. the Prince, when he sees Kotertashiel Y. the great, awesome, and honored Prince, would remove the crown of glory from atop his head and fall upon his face. And why is his name called Kotertashiel? Because he is appointed in authority over the four headwaters of the River of Fire beneath the Throne of Glory. And every prince from whom a voice goes out and who enters before the Shekhinah only goes out and enters by his permission, forasmuch as the walls of the four headwaters of the River of Fire are entrusted to his hand. Moreover, the height of his stature is seventy thousand myriads of parasangs, and he is the crown of fire of the River of Fire, and he goes out and enters before the Shekhinah to declare the merit of all who come into the world, as it is said: "The judgment was set, and the books were opened." 

And Kotertashiel Y. the Prince, when he sees Sheked-Hazaya Y. the great, mighty, awesome, and honored Prince, would remove the crown of glory from atop his head and fall upon his face. And why is his name called Sheked-Hazaya? Because he weighs [*shokel*] all merits in the scale-pan before the Holy One, Blessed be He. And Sheked-Hazaya Y. the Prince, when he sees Zephanurya Y. the great, mighty, awesome, honored, and majestic Prince, who is revered by all the heavenly host, removes the crown of glory from atop his head and falls upon his face. english: ...and wells. The Arabs used to say, "Thabir has brightened, so that we may raid [the others]." It is called Jam' and the <term>Mash'ar al-Haram</term> <gloss>The Sacred Monument</gloss>. 'Arafa is a village containing farms, greenery, and melon patches. It has fine houses for the people of Mecca, which they stay in on the day of 'Arafa. The standing place is on its plain near a mountain. There are watering places, a canal flowing through it, and a sign the Imam built behind him for prayer, with people around him. On the mountains near it are lamps. The prayer hall is on the edge of the Wadi 'Arana at the borders of 'Arafa, and standing in the valley is not permitted. Whoever goes out to it before the sun sets, a blood sacrifice becomes mandatory for him. At the edge of 'Arafa are white landmarks. In the prayer hall is a pulpit made of brick, and behind it is a large basin. Two miles before it are the two <term>Ma'zamayn</term> <gloss>the two narrow passes</gloss>, which are the boundary of the <term>Haram</term>. <term>Batn Muhassir</term> <gloss>the valley of Muhassir</gloss> is a valley between Mina and Al-Muzdalifa; it is the boundary of Al-Muzdalifa. Al-Tan'im is a place with mosques around the mosque of 'Aisha and watering places on the road to Medina, from which the Meccans enter the state of <term>ihram</term> <gloss>pilgrimage consecration</gloss> for the Umra. White landmarks surround the <term>Haram</term>. From the direction of the west, Al-Tan'im is three miles away; from the direction of Iraq, nine miles; from the direction of Yemen, seven miles; from the direction of Ta'if, eleven miles; and from the direction of the main road, ten miles. Dhu al-Hulayfa is a village near Yathrib containing a well-maintained mosque and nearby wells, but no dwellings are seen there. Al-Juhfa is a city inhabited by the Banu Ja'far; it has a fortress with two gates and a few wells. Two miles away is a spring, and it has a large cistern which sometimes lacks water, and it is plentiful.

6. Καὶ ἔσται τὸ παιδίον ὃ ἐὰν τέκῃ, κατασταθήσεται ἐκ τοῦ ὀνόματος τοῦ τετελευτηκότος, καὶ οὐκ ἐξαλειφθήσεται τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ ἐξ Ἰσραήλ.
7. Ἐὰν δὲ μὴ βούληται ὁ ἄνθρωπος λαβεῖν τὴν γυναῖκα τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἀναβήσεται ἡ γυνὴ ἐπὶ τὴν πύλην ἐπὶ τὴν γερουσίαν, καὶ ἐρεῖ· Οὐ θέλει ὁ ἀδελφὸς τοῦ ἀνδρός μου ἀναστῆσαι τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ αὐτοῦ ἐν Ἰσραήλ, οὐκ ἠθέλησεν ὁ ἀδελφὸς τοῦ ἀνδρός μου.
8. Καὶ καλέσουσιν αὐτὸν ἡ γερουσία τῆς πόλεως αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἐροῦσιν αὐτῷ, καὶ στὰς εἴπῃ· Οὐ βούλομαι λαβεῖν αὐτήν·
9. καὶ προσελθοῦσα ἡ γυνὴ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ αὐτοῦ ἔναντι τῆς γερουσίας, καὶ ὑπολύσει τὸ ὑπόδημα αὐτοῦ τὸ ἓν ἀπὸ τοῦ ποδὸς αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἐμπτύσεται κατὰ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἀποκριθεῖσα ἐρεῖ· Οὕτω ποιήσουσι τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ ὃς οὐκ οἰκοδομήσει τὸν οἶκον τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ αὐτοῦ ἐν Ἰσραήλ,
10. καὶ κληθήσεται τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ ἐν Ἰσραήλ, οἶκος τοῦ ὑπολυθέντος τὸ ὑπόδημα.
11. Ἐὰν δὲ μάχωνται ἄνθρωποι ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ, ἄνθρωπος μετὰ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ αὐτοῦ, καὶ προσέλθῃ ἡ γυνὴ ἑνὸς αὐτῶν ἐξελέσθαι τὸν ἄνδρα αὐτῆς ἐκ χειρὸς τοῦ τύπτοντος αὐτὸν, καὶ ἐκτείνασα τὴν χεῖρα ἐπιλάβηται τῶν διδύμων αὐτοῦ,
12. ἀποκόψεις τὴν χεῖρα· οὐ φείσεται ὁ ὀφθαλμός σου ἐπ’ αὐτῇ.
13. Οὐκ ἔσται ἐν τῷ μαρσίππῳ σου στάθμιον καὶ στάθμιον, μέγα ἢ μικρόν.
14. Οὐκ ἔσται ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ σου μέτρον καὶ μέτρον, μέγα ἢ μικρόν·
15. στάθμιον ἀληθινὸν καὶ δίκαιον ἔσται σοι, καὶ μέτρον ἀληθινὸν καὶ δίκαιον ἔσται σοι, ἵνα πολυήμερος γένῃ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ἧς Κύριος ὁ Θεός σου δίδωσί σοι ἐν κλήρῳ·
16. ὅτι βδέλυγμα Κυρίῳ τῷ Θεῷ σου πᾶς ποιῶν ταῦτα, πᾶς ποιῶν ἄδικον.
17. Μνήσθητι ὅσα ἐποίησέ σοι Ἀμαλὴκ ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ, ἐκπορευομένου σου ἐκ γῆς Αἰγύπτου,
18. πῶς ἀντέστη σοι ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ, καὶ ἔκοψέ σου τὴν οὐραγίαν τοὺς κοπιῶντας ὀπίσω σου, σὺ δὲ ἐπείνας καὶ ἐκοπίας, καὶ οὐκ ἐφοβήθη τὸν Θεόν.
19. Καὶ ἔσται, ἡνίκα ἐὰν καταπαύσῃ σε Κύριος ὁ Θεός σου ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν ἐχθρῶν σου τῶν κύκλῳ σου ἐν τῇ γῇ ᾗ Κύριος ὁ Θεός σου δίδωσί σοι κληρονομῆσαι, ἐξαλείψεις τὸ ὄνομα Ἀμαλὴκ ἐκ τῆς ὑπὸ τὸν οὐρανὸν, καὶ οὐ μὴ ἐπιλάθῃ.

### ΚΕΦΑΛΑΙΟΝ ΚϚ'.

1. Καὶ ἔσται, ἐὰν εἰσέλθῃς εἰς τὴν γῆν ἣν Κύριος ὁ Θεός σου δίδωσί σοι κληρονομῆσαι, καὶ κατακληρονομήσῃς αὐτὴν, καὶ κατοικήσῃς ἐπ’ αὐτὴν,
2. καὶ λήψῃ ἀπὸ τῆς ἀπαρχῆς τῶν καρπῶν τῆς γῆς σου ἧς Κύριος ὁ Θεός σου δίδωσί σοι, καὶ ἐμβαλεῖς εἰς κάρταλλον, καὶ πορεύσῃ εἰς τὸν τόπον ὃν ἂν ἐκλέξηται Κύριος ὁ Θεός σου ἐπικληθῆναι τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ ἐκεῖ.
3. Καὶ ἐλεύσῃ πρὸς τὸν ἱερέα ὃς ἔσται ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις ἐκείναις, καὶ ἐρεῖς πρὸς αὐτόν· Ἀναγγέλλω σήμερον Κυρίῳ τῷ Θεῷ μου, ὅτι εἰσελήλυθα εἰς τὴν γῆν ἣν ὤμοσε Κύριος τοῖς πατράσιν ἡμῶν δοῦναι ἡμῖν.

6. Et erit infans quicumque natus fuerit, constituetur ex defuncti nomine, et non delebitur nomen ejus ex Israel.
7. Si autem noluerit homo accipere uxorem fratris sui, et ascendet mulier in porta ad senatum, et dicet : Non vult frater viri mei suscitare nomen fratris sui in Israel, noluit frater viri mei.
8. Et vocabunt eum seniores civitatis ejus, et dicent ei , et stans dixerit : Nolo accipere eam :
9. et accedens uxor fratris ejus ante seniores, et solvet calceamentum ejus unum de pede ejus, et spuet in faciem ejus, et respondens dicet : Sic facient homini qui non ædificabit domum fratris sui in Israel ,
10. et vocabitur nomen ejus in Israel, domus discalceati calceamentum.
11. Si autem rixati fuerint homines pariter, homo cum fratre suo , et accesserit uxor unius eorum ad eruendum virum suum de manu verberantis eum, et extendens manum apprehenderit testes ejus,
12. abscindes manum : non parcet oculus tuus super eam.
13. Non erit in marsupio tuo pondus et pondus , magnum aut parvum.
14 Non erit in domo tua mensura et mensura, magna vel parva.
15. Pondus verax et justum erit tibi , et mensura verax et justa erit tibi , ut longævus sis super terram quam Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi in sorte :
16. quoniam abominatio Domino Deo tuo omnis faciens hæc , omnis faciens injustum.
17. Recordare quæcumque fecit tibi Amalec in via , exeunte te de terra Ægypti,
18. quomodo restitit tibi in via, et percussit caudam agminis tui, defessos post te, tu autem esuriebas et laborabas, et non timuit Deum.
19. Et erit , postquam quiescere fecerit te Dominus Deus tuus ab omnibus inimicis tuis qui in circuitu tuo in terra quam Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi hæreditare, delebis nomen Amalec de sub cœlo , et non obliviscaris.

### CAPUT XXVI.

1. Et erit , si intraveris in terram quam Dominus tuus dat tibi hæreditare, et hæreditaveris eam, et habitaveris in ea,
2. et sumes de primitiis fructuum terræ tuæ quam Dominus Deus tuus dat tibi, et mittes in cartallum , et ibis in locum quem elegerit Dominus Deus tuus ut invocetur nomen suum ibi.
3. Et venies ad sacerdotem qui erit in diebus illis , et dices ad eum : Annuntio hodie Domino Deo meo , quia intravi in terram quam juravit Dominus patribus nostris dare nobis.

6. And it shall be that the child whom she bears shall be established by the name of the one who is dead, and his name shall not be blotted out from Israel.
7. But if the man does not wish to take his brother's wife, the woman shall go up to the gate to the elders <note>original: "gerousian"</note>, and shall say: "My husband's brother refuses to raise up the name of his brother in Israel; my husband's brother has refused."
8. Then the elders of his city shall call him and speak to him, and if he stands and says: "I do not wish to take her,"
9. then his brother's wife shall approach before the elders, and shall loosen one of his sandals from his foot, and shall spit in his face, and answering shall say: "Thus shall they do to the man who will not build the house of his brother in Israel,"
10. and his name shall be called in Israel: "The house of him whose sandal was loosened."
11. If men are fighting together, a man with his brother, and the wife of one of them approaches to rescue her husband from the hand of the one striking him, and stretching out her hand she seizes his private parts,
12. you shall cut off her hand; your eye shall not spare her.
13. There shall not be in your pouch a weight and a weight, a large one or a small one.
14. There shall not be in your house a measure and a measure, a large one or a small one;
15. a true and righteous weight shall be yours, and a true and righteous measure shall be yours, so that you may live long upon the land which the Lord your God gives you as an inheritance;
16. for everyone who does these things, everyone who does unrighteousness, is an abomination to the Lord your God.
17. Remember what <term>Amalek</term> <gloss>an ancient enemy of Israel</gloss> did to you on the way, when you were coming out of the land of <term>Aigyptos</term> <gloss>Egypt</gloss>,
18. how he stood against you on the way, and cut off your rear guard, those who were weary behind you, and you were hungry and tired, and he did not fear God.
19. And it shall be, when the Lord your God gives you rest from all your enemies around you in the land which the Lord your God gives you to inherit, you shall blot out the name of <term>Amalek</term> from under heaven, and you shall not forget.

### CHAPTER 26.

1. And it shall be, when you enter the land which the Lord your God gives you to inherit, and you take possession of it, and dwell in it,
2. that you shall take from the first fruits of the fruits of your land which the Lord your God gives you, and you shall put them into a basket, and go to the place which the Lord your God chooses for His name to be called there.
3. And you shall come to the priest who shall be in those days, and say to him: "I declare today to the Lord my God that I have entered into the land which the Lord swore to our fathers to give us."

<column-break/>

6. And it shall be that the infant who is born shall be established from the name of the deceased, and his name shall not be deleted from Israel.
7. But if the man is unwilling to take the wife of his brother, and the woman shall go up to the gate to the senate <note>original: "senatum"</note>, and shall say: "My husband's brother does not wish to raise up the name of his brother in Israel; my husband's brother has refused."
8. And the elders of his city shall call him, and they shall say to him, and he, standing, shall say: "I do not wish to take her."
9. And the wife of his brother, approaching before the elders, shall loosen one of his shoes from his foot, and shall spit in his face, and answering she shall say: "Thus they shall do to the man who will not build the house of his brother in Israel,"
10. and his name shall be called in Israel: "The house of the unshod."
11. If men are fighting together, a man with his brother, and the wife of one of them approaches to rescue her husband from the hand of the one striking him, and extending her hand she seizes his testicles,
12. you shall cut off her hand: your eye shall not spare her.
13. There shall not be in your bag a weight and a weight, large or small.
14. There shall not be in your house a measure and a measure, large or small.
15. A true and just weight shall be for you, and a true and just measure shall be for you, so that you may be long-lived upon the land which the Lord your God gives you by lot:
16. for every one who does these things, every one who does injustice, is an abomination to the Lord your God.
17. Remember whatever <term>Amalec</term> <gloss>Amalek</gloss> did to you on the way, when you were leaving the land of <term>Aegyptus</term> <gloss>Egypt</gloss>,
18. how he resisted you on the way, and struck the tail of your column, the weary ones behind you, and you were hungry and laboring, and he did not fear God.
19. And it shall be, after the Lord your God has made you rest from all your enemies who are around you in the land which the Lord your God gives you to inherit, you shall delete the name of <term>Amalec</term> from under heaven, and you shall not forget.

### CHAPTER 26.

1. And it shall be, if you have entered into the land which the Lord your God gives you to inherit, and you have inherited it, and have dwelt in it,
2. and you take from the first-fruits of the fruits of the land which the Lord your God gives you, and you put them in a basket, and you go to the place which the Lord your God has chosen for His name to be invoked there.
3. And you shall come to the priest who shall be in those days, and you shall say to him: "I announce today to the Lord my God, that I have entered into the land which the Lord swore to our fathers to give to us."
